items.stem: Two point masses m₁ = 1.5 kg and m₂ = 2.0 kg slide on a light frictionless horizontal rod rotating about a vertical axis at ω_i = 6.0 rad s⁻¹. Initially r₁ = 0.40 m and r₂ = 0.50 m. An internal cord then pulls both masses inward at the same time to half their initial radii.
items.workedSolution: (a) I_i = 0.740 kg m². (b) L = 4.44 J s. (c) ω_f = 24.0 rad s⁻¹. (d) W_int = 40.0 J. (e) with zero net external torque angular momentum remains constant, so decreasing the moment of inertia increases both angular speed and rotational kinetic energy because internal forces do positive work.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates I_i = Σmr² = 0.740 kg m².
Applies L = I_i ω_i to obtain 4.44 J s.
Recognizes I_f = I_i / 4 and applies I_i ω_i = I_f ω_f.
Obtains ω_f = 24.0 rad s⁻¹.
Computes ΔE_k = ½I_f ω_f² − ½I_i ω_i².
Obtains internal work done = 40.0 J.
Notes zero external torque conserves L so E_k = L²/(2I) rises as I falls.
Identifies positive mechanical work done by internal radial forces.

items.stem: A small stone is thrown from flat ground with an initial speed of 30 m s⁻¹ at 62° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes v_y = 0 at apex so v_apex = u cos θ.
Obtains 14.1 m s⁻¹.
Applies h_max = (u sin θ)² / (2g).
Obtains 35.8 m.
Evaluates R = u_x × (2u_y / g).
Obtains 76.1 m.

items.stem: A steel ball is fired from a spring launcher on level ground at 32 m s⁻¹ and 60° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the total time of flight before returning to the ground.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 32 sin 60° = 27.7 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 32 cos 60° = 16.0 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.81 = 5.65 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 90.4 m. Target = 5.65 s.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 5.65 s (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes time to reach the apex u sin θ / g rather than full time of flight.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Swaps sin θ and cos θ when resolving vertical launch speed.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses total speed u instead of vertical component u sin θ.

items.stem: A steel ball of mass 2.5 kg is attached to a rubber cord of natural length 4 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.45 m in 0.34 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum tension in the cord at the lowest point B.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 4 + 0.45 = 4.45 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 1.08 × 10³ N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 485 N. Target = 485 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (4 + 0.45) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 485 N (C).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a horizontal wooden bar of length L = 2.8 m and mass 26 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light vertical wires at A and B. The wires are 1.8 m apart. Its centre of gravity G lies 1.15 m to the right of A and 0.65 m to the left of B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B yield T₁ = 92.11 N ≈ 92.1 N. (b) Force balance gives T₂ = 163.0 N ≈ 163 N. (c) wire B carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire B.

markScheme.criterion: Applies moment balance about attachment B.
Applies ΣF_y = 0 to obtain T₂.
Identifies the wire closer to G as carrying greater tension.
Justifies using equal opposite moments about G with shorter lever arm.

items.stem: A steel ball of mass 1.2 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.2 m on a light string. The string breaks if the tension exceeds 29 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the ball at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((29/1.2) − 9.81) × 1.2] = 4.15 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 4.15 m s⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds g instead of subtracting g when rearranging T_max − mg = mv²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.workedSolution: (a) Static equilibrium requires zero resultant force and zero resultant moment about any point. (b) Torque of the couple is T = F d_perp = 57.48 N m ≈ 57.5 N m (note N m, not J).

markScheme.criterion: Zero resultant force.

Torque = 57.5 N m with unit N m.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 1.4 m and mass 12 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 4 kg hangs so its centre of gravity acts 1.2 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at 54° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal component of force exerted on the rod by hinge O.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about hinge O: T sin 54° × 1.4 = (12 × 0.7 + 4 × 1.2) × 9.81 = 129.5 N m. Hence T sin 54° = 92.49 N and T = 114.3 N ≈ 114 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos 54° = 67.20 N ≈ 67.2 N. Vertical balance: R_y = (12 + 4) × 9.81 − 92.49 = 64.47 N ≈ 64.5 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 67.2 N.

items.stem: A plastic box of mass 12.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough ramp. The slope is 11.5 m long and inclined at 28° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 5.97 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = mgL sin θ.
Obtains 662 J.
Subtracts ½mv² from ΔE_p.
Obtains 439 J.
Applies W_f = μ(mg cos θ)L.
Obtains 0.353.

items.stem: In Searle's Young modulus investigation (RP4), a student tests a copper wire of unstretched length $(2.10 \pm 0.002)$ m. Micrometer diameter readings in perpendicular directions at three places average to 0.48 mm, 0.46 mm, and 0.47 mm (each $\pm 0.01$ mm). A graph of load $F$ against extension $e$ is a straight line through the origin of gradient 9.8 N mm⁻¹ ($\pm 1.8\%$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $A = \pi d^2/4 = 1.73 × 10⁻⁷ m²$. (b) $E = L(\mathrm{grad})/A = 119 GPa$. (c) $\%\Delta E = 6.15\%$. (d) an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while perpendicular micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Averages three diameters and converts mm to m in $A = \pi d^2/4$.
Cross-sectional area $A = 1.73 × 10⁻⁷ m²$.
Converts gradient to N m⁻¹ and substitutes into $E = (L/A)\,\mathrm{grad}$.
Young modulus $E = 119 GPa$.
Combines $\%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad}$.
Percentage uncertainty in $E = 6.15\%$.
Identical reference wire compensates both support sag and temperature expansion.
Perpendicular micrometer readings at >= 3 positions detect non-uniformity/oval cross-section.

Determine the Young modulus $E$ of the wire in GPa.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $E$.

parts.expectedAnswer: an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while perpendicular micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty

Perpendicular readings at 3 positions check circularity and reduce random error in d².

items.stem: A brass bob of mass 0.9 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.6 m on a light nylon cord. At the lowest point, its speed is 8 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the cord at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 0.9 × 8² / 0.6 = 96.0 N, so T = 96.0 + 0.9 × 9.81 = 105 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 105 N (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A marine thruster rotor of moment of inertia 3.60 kg m² reverses from $+20.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ to $-10.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ in 1.80 s under a uniform braking-and-reversing pulse. What is the magnitude of the mean external torque acting on the rotor?
items.workedSolution: $|\Delta L| = I|\omega_2 - \omega_1| = 3.60(30.0) = 108\text{ N m s}$. Mean torque $|T| = \frac{|\Delta L|}{\Delta t} = \frac{108}{1.80} = 60.0 N m$.

markScheme.criterion: Magnitude of mean torque equals 60.0 N m.

items.stem: Engineers evaluate a composite flywheel of moment of inertia 1.90 kg m² operating between 580 rad s⁻¹ and 240 rad s⁻¹ inside a municipal hybrid bus of total mass 1.15 × 10³ kg. On a test incline of road length 200 m rising 15.0 m vertically, the mean resistive drag force is 220 N. Take $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = 2.65 × 10⁵ J$. (b) $\Delta E_{\mathrm{p}} = 1.69 × 10⁵ J$. (c) Subtracting drag work 4.40 × 10⁴ J and dividing by $mg$ gives $h_{\max} = 19.6 m$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_{\max}^2 - \omega_{\min}^2)$.
Obtains 2.65 × 10⁵ J.
Uses $mgh$ with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Obtains 1.69 × 10⁵ J.
Computes drag work $F_{\mathrm{d}}s$ and subtracts from flywheel energy release.
Equates remaining energy to $mg h_{\max}$.

items.workedSolution: Because drag always opposes the instantaneous velocity, its horizontal component acts backwards throughout both ascent and descent. options.text: The horizontal velocity component remains strictly constant because gravity acts solely in the vertical direction.
options.distractorRationale: Constant horizontal velocity holds only when fluid resistance is negligible.

options.label: B
options.text: The horizontal velocity component decreases during the ascent and then increases back to its launch value during the descent.
options.distractorRationale: Air resistance always has a backward horizontal component whenever horizontal velocity is forward, so horizontal speed never recovers.

options.label: C
options.text: Fluid resistance opposes the instantaneous velocity so the horizontal velocity component decreases continuously throughout flight.

options.label: D
options.text: The horizontal velocity component drops instantaneously to zero at the highest point of the path.
options.distractorRationale: At the apex only the vertical velocity component is zero; horizontal motion continues forwards while decelerating.

items.stem: Two stationary dynamics trolleys A ($2.00\text{ kg}$) and B ($5.00\text{ kg}$) are pushed apart on a frictionless horizontal track by releasing an internal spring. Trolley A moves to the left at $7.50\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $v_{\text{B}} = 3.00 m s⁻¹$. (b) $E_{\text{total}} = 78.8 J$. (c) in an isolated one-dimensional explosion from rest total linear momentum remains zero while kinetic energy is shared inversely with fragment mass.

markScheme.criterion: Applies conservation of momentum 0 = −m_A v_A + m_B v_B.
Obtains v_B = 3.00 m s⁻¹.
Computes E_kA = ½m_A v_A² = 56.3 J.
Computes E_kB = ½m_B v_B² = 22.5 J and adds both energies.
Obtains total kinetic energy 78.8 J.
Notes equal opposite momentum magnitudes p = m_A v_A = m_B v_B.
Uses E_k = p²/(2m) to explain inverse mass sharing (in an isolated one-dimensional explosion from rest total linear momentum remains zero while kinetic energy is shared inversely with fragment mass).

items.stem: A compressed spring launches a block along a rough track and up a ramp. How is the change in total mechanical energy ($E_{\text{k}} + E_{\text{p}} + E_{\text{H}}$) of the block-spring-Earth system interpreted?
items.workedSolution: By the work-energy principle, W_nc = Δ(E_k + E_p + E_H), so resistive friction reduces mechanical energy by the work done against it. Therefore the correct statement is: When resistive non-conservative forces act the decrease in total mechanical energy equals the magnitude of work done against the resistive force.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: when resistive non-conservative forces act the decrease in total mechanical energy equals the magnitude of work done against the resistive force.

options.text: When resistive non-conservative forces act the decrease in total mechanical energy equals the magnitude of work done against the resistive force.

options.label: B
options.text: Total mechanical energy always remains strictly constant even when dynamic friction acts along the track.
options.distractorRationale: Total energy of the universe is conserved, but mechanical energy decreases as thermal energy is dissipated by friction.

options.label: C
options.text: Total mechanical energy increases by the work done against friction because thermal energy adds to kinetic energy.
options.distractorRationale: Friction opposes motion (doing negative mechanical work), reducing total mechanical energy.

options.label: D
options.text: Elastic potential energy cannot convert into gravitational potential energy when friction is present.
options.distractorRationale: Elastic potential energy still converts into gravitational PE and KE, minus the thermal energy transferred via friction.

items.stem: An electric motor applies a constant driving torque to a fan blade starting from rest. This produces a curved $\omega$–$t$ graph whose slope falls to zero at a steady top speed. Why is the angular acceleration non-uniform?
items.workedSolution: From $T_{\text{drive}} - T_{\text{drag}} = I\alpha$, the decreasing gradient shows net torque falling as resistive drag torque increases toward driving torque.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that decreasing gradient shows net torque falling as resistive drag torque increases toward driving torque.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a heavy non-uniform trapdoor of length L = 1.2 m and mass 18 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.46 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 36° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) T = 83.67 N ≈ 83.7 N. (b) the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium. (c)(i) R_x = 49.18 N, R_y = 108.9 N, so R = 119.5 N ≈ 119 N. (c)(ii) α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 65.69° ≈ 65.7° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Στ = 0 about O using T cos(angle to vertical) × L = m g x_G.
Obtains T = 83.67 N (83.7 N) matching 84 N.
Identifies horizontal component of angled cable tension directed toward the wall.
States hinge must exert an equal opposite horizontal force away from the wall for ΣF_x = 0.
Computes R_x = 49.18 N and R_y = 108.9 N and applies Pythagoras.
Resultant hinge reaction magnitude R = 119 N.
Uses tan α = R_y / R_x with both hinge components.
Direction α = 65.7° above the horizontal.

workingSteps: Identify that the inclined cable pulls horizontally toward the wall.

items.stem: A sandbag of mass 3 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 1.8 m. It falls freely from rest at the fixed support to point A, where the cord becomes taut. It then stretches the cord by 0.8 m over 0.18 s before stopping at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 5.94 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (3 × 5.94) / 0.18 = 99.0 N.
Obtains 128 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 191 N.

items.stem: A minibus of mass 1600 kg accelerates along a level road while a small metal bob hangs from its ceiling at 26° to the vertical. Later, the minibus climbs a straight 8° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 70 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.6. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 18 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 620 N toward the exit. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg => a = g tan θ.
Obtains 4.78 m s⁻².
Applies μ_s mg = m v_max² / R.
Obtains 20.3 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts resistive work F_res(πR) from initial kinetic energy ½mu².
Obtains 12.4 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By resolving forces on the bob, calculate the horizontal acceleration when the string hangs at 26° to the vertical.
Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular road without sliding.
Calculate the speed of the minibus when it reaches the exit at the end of the semicircular bend.

items.stem: A steel ball of mass 0.6 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 2.2 m attached to a light string. The maximum tension the string can hold without breaking is 29 N. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Writes T_max − mg = m v_max² / r at the lowest point.
Obtains 9.21 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By considering the forces acting on the ball at the lowest point, calculate the maximum speed at the bottom so the string does not break.

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 0.3 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.4 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 0.3 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string just before the bob strikes the putty.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 5.24 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 8.83 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 2.62 m s⁻¹. Target = 8.83 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 8.83 N (C).

items.stem: A 240 N traffic signal hangs in equilibrium from two cables below a horizontal ceiling. The left cable (tension T₁) makes an angle of 30° and the right cable (tension T₂) makes 60° below the ceiling, forming a right-angled vector triangle. Calculate the tension T₁ in the left cable.
items.workedSolution: Since 30° + 60° = 90°, the two cables meet at 90° and T₁ = W sin 30° = 240 × 0.500 = 120 N.

markScheme.criterion: Finds cable tension T₁ = 120 N.

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 10.5 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 1.8 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.55 m in 0.38 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the spring constant of the cord.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 1.8 + 0.55 = 2.35 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 1.60 × 10³ N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 879 N. Target = 1.60 × 10³ N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (1.8 + 0.55) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 1.60 × 10³ N m⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a timber-yard log crane has total length L = 24 m and mass 700 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 5.5 m from rear end A. A 2600 kg concrete counterweight sits 4.7 m to the left of P (0.8 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 3.5 m to the right of P (9 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 17.5 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) M_cw = 1.199 × 10⁵ N m ≈ 1.20 × 10⁵ N m. (b) Equating clockwise and anticlockwise moments about P gives m_max = 558.3 kg ≈ 558 kg. (c) Vertical force balance yields R = 3.785 × 10⁴ N ≈ 3.78 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses M = m g d with counterweight mass and lever arm from P.
Counterweight moment = 1.20 × 10⁵ N m.
Subtracts boom self-weight moment from counterweight moment and divides by g × load lever arm.
Maximum safe load mass = 558 kg.
Applies vertical force balance summing counterweight, boom, and load weights.
Upward mast reaction R = 3.78 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: On a horizontal frictionless air track, glider X of mass 1.6 kg moves right at 6 m s⁻¹ and collides with stationary glider Y of mass 0.8 kg. Immediately after impact, glider Y moves right at 5.06 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of glider X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Momentum conservation: (1.6)(6) = (1.6)v_X + (0.8)(5.06), giving v_X = 3.47 m s⁻¹. K_i = 28.8 J and K_f = 19.9 J, so ΔK_lost = K_i − K_f = 8.93 J. Target = 3.47 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves linear momentum and evaluates kinetic energy budget to obtain 3.47 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: A steel ball bearing of radius 3.00 mm and density 7850 kg m⁻³ is dropped gently into a deep column of castor oil. The oil has density 910 kg m⁻³ and viscosity 0.780 Pa s, and the flow is laminar ($g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$).
items.workedSolution: (a) U = 1.01 mN. (b) F = 7.70 mN. (c) v = 0.175 m s⁻¹. (d) increasing liquid temperature weakens intermolecular cohesion so liquid viscosity decreases and terminal speed increases.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates sphere volume V = (4/3)πr³ with r in metres.
Obtains upthrust U = 1.01 mN.
Computes weight W and applies equilibrium F = W − U.
Obtains terminal drag F = 7.70 mN.
Rearranges Stokes' law v = F / (6πηr).
Obtains terminal speed v = 0.175 m s⁻¹.
States higher temperature lowers liquid viscosity due to reduced intermolecular cohesion.
Concludes terminal velocity increases (increasing liquid temperature weakens intermolecular cohesion so liquid viscosity decreases and terminal speed increases).

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 2 kg moves right at 15 m s⁻¹ and strikes stationary trolley Y of mass 5.2 kg. Immediately after impact, trolley Y moves right at 6.67 m s⁻¹ and trolley X rebounds to the left. Calculate the total kinetic energy of the two objects immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward positive, (2)(15) = (2)v_X + (5.2)(6.67) gives v_X = -2.34 m s⁻¹ (2.34 m s⁻¹ to the left). Scalar final kinetic energies add: K_f = ½(2)(2.34)² + ½(5.2)(6.67)² = 121 J. Energy lost = 225 J − K_f = 104 J. Target = 121 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds rebound speed 2.34 m s⁻¹ and sums scalar kinetic energies to obtain 121 J (B).

items.stem: A football is kicked from a level sports field with an initial speed of 42 m s⁻¹ at 28° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.
items.workedSolution: (a) v_apex = 42 × cos 28°. Answer: 37.1 m s⁻¹. (b) u_y = 42 × sin 28° = 19.7 m s⁻¹. h_max = u_y² / (2 × 9.8). Answer: 19.8 m. (c) T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 4.02 s. R = 37.1 × T. Answer: 149 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes v_y = 0 at apex so v_apex = u cos θ.
Obtains 37.1 m s⁻¹.
Applies h_max = (u sin θ)² / (2g).
Obtains 19.8 m.
Evaluates R = u_x × (2u_y / g).
Obtains 149 m.

parts.prompt: Determine the speed of the projectile at the highest point of its path.

items.stem: A small steel ball of mass 2.8 kg hangs on a light string of length 0.9 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a block of clay of mass 5.6 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy lost during the collision.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 4.20 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 1.40 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.100 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 16.5 J. Target = 16.5 J.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 16.5 J (B).

items.stem: In a statics experiment, a steel bar AB has length L = 4.4 m and mass 16 kg. Its centre of gravity G lies 2.2 m from end A. It is balanced horizontally on a pivot P at 1.58 m from end A by placing a 30 kg block to the left of P. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) The moment of a force is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. (b) Moment balance about P gives d = 0.3307 m left of P, so distance from end B is 3.151 m ≈ 3.15 m.

markScheme.criterion: Force multiplied by distance from pivot.
Perpendicular distance to the line of action.
Correct moment balance about P yielding lever arm d = 0.3307 m.
Converts cleanly to distance from end B = 3.15 m.

parts.prompt: Determine the distance from end B at which the calibration block must be placed so that the beam balances horizontally.
workingSteps: Clockwise moment of beam weight about P = 16 × 9.81 × 0.6200.

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 13 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 4.6 m. It falls freely from rest at the fixed support to point A, where the cord becomes taut. It then stretches the cord by 0.9 m over 0.24 s before stopping at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 9.50 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (13 × 9.50) / 0.24 = 515 N.
Obtains 642 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 1.56 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Students place an overhead camera above a level air table to record a two-dimensional collision between two pucks. They use the video to test momentum conservation and elasticity.
items.workedSolution: Resolve momentum vectors into perpendicular components to find recoil velocity and test elasticity using p squared over 2m. Measure masses m₁, m₂ on a top-pan balance and place a calibrated metre rule in the horizontal plane of the pucks to avoid parallax. Track frame-by-frame displacements over known Δt = 1/f_frame to compute velocities u₁, v₁, v₂ and scattering angles θ₁, θ₂. Check Σp_x = m₁u₁ = m₁v₁cosθ₁ + m₂v₂cosθ₂ and Σp_y = 0 = m₁v₁sinθ₁ − m₂v₂sinθ₂ (or closed momentum triangle). Compare p₀²/(2m₁) with p₁²/(2m₁) + p₂²/(2m₂) to test elasticity.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Measures both puck masses on a balance and levels the air table to minimise net external horizontal force.
L1: Places a calibration scale in the puck plane and mounts camera vertically overhead to prevent parallax error.
L2: Computes speed magnitudes from frame displacements divided by frame interval Δt and measures angles θ₁ and θ₂.
L2: Verifies vector conservation along perpendicular axes: m₁u₁ = m₁v₁cosθ₁ + m₂v₂cosθ₂ and m₁v₁sinθ₁ = m₂v₂sinθ₂.
L3: Notes that vector conservation also forms a closed momentum triangle p₀ = p₁ + p₂.
L3: Compares total kinetic energy before and after using E_k = p²/(2m) to test whether the collision is elastic.

parts.prompt: Explain how the students collect measurements from the video, verify two-dimensional conservation of linear momentum using components or a vector triangle, and determine whether the collision is elastic using E_k = p²/(2m). [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Resolve momentum vectors into perpendicular components to find recoil velocity and test elasticity using p squared over 2m. Measure masses m₁, m₂ on a top-pan balance and place a calibrated metre rule in the horizontal plane of the pucks to avoid parallax. Track frame-by-frame displacements over known Δt = 1/f_frame to compute velocities u₁, v₁, v₂ and scattering angles θ₁, θ₂. Check Σp_x = m₁u₁ = m₁v₁cosθ₁ + m₂v₂cosθ₂ and Σp_y = 0 = m₁v₁sinθ₁ − m₂v₂sinθ₂ (or closed momentum triangle). Compare p₀²/(2m₁) with p₁²/(2m₁) + p₂²/(2m₂) to test elasticity.
workingSteps: Detail mass measurement, level frictionless table, overhead camera calibration scale, and frame-rate timing.
Resolve initial and final momenta along perpendicular x and y axes (or construct a closed vector triangle).
Evaluate initial and final kinetic energy via E_k = p²/(2m) to distinguish elastic from inelastic impact.

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 3 kg moves to the right at 9 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with trolley Y of mass 1.2 kg moving to the left at 5.5 m s⁻¹ (arrow on Y not shown). Immediately after impact, trolley Y moves to the right at 1.5 m s⁻¹. Take motion to the right as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) p_before = 3 × 9 + 1.2 × (−5.5) = 20.4 kg m s⁻¹. Answer: 20.4 kg m s⁻¹ to the right. (b) v_X = (20.4 − 1.2 × 1.5) / 3 = 6.20 m s⁻¹. Answer: 6.20 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m_X u_X − m_Y |u_Y| with correct signs.
Obtains 20.4 kg m s⁻¹ to the right.
Solves p_before = m_X v_X + m_Y v_Y for v_X.
Obtains 6.20 m s⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform timber board of total length L = 4.8 m and mass 36 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is 0.8 m from the left end, and support B is 2.2 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 1.8 m. A technician of mass 48 kg initially stands 2.5 m from the left end of the plank. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B give F₁ = 203.3 N ≈ 203 N. (b) Vertical equilibrium gives F₂ = 620.7 N ≈ 621 N. (c) the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases. (d) Setting F₁ = 0 about B yields d_tip = 0.4500 m ≈ 0.450 m.

markScheme.criterion: Takes moments about B summing plank and technician anticlockwise moments.
Support A reaction F₁ = 203 N.
Support B reaction F₂ = 621 N via vertical force balance.
States that the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.
Sets F₁ = 0 and equates clockwise overhang moment to restoring plank moment about B.
Tipping distance past B = 0.450 m.

parts.prompt: By taking moments about support B, calculate the upward reaction force F₁ at support A while the technician is at the initial position.
workingSteps: Clockwise moment of F₁ about B = F₁ × 2.2.

parts.prompt: Deduce the upward reaction force F₂ at support B.
State qualitatively how the reaction forces at supports A and B change as the technician walks slowly toward the right-hand overhang.
parts.expectedAnswer: As the technician moves toward the overhang, the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.
workingSteps: Explain that shifting weight toward support B reduces the anticlockwise moment about B so support A carries less load while support B carries more.

parts.prompt: Calculate the maximum distance past support B that the technician can walk onto the overhang before the plank begins to tip.
workingSteps: At the tipping limit, F₁ = 0; take moments about B: 48 g d_tip = 36 g (0.6000).

items.stem: A steel ball is fired from a spring launcher on level ground at 40 m s⁻¹ and 30° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the total time of flight before returning to the ground.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 40 sin 30° = 20.0 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 40 cos 30° = 34.6 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 4.08 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 141 m. Target = 4.08 s.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 4.08 s (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes time to reach the apex u sin θ / g rather than full time of flight.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Swaps sin θ and cos θ when resolving vertical launch speed.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses total speed u instead of vertical component u sin θ.

items.stem: A car of mass 1400 kg accelerates along a level road while a small steel bob hangs from its ceiling at 34° to the vertical. Later, the car climbs a straight 14° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 75 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.5. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 18 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 470 N toward the finish line. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg => a = g tan θ.
Obtains 6.61 m s⁻².
Applies μ_s mg = m v_max² / R.
Obtains 19.2 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts resistive work F_res(πR) from initial kinetic energy ½mu².
Obtains 12.9 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By resolving forces on the bob, calculate the horizontal acceleration when the string hangs at 34° to the vertical.
Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular road without sliding.
Calculate the speed of the car when it reaches the finish line at the end of the semicircular bend.

items.stem: A $1400\text{ kg}$ car travelling at $12.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ crashes into a barrier and comes to rest in $0.300\text{ s}$ with its crumple zone deforming.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta p = 1.68 \times 10^4\text{ N s}$; $F = 5.60 \times 10^4\text{ N}$. (b) same change in momentum over a longer impact time reduces average force on occupants.

markScheme.criterion: Impulse $= 1.68 × 10⁴ N s$.
Apply $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$.
Average force $= 5.60 × 10⁴ N$.
Same change in momentum (equal area under F–t graph).
Longer impact time reduces average force F = Δp/Δt on occupants.

parts.expectedAnswer: The area under the $F\text{–}t$ graph equals impulse $\Delta p$, so same change in momentum over a longer impact time reduces average force on occupants.
workingSteps: Area under F-t is fixed Δp; longer Δt gives smaller average/peak force F = Δp/Δt.

items.stem: A parcel of mass 3.5 kg slides from rest down a rough ramp of length 10 m inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 5.45 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. If the parcel is instead released from rest halfway down the ramp, calculate its speed at the bottom.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 30° − ½mv² = 120 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 10 = 12.0 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.85 m s⁻¹. Target = 3.85 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 3.85 m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: A sled of mass 4.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a snowy slope of length 5 m, inclined at 28° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 4.54 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the coefficient of dynamic friction μ_d between the sled and the slope.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 28° = 104 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(4.5)(4.54)² = 46.4 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 57.1 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 28°)L, μ = 0.294. Target = 0.294.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 28° accurately to obtain 0.294 (B).

items.stem: A lead bob of mass 1.7 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.7 m on a light steel cable. At the lowest point, its speed is 9.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the cable at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.7 × 9.5² / 1.7 = 90.2 N, so T = 90.2 + 1.7 × 9.8 = 107 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 107 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A uniform mortar channel of length L = 3.10 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a semi-annular cross-section of outer diameter D = 18.0 cm and inner diameter d = 10.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2250 kg m⁻³. It is uniform along its length, so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. A workshop electric winch of electrical input power 360 W and efficiency 72% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 8.796 × 10⁻³ m², V = A L = 0.02727 m³, m = ρ V = 61.36 kg ≈ 61.4 kg. (b) W = 601.9 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 300.9 N ≈ 301 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.550 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 932.9 J ≈ 933 J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.72 × 360 = 259.2 W, so t = 932.9 / 259.2 = 3.599 s ≈ 3.60 s. (e) density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

markScheme.criterion: Computes semi-annular cross-section A = (π/8)(D² − d²) = 8.796 × 10⁻³ m² with cm → m conversion.
Calculates V = A L = 0.02727 m³ and substitutes m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 61.36 kg rounding clearly to 61.4 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 3.10 = m g × 1.550.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 301 N (4 s.f. 300.9 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.550 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 933 J (4 s.f. 932.9 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 259.2 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 3.60 s (4 s.f. 3.599 s).
States valid physical assumption: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

items.stem: A steel bob of mass 0.4 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.1 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a lump of modelling clay of mass 0.32 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height above the lowest point reached by the joined objects.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 4.64 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 2.58 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.340 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 1.92 J. Target = 0.340 m.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 0.340 m (C).

items.stem: A uniform granite trough of length L = 2.40 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a semi-annular cross-section of outer diameter D = 24.0 cm and inner diameter d = 14.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2650 kg m⁻³. It is uniform along its length, so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. An electric hoist motor of electrical input power 540 W and efficiency 78% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.01492 m², V = A L = 0.03581 m³, m = ρ V = 94.91 kg ≈ 94.9 kg. (b) W = 931.0 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 465.5 N ≈ 466 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.200 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 1117 J ≈ 1.12 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.78 × 540 = 421.2 W, so t = 1117 / 421.2 = 2.653 s ≈ 2.65 s. (e) electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates cross-section A = 0.01492 m², volume V = 0.03581 m³, and applies m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 94.91 kg confirming 94.9 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 2.40 = m g × 1.200.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 466 N (4 s.f. 465.5 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.200 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 1.12 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 1117 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 421.2 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 2.65 s (4 s.f. 2.653 s).
Identifies electrical heating in motor windings and mechanical friction in hoist gears.
Links losses to thermal energy dissipated to the surroundings (electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings).

items.stem: During Required Practical 3, a steel sphere drops through two light gates separated by height $h$. Plotting $2h/t$ against $t$ yields a straight line of gradient 9.74 m s⁻² and vertical intercept 2.28 m s⁻¹. What was the speed $u$ of the sphere as it passed the upper light gate?
items.workedSolution: From $h = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^2$, rearranging gives $2h/t = gt + 2u$. Thus $g = 9.74$ m s⁻², $u = 2.28 / 2 = 1.14 m s⁻¹$, and percentage difference $= |9.74 - 9.81|/9.81 \times 100\% = 0.714\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates initialSpeedU $= 1.14 m s⁻¹$.

items.stem: A student releases a dense steel ball from an electromagnet to a trapdoor switch (RP3) across several heights and plots $h$ against $t^2$. The best-fit straight line has gradient 4.76 m s⁻². Determine the experimental value of $g$.
items.workedSolution: Comparing $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ with $y = mx$, the gradient equals $g/2$, so $g = 2 \times 4.76 = 9.52 m s⁻²$.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates $g = 9.52 m s⁻²$.

items.stem: Two light springs of constants $k_1 = 45.0\text{ N m}^{-1}$ and $k_2 = 90.0\text{ N m}^{-1}$ obey Hooke's law. They support an 18.0 N weight, first in series and then in parallel.
items.workedSolution: (a) k_s = 30.0 N m⁻¹. (b) k_p = 135 N m⁻¹. (c) E_s = 5.40 J. (d) springs in parallel share the same extension while their tensions add giving effective stiffness k1 plus k2.

markScheme.criterion: Applies reciprocal sum 1/k_s = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂.
Obtains k_s = 30.0 N m⁻¹.
Adds k₁ + k₂ to obtain k_p = 135 N m⁻¹.
Finds series extension x_s = F/k_s and applies E = ½Fx_s (or F²/(2k_s)).
Obtains stored energy E_s = 5.40 J.
States parallel springs have the same extension x and share total load F = F₁ + F₂.
Substitutes F₁ = k₁x, F₂ = k₂x to obtain k_p = k₁ + k₂ (springs in parallel share the same extension while their tensions add giving effective stiffness k1 plus k2).

items.stem: At 15.0 m s⁻¹, a 1200 kg hatchback has a reaction time of 0.600 s (thinking distance 9.00 m) and brakes at 5.00 m s⁻² (braking distance 22.5 m). If the same driver doubles the speed to 30.0 m s⁻¹ on the same road, what is the new total stopping distance?
items.workedSolution: At doubled speed: d_think' = 2 × 9.00 = 18.0 m and d_brake' = 4 × 22.5 = 90.0 m, so d_stop' = 18.0 + 90.0 = 108 m.

markScheme.criterion: Doubles thinking distance and quadruples braking distance to obtain 108 m.

items.stem: A student uses Searle's dual-wire apparatus hanging from a rigid ceiling beam. They want to measure the Young modulus of a long steel wire.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Wear safety goggles in case the taut wire snaps and place a sand tray or cushioned pad directly beneath the hanging slotted masses, keeping feet clear. Hang a long thin test wire alongside an identical reference wire carrying a small constant mass from the same rigid beam so ceiling sag and thermal expansion cancel equally. Check micrometer zero error, then use the ratchet to measure wire diameter in perpendicular directions at least three positions along the wire; average d and compute A = πd²/4. Measure original length L from clamp to Vernier marker with a metre ruler after applying a small initial load to remove kinks. Add known masses incrementally (F = mg, g = 9.81 m s⁻²), recording Vernier extension e at eye level, then record extensions while unloading to verify the elastic limit was not exceeded. Plot F against e, draw a best-fit line through the linear elastic region, determine gradient from > 50% span, and evaluate E = (L / A) × gradient.

markScheme.criterion: States safety precautions: wear safety goggles for snapping wire and place a sand tray/cushion under slotted masses.
Explains that the identical reference wire compensates both ceiling-beam sag and thermal expansion.
Measures diameter using a zero-checked micrometer with ratchet at >= 3 places in perpendicular directions to find A = πd²/4.
Applies a small initial straightening load, measures original length L with a metre ruler, and records incremental Vernier extensions e for loads F = mg.
Takes unloading readings to confirm the wire returns to original readings (elastic limit not exceeded).
Plots F against e (or stress against strain) and extracts E = (L / A) × gradient from a best-fit straight line.

parts.prompt: Describe a detailed, safe experimental method to obtain an accurate value for the Young modulus, explaining all measurements, instrument techniques, error controls, and graphical analysis. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Wear safety goggles and place a sand tray beneath the slotted masses; an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while perpendicular micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty; measure unstretched length L with a metre ruler, apply incremental loads F = mg while reading Vernier extensions during both loading and unloading, plot F against e, and obtain E = (L/A) × gradient.
workingSteps: Level 1: Safety goggles + sand tray beneath slotted masses; long thin test wire and identical reference wire.
Level 2: Micrometer with ratchet (zero-error checked) at >= 3 perpendicular pairs for d -> A = πd²/4; ruler for L; initial straightening load + Vernier extension readings.
Level 3: Repeat readings during unloading to confirm elastic limit, plot F vs e (straight line through origin), compute E = L × gradient / A.

items.stem: A solid sphere (I = 2/5 mR²) and a thin hollow hoop (I = mR²) have the same mass and radius. Both are released from rest at the same time to roll without slipping down the same slope. Which reaches the bottom first, and why?
items.workedSolution: Because v = √(2gh / (1 + k_I)), the solid sphere (k_I = 0.40) retains 5/7 of mgΔh as translational KE whereas the hollow hoop (k_I = 1.0) retains only 1/2. Therefore the correct statement is: Comparing their energy split, the solid sphere reaches the bottom first because it has the smallest moment of inertia factor, so a greater proportion of gravitational potential energy becomes translational kinetic energy rather than rotational kinetic energy.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: the solid sphere reaches the bottom first because it has the smallest moment of inertia factor, so a greater proportion of gravitational potential energy becomes translational kinetic energy rather than rotational kinetic energy.

options.label: A
options.text: Comparing their energy split, the hollow hoop reaches the bottom first because distributing mass at the rim maximizes angular momentum and forward push.
options.distractorRationale: A larger moment of inertia diverts a larger share (50% vs 29%) of gravitational PE into rotational KE, leaving less translational speed.

options.label: B
options.text: Comparing their energy split, the solid sphere reaches the bottom first because it has the smallest moment of inertia factor, so a greater proportion of gravitational potential energy becomes translational kinetic energy rather than rotational kinetic energy.

options.label: C
options.text: Comparing their energy split, both reach the bottom at the exact same instant because gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m s⁻² is independent of mass distribution.
options.distractorRationale: True for frictionless sliding, but for rolling without slipping a = g sin θ / (1 + I/(mR²)) depends explicitly on mass distribution.

options.label: D
options.text: Comparing their energy split, the solid sphere reaches the bottom first only if its mass exceeds the hoop's mass, since translational speed scales with √m.
options.distractorRationale: Both mass m and radius R cancel out of v = √(2gh / (1 + k_I)); only the dimensionless shape factor k_I matters.

items.stem: A steel ball is fired from a spring launcher on level ground at 36 m s⁻¹ and 33° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height reached above the ground.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 33° = 30.2 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 33°)² / (2g) = 19.6 m. Target = 19.6 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 33° at apex to obtain 19.6 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Converts all initial kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy, forgetting non-zero horizontal speed u cos θ at the apex.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses horizontal component u cos θ instead of vertical component u sin θ in h = u_y² / (2g).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of two in the denominator of h_max = u_y² / (2g).

items.stem: A tennis ball is fired from a launcher on a level pitch at a speed of 20 m s⁻¹ and an angle of 38° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates u_y = u sin θ.
Obtains 12.3 m s⁻¹.
Applies T = 2u_y / g.
Obtains 2.51 s.
Multiplies u cos θ by flight time T.
Obtains 39.6 m.

items.stem: A metal cylinder of mass 5 kg is attached to an elastic rope of natural length 3.2 m. It falls from rest at the fixed upper support, and the rope obeys Hooke's law once it becomes taut at point A. The rope stretches by a maximum extension of 0.45 m in 0.28 s before the cylinder stops at the lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Uses free-fall relation v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 7.92 m s⁻¹.
Equates mg(L + x) = ½kx² over the complete vertical drop.
Obtains 1.77 × 10³ N m⁻¹.
Evaluates a_B = (kx − mg) / m.
Obtains 149 m s⁻².

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a horizontal beam of length L = 2.8 m and mass 8 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light vertical wires at A and B. The wires are 2.1 m apart. Its centre of gravity G lies 0.76 m to the right of A and 1.34 m to the left of B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the tension T₁ in wire A.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: T₁_y × 2.1 = 8 × 9.81 × 1.34 ⇒ T₁_y = 50.08 N, T₂_y = 28.40 N. For vertical wires, T₁ = 50.08 N ≈ 50.1 N and T₂ = 28.40 N ≈ 28.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct wire tension = 50.1 N.

items.stem: A lead bob of mass 3 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 2 m on a light steel cable. The cable breaks if the tension exceeds 106 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the bob at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((106/3) − 9.81) × 2] = 7.14 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 7.14 m s⁻¹ (C).

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a steering bar has length d = 0.36 m. Two equal and opposite parallel forces of magnitude F = 74 N act at its ends, each at 55° to the bar. What is the magnitude of the torque of this couple?
items.workedSolution: Perpendicular separation between the parallel lines of action is d_perp = d sin 55° = 0.2949 m. Torque of the couple: T = F d_perp = 74 × 0.2949 = 21.82 N m ≈ 21.8 N m.

markScheme.criterion: Correct couple torque = 21.8 N m.

items.stem: A sled of weight 280 N slides at a constant speed down a snowy slope. The slope has length 33 m and vertical height 10.6 m. Calculate the magnitude of the resistive force opposing motion along the slope.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 2 m and mass 10 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 6.5 kg hangs so its centre of gravity acts 1.5 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at 32° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about O give T = 182.8 N ≈ 183 N. (b) Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos θ = 155.0 N ≈ 155 N. (c) Vertical balance: R_y = W_total − T sin θ = 64.99 N ≈ 65.0 N.

markScheme.criterion: Writes full moment balance about hinge O including both rod and sign moments with T sin θ.
Evaluates T = 182.8 N (183 N) showing agreement with 1.8 × 10² N.
Applies horizontal equilibrium R_x = T cos θ.
R_x = 155 N away from the wall.
Applies vertical equilibrium R_y = W_total − T sin θ.
R_y = 65.0 N upwards.

parts.prompt: By taking moments about hinge O, show clearly that the tension T in the angled wire is approximately 1.8 × 10² N.
workingSteps: Clockwise moment about O = (10 × 1 + 6.5 × 1.5) × 9.81 = 193.7 N m.
T = 182.8 N ≈ 183 N, which rounds to 1.8 × 10² N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the horizontal component of the force exerted by hinge O on the rod.
workingSteps: Horizontal equilibrium: R_x = T cos 32° = 182.8 × cos 32° = 155.0 N ≈ 155 N away from the wall.

parts.prompt: Calculate the vertical component of the force exerted by hinge O on the rod.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium: R_y = W − T sin 32° = 64.99 N ≈ 65.0 N upwards.

items.stem: A plastic box of mass 13.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough ramp of length 11.5 m, inclined at 44° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 6.51 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy dissipated against friction during the slide.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 44° = 1.06 × 10³ J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(13.5)(6.51)² = 286 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 772 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 44°)L, μ = 0.705. Target = 772 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 44° accurately to obtain 772 J (D).

items.stem: In Required Practical 4, a copper wire has length $(2.10 \pm 0.002)$ m. Perpendicular micrometer readings give mean diameters 0.48 mm, 0.46 mm, and 0.47 mm (uncertainty $\pm 0.01$ mm). The $F$ against $e$ graph has percentage uncertainty 1.8% in its gradient. Calculate the total percentage uncertainty in the Young modulus $E$.
items.workedSolution: Mean diameter $d = 0.47$ mm gives $A = \pi d^2/4 = 1.73 × 10⁻⁷ m²$. $E = L \times \mathrm{grad} / A = 119 GPa$. Percentage uncertainty $\%\Delta E = \%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad} = 0.0952 + 2(2.13) + 1.8 = 6.15\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates pctUncE $= 6.15\%$.

items.stem: A small metal sphere of mass 1.1 kg is attached to a light wire of length 2 m. It moves in a vertical circle and passes through the lowest point at 7.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_c = mv² / r.
Obtains 30.9 N.
Applies T − mg = F_c => T = F_c + mg.
Obtains 41.7 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant centripetal force on the sphere at the lowest point.
Hence calculate the tension in the wire at the lowest point.

items.stem: A spinning space probe with extended sensor arms has moment of inertia 16.0 kg m² and spins at 3.00 rad s⁻¹ with zero external torque. Internal motors pull the arms inward, reducing the moment of inertia to 6.40 kg m².
items.workedSolution: (a) $\omega_2 = 7.50 rad s⁻¹$. (b) Work done $= \frac{1}{2}I_2\omega_2^2 - \frac{1}{2}I_1\omega_1^2 = 108 J$. (c) Internal radial forces do positive work pulling masses inward so rotational kinetic energy increases.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$.
Obtains $\omega_2 = 7.50 rad s⁻¹$.
Calculates initial rotational KE $\frac{1}{2}I_1\omega_1^2$.
Calculates final rotational KE $\frac{1}{2}I_2\omega_2^2$ and finds difference.
Obtains internal work $= 108 J$.
Explains that internal radial forces produce zero torque about the spin axis.
States that internal radial forces do positive work pulling the pods inward.

items.stem: A 1350 kg delivery van uses a KERS flywheel to climb a 250 m slope that rises 16.0 m vertically against a mean resistive force of 280 N. Take $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$. The flywheel slows from 620 rad s⁻¹ to 260 rad s⁻¹ with zero energy loss in transmission. Calculate its minimum moment of inertia.
items.workedSolution: Required energy $E = mgh + F_{\mathrm{d}}s = 1350(9.81)(16.0) + 280(250) = 2.82 × 10⁵ J$. Setting $\frac{1}{2}I(\omega_1^2 - \omega_2^2) = E$ gives $I = \frac{2E}{620^2 - 260^2} = 1.78 kg m²$.

markScheme.criterion: Minimum flywheel moment of inertia equals 1.78 kg m².

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Includes gravitational potential gain $mgh$ but ignores work done against drag $F_{\mathrm{d}}s$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses $(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$ instead of $(\omega_1^2 - \omega_2^2)$.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of $2$ when rearranging $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_1^2 - \omega_2^2)$.

items.stem: A heavy box of weight 900 N slides down a straight ramp at a constant speed of 6.5 m s⁻¹. The ramp is 22 m long and drops by 8.8 m vertically. Calculate the rate at which mechanical energy is transferred to thermal energy.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed, friction balances downslope weight: F_f = W(h/L) = 900 × (8.8/22) = 360 N. Rate of thermal energy generation P = F_f v = 2.34 × 10³ W. Target = 2.34 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_f = Wh/L and P = F_f v to obtain 2.34 × 10³ W (B).

items.stem: A weather sensor released from a hovering balloon reaches terminal velocity $30.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ along the curved velocity–time graph shown. At point P ($t = 3.00\text{ s}$), the sensor's speed is $15.8 m s⁻¹$ and the tangent at P meets the vertical velocity axis at $5.20 m s⁻¹$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Tangent slope gives $a = 3.54 m s⁻²$. (b) Average acceleration $a_{\text{avg}} = 5.28 m s⁻²$. (c) as speed rises fluid resistance increases until it balances weight so resultant force and acceleration fall to zero at terminal speed.

markScheme.criterion: Uses tangent coordinates to evaluate gradient Δv/Δt.
Obtains instantaneous acceleration 3.54 m s⁻².
Computes average acceleration as total Δv divided by 3.00 s.
Obtains average acceleration 5.28 m s⁻².
States weight remains constant downwards while upward fluid resistance grows with speed.
Deduces resultant downward force and acceleration decrease continuously.
Concludes zero resultant force at terminal velocity (as speed rises fluid resistance increases until it balances weight so resultant force and acceleration fall to zero at terminal speed).

items.stem: Two stationary trolleys of unequal mass held together by a compressed spring are released on a frictionless horizontal track. How do their momenta and kinetic energies compare after separation?
items.workedSolution: With zero external impulse, p_A + p_B = 0 gives equal momentum magnitudes p, so E_k = p²/(2m) implies E_k ∝ 1/m. Therefore the correct statement is: In an isolated one-dimensional explosion from rest total linear momentum remains zero while kinetic energy is shared inversely with fragment mass.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: in an isolated one-dimensional explosion from rest total linear momentum remains zero while kinetic energy is shared inversely with fragment mass.

items.stem: The diagram shows the rotor of a high-speed textile winding drum. Its central hub has moment of inertia 1.60 kg m² and carries 6 rim masses of 1.40 kg each at radius 0.350 m. During a test run lasting 10.0 s, the rotational speed changes uniformly from 14.0 rev s⁻¹ to 2.00 rev s⁻¹ while a constant bearing friction torque of 2.00 N m opposes rotation.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I = 2.63 kg m²$. (b) $|\alpha| = \frac{2\pi|f_2 - f_1|}{t} = 7.54 rad s⁻²$. (c) Applied torque $T_{\mathrm{app}} = 17.8 N m$. (d) Peak power $P_{\max} = T_{\mathrm{app}}\omega_{\max} = 1.57 × 10³ W$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $I = I_{\mathrm{hub}} + \sum m r^2$ with squared radius.
Obtains $I = 2.63 kg m²$.
Converts $\text{rev s}^{-1}$ to $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ via $2\pi$ and divides change by $t$.
Obtains $|\alpha| = 7.54 rad s⁻²$.
Combines $I|\alpha|$ with bearing friction torque in the correct sense.
Obtains applied torque $= 17.8 N m$.
Applies $P = T\omega$ at the highest angular speed.
Obtains maximum power $= 1.57 × 10³ W$.

items.stem: A natural-gas power station shown in the Sankey diagram uses fuel of specific energy $50.0\text{ MJ kg}^{-1}$ at an input power of $800\text{ MW}$. It produces $300\text{ MW}$ of electrical power and loses $360\text{ MW}$ in hot exhaust gases.
items.workedSolution: (a) $P_{\text{cool}} = 140 MW$. (b) $\eta = 37.5\%$. (c) $\Delta m/\Delta t = 16.0 kg s⁻¹$. (d) the width of every arrow in a Sankey diagram is directly proportional to the energy or power transferred and input width equals the sum of all output widths.

markScheme.criterion: Applies energy conservation to find 140 MW.
Applies η = P_output / P_input.
Obtains efficiency 37.5%.
Divides input power (not electrical output) by specific energy.
Obtains mass burn rate 16.0 kg s⁻¹.
States arrow width is proportional to energy or power flow.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a non-uniform access door of length L = 2.2 m and mass 32 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.88 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 28° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the angle above the horizontal at which the resultant reaction force R from hinge O acts.
items.workedSolution: Moments about O: T cos 28° × 2.2 = 32 × 9.81 × 0.88 ⇒ T = 142.2 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T sin 28° = 66.77 N. Vertical balance: R_y = 32 × 9.81 − T cos 28° = 188.4 N. Resultant R = √(R_x² + R_y²) = 199.8 N ≈ 200 N, at angle α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 70.48° ≈ 70.5° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 70.5°.

items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.8 × 2.6) = 7.14 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.33 + 6(9.8) = 189 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 189 N (D).

items.stem: A small lorry of mass 1700 kg accelerates along a level road while a small plumb bob hangs from its ceiling at 22° to the vertical. Later, the lorry climbs a straight 12° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 50 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.85. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 22 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 530 N toward the stop sign. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 22°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 22° = ma and T cos 22° = mg => a = g tan 22° = 3.96 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.85 × 9.81 × 50) = 20.4 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1700)(22)² / 530 = 776 m. Target = 3.96 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 3.96 m s⁻² (C).

options.label: B

options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: A heavy ball of mass 0.5 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.8 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a wooden block of mass 0.5 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string just before the ball strikes the block.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 5.94 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 14.7 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 2.97 m s⁻¹. Target = 14.7 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 14.7 N (A).

items.stem: Two dynamics trolleys of masses m₁ = 1.2 kg and m₂ = 3.6 kg are held at rest against a compressed spring on a smooth horizontal track. When released, the 1.2 kg trolley moves left at 2.7 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) 0.900 m s⁻¹. (b) 5.83 J. (c) 3.00. (d) because both fragments gain equal and opposite momenta from rest, the lighter mass moves faster and gains the greater proportion of the released kinetic energy.

markScheme.criterion: Applies 0 = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
Obtains v₂ = 0.900 m s⁻¹.
Computes ½m₁v₁² + ½m₂v₂².
Obtains total KE = 5.83 J.
Finds ratio = 3.00.
States equal momentum magnitudes p₁ = p₂.
Links smaller mass to greater speed and larger E_k = p²/(2m).

items.stem: A metal cylinder of mass 5.5 kg is attached to an elastic rope of natural length 3 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.45 m in 0.26 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the spring constant of the rope.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 3 + 0.45 = 3.45 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 1.84 × 10³ N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 826 N. Target = 1.84 × 10³ N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (3 + 0.45) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 1.84 × 10³ N m⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a construction crane has total length L = 16 m and mass 800 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 5.5 m from rear end A. A 3800 kg concrete counterweight sits 4.1 m to the left of P (1.4 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 4 m to the right of P (9.5 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 10 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum safe load weight at the hook without tipping clockwise about P.
items.workedSolution: Anticlockwise counterweight moment about P: M_cw = 3800 × 9.81 × 4.1 = 1.528 × 10⁵ N m. Clockwise boom moment: M_boom = 800 × 9.81 × 4 = 3.139 × 10⁴ N m. Remaining clockwise moment available for load: W_max × 10 = 1.214 × 10⁵ N m ⇒ W_max = 1.214 × 10⁴ N ≈ 1.21 × 10⁴ N, m_max = W_max / 9.81 = 1238 kg ≈ 1.24 × 10³ kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct maximum safe load weight = 1.21 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform metal beam AB has total length L = 4.4 m and mass 16 kg. Its centre of gravity G is at its midpoint, 2.2 m from end A. It rests horizontally on a sharp pivot P at 1.67 m from end A. A counterbalance block of unknown mass sits 0.33 m from end A. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the mass of the counterbalance block needed for horizontal equilibrium.
items.workedSolution: Take moments about pivot P. Lever arm of beam CG is d_G = 2.2 − 1.67 = 0.5300 m. Lever arm of counterbalance is d_load = 1.67 − 0.33 = 1.340 m. Balancing moments: m_load g d_load = m_beam g d_G ⇒ m_load = (16 × 0.5300) / 1.340 = 6.328 kg ≈ 6.33 kg. Vertical equilibrium gives R = (m_beam + m_load)g = (16 + 6.328) × 9.81 = 219.0 N ≈ 219 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct balancing mass m_load = 6.33 kg.

items.stem: A heavy block of mass 2 kg is attached to a rubber rope of natural length 2.6 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the rope becomes taut, and then stretches it by 1.2 m in 0.33 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward force exerted by the rope between A and B.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.81 × 2.6) = 7.14 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.33 + 2(9.81) = 62.9 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 62.9 N (D).

items.stem: A particle's kinetic energy can be written in terms of momentum $p$ and mass $m$ as $E_k = p^2/(2m)$. Which conclusion follows directly from this relation?
items.workedSolution: From E_k = p²/(2m), for constant mass E_k ∝ p², so doubling p increases E_k by a factor of 2² = 4. Therefore the correct statement is: For a particle of fixed mass kinetic energy equals p squared divided by 2m so doubling momentum quadruples kinetic energy.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: for a particle of fixed mass kinetic energy equals p squared divided by 2m so doubling momentum quadruples kinetic energy.

options.text: For a particle of fixed mass doubling its momentum merely doubles its kinetic energy.
options.distractorRationale: Kinetic energy varies as the square of momentum (p²), not linearly with p.

options.label: B
options.text: Two particles carrying the same momentum always possess the same kinetic energy regardless of their masses.
options.distractorRationale: At identical momentum p, the lighter particle has greater kinetic energy since E_k ∝ 1/m.

options.label: C
options.text: For a particle of fixed mass kinetic energy equals p squared divided by 2m so doubling momentum quadruples kinetic energy.

options.label: D
options.text: Halving a particle's mass at fixed momentum halves its kinetic energy.
options.distractorRationale: Mass sits in the denominator of p²/(2m), so halving mass doubles kinetic energy.

items.stem: On a horizontal frictionless air track, glider X of mass 2 kg moves to the right at 13 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with glider Y of mass 3.6 kg moving to the left at 6 m s⁻¹ (arrow not shown). Immediately after the collision, glider Y moves right at 4 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of glider X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward as positive: p_before = (2)(13) + (3.6)(−6) = 4.40 kg m s⁻¹. From p_before = (2)v_X + (3.6)(4), v_X = -5.00 m s⁻¹, which is 5.00 m s⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: Uses signed head-on momentum p_before = 4.40 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 5.00 m s⁻¹ to the left (C).

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform wooden plank of total length L = 5.4 m and mass 48 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is 0.6 m from the left end, and support B is 3.2 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 1.6 m. A technician of mass 66 kg initially stands 2.1 m from the left end of the plank. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate how far past support B the technician can walk before the plank begins to tip.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: F₁ × 3.2 = (48 × 1.100 + 66 × 1.700) × 9.81 ⇒ F₁ = 505.8 N ≈ 506 N. At tipping (F₁ = 0): m_load × d_tip = m_beam × (x_B − x_G) ⇒ d_tip = (48 × 1.100) / 66 = 0.8000 m ≈ 0.800 m. At the very tip (overhang 1.6 m): m_end = (48 × 1.100) / 1.6 = 33.00 kg ≈ 33.0 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct solver-verified answer = 0.800 m.

items.stem: A steel ball is fired from a spring launcher on level ground at 38 m s⁻¹ and 52° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the ground.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 38 sin 52° = 29.9 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 38 cos 52° = 23.4 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 6.11 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 143 m. Target = 143 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 143 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies horizontal speed by ascent time u sin θ / g instead of full flight time 2u sin θ / g.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cos θ for sin θ in the flight-time expression.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: An electric car of mass 1700 kg accelerates along a level road while a small steel sphere hangs from its ceiling at 38° to the vertical. Later, the car climbs a straight 8° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 70 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.8. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 22 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 620 N toward the marker. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular bend of radius 70 m without skidding.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 38° = ma and T cos 38° = mg => a = g tan 38° = 7.66 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.8 × 9.8 × 70) = 23.4 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1700)(22)² / 620 = 664 m. Target = 23.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 23.4 m s⁻¹ (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the static friction coefficient μ_s in μ_s mg = mv²/R.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides by μ_s instead of multiplying by μ_s.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes v² = μ_s g R without taking the square root.

items.stem: A student uses the curved velocity–time graph of a falling skydiver. They want to find the acceleration at point P and the distance fallen from release to point Q. Which method is physically valid?
items.workedSolution: Because acceleration decreases continuously as drag grows, constant acceleration equations are invalid; use tangent gradient for acceleration and area under the $v\text{–}t$ graph for distance. Therefore option A is correct: constant acceleration equations are invalid so use tangent gradient and area under velocity time graph.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: constant acceleration equations are invalid so use tangent gradient and area under velocity time graph.

items.stem: A rubber block of mass 13.5 kg slides from rest down a rough concrete slope of length 7.5 m inclined at 34° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 5.44 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the magnitude of the constant friction force opposing its motion.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 34° − ½mv² = 356 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 7.5 = 47.4 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.85 m s⁻¹. Target = 47.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 47.4 N (A).

items.stem: A plastic box of mass 6.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough ramp of length 10 m, inclined at 32° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 6.22 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the coefficient of dynamic friction μ_d between the box and the ramp.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 32° = 338 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(6.5)(6.22)² = 126 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 212 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 32°)L, μ = 0.392. Target = 0.392.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 32° accurately to obtain 0.392 (D).

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 0.9 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.7 m on a strong string. At the lowest point, its speed is 5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 0.9 × 5² / 0.7 = 32.1 N, so T = 32.1 + 0.9 × 9.8 = 41.0 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 41.0 N (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A non-uniform cast-iron bar of length L = 2.20 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a rectangular cross-section of width w = 16.0 cm and thickness h = 8.0 cm, with average density ρ = 7200 kg m⁻³. Its centre of gravity G lies at distance x = 0.99 m from end A. An electric chain hoist of electrical input power 850 W and efficiency 84% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.01280 m², V = A L = 0.02816 m³, m = ρ V = 202.8 kg ≈ 203 kg. (b) W = 1989 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 895.0 N ≈ 895 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 0.9900 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 1969 J ≈ 1.97 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.84 × 850 = 714.0 W, so t = 1969 / 714.0 = 2.758 s ≈ 2.76 s. (e) density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

markScheme.criterion: Computes cross-section A = w h = 0.01280 m² with cm → m conversion.
Calculates V = A L = 0.02816 m³ and substitutes m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 202.8 kg rounding clearly to 203 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 2.20 = m g × 0.9900.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 895 N (4 s.f. 895.0 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 0.9900 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 1.97 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 1969 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 714.0 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 2.76 s (4 s.f. 2.758 s).
States valid physical assumption: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

items.stem: A steel bob of mass 2.4 kg hangs on a light string of length 2.3 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a lump of modelling clay of mass 6 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height above the lowest point reached by the joined objects.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 6.71 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 1.92 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.188 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 38.6 J. Target = 0.188 m.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 0.188 m (A).

items.stem: A uniform ceramic channel of length L = 3.40 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a semi-annular cross-section of outer diameter D = 19.0 cm and inner diameter d = 11.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2320 kg m⁻³. It is uniform along its length, so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. An electric yard winch of electrical input power 450 W and efficiency 74% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 9.425 × 10⁻³ m², V = A L = 0.03204 m³, m = ρ V = 74.34 kg ≈ 74.3 kg. (b) W = 729.3 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 364.7 N ≈ 365 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.700 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 1240 J ≈ 1.24 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.74 × 450 = 333.0 W, so t = 1240 / 333.0 = 3.723 s ≈ 3.72 s. (e) electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates cross-section A = 9.425 × 10⁻³ m², volume V = 0.03204 m³, and applies m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 74.34 kg confirming 74.3 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 3.40 = m g × 1.700.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 365 N (4 s.f. 364.7 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.700 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 1.24 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 1240 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 333.0 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 3.72 s (4 s.f. 3.723 s).
Identifies electrical heating in motor windings and mechanical friction in hoist gears.
Links losses to thermal energy dissipated to the surroundings (electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings).
