items.stem: In Required Practical 3, a student drops a dense steel sphere through two light gates and plots $2h/t$ against $t$. The best-fit straight line has gradient 9.92 m s⁻² (with percentage uncertainty 1.8%) and vertical intercept 3.16 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $u = 3.16/2 = 1.58 m s⁻¹$. (b) $\Delta g = 0.179 m s⁻²$. (c) Percentage difference $= 1.12\%$ (smaller than the 1.8% experimental uncertainty, so result is consistent with 9.81 m s⁻²). (d) use a plumb line to align the metre ruler vertically and plot two h over t against t so the gradient equals gravitational field strength independently of initial speed.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies vertical intercept equals $2u$.
Initial speed $u = 1.58 m s⁻¹$.
Multiplies measured $g$ by fractional uncertainty.
Absolute uncertainty $\Delta g = 0.179 m s⁻²$.
Computes $|g_{\mathrm{meas}} - 9.81|/9.81 \times 100\%$.
Percentage difference $= 1.12\%$.
Uses a plumb line / set square against bench to ensure ruler is completely vertical.
Shows $2h/t = gt + 2u$ keeps gradient equal to $g$ regardless of initial speed $u$.

Calculate the absolute uncertainty in the measured value of $g$.
Calculate the percentage difference between the measured $g$ and accepted value $9.81$ m s⁻².
Explain how the ruler is aligned vertically and why plotting $2h/t$ against $t$ removes error from the unknown release height above Gate 1.
parts.expectedAnswer: use a plumb line to align the metre ruler vertically and plot two h over t against t so the gradient equals gravitational field strength independently of initial speed
workingSteps: Align clamped metre ruler against a plumb line (reject bare 'pendulum').
2h/t = gt + 2u separates unknown u into the vertical intercept while gradient stays g.

items.stem: In the electromagnet-and-trapdoor arrangement of Required Practical 3, plotting drop height $h$ against $t^2$ produces a straight line of gradient 4.76 m s⁻². In an individual drop from $h = 1.15$ m, the digital timer records 0.4982 s because residual magnetism delays release by 14 ms.
items.workedSolution: (a) $g = 2 \times 4.76 = 9.52 m s⁻²$. (b) Percentage difference $= 2.96\%$. (c) Single drop gives $g = 9.27 m s⁻²$. (d) residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $g = 2 \times \mathrm{gradient}$.
Measured $g = 9.52 m s⁻²$.
Divides absolute discrepancy by accepted $9.81$ m s⁻².
Percentage difference $= 2.96\%$.
Substitutes into $g = 2h/t^2$.
Apparent $g = 9.27 m s⁻²$.
Residual magnetism delays release so recorded $t$ is systematically too large.
Suggests reducing electromagnet current / inserting paper spacer / using two light gates.

Calculate the apparent value of $g$ obtained from the single drop at $h = 1.15$ m.
Explain why residual magnetism produces a systematic underestimate of $g$ and suggest one way to minimise it.
parts.expectedAnswer: residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g; minimise by reducing electromagnet current to the minimum needed to hold the sphere or inserting a thin sheet of paper.
workingSteps: Timer starts when current switches off, before sphere detaches -> t too large -> 2h/t² too small.

markScheme.criterion: Computes k_p = 80.0 N m⁻¹ and elastic strain energy 2.50 J.

items.stem: Highway safety campaigns emphasise that small increases in urban driving speed dramatically increase stopping distance and collision severity.
items.workedSolution: Stopping distance sums linear thinking distance vt and quadratic braking distance v squared over 2a determined by reaction time and road friction. Total stopping distance is d_stop = d_think + d_brake. During reaction time t_r the car moves at constant speed v, so d_think = v t_r (proportional to v). Under constant braking force F, work done against friction equals initial kinetic energy: F d_brake = ½mv², giving d_brake = mv²/(2F) = v²/(2a) (proportional to v²). Doubling speed doubles thinking distance but quadruples braking distance. Driver fatigue, alcohol, drugs, and distractions lengthen t_r (thinking distance only), whereas wet/icy roads, worn tyres, defective brakes, and greater vehicle mass increase braking distance.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Defines stopping distance as the sum of thinking distance and braking distance.
L1: Shows thinking distance d_think = v t_r is directly proportional to speed v for constant reaction time.
L2: Equates braking work F d_brake to kinetic energy ½mv² to derive d_brake = mv²/(2F) = v²/(2a).
L2: Explains doubling speed doubles thinking distance while quadrupling braking distance.
L3: Correctly assigns driver factors (tiredness, alcohol, drugs, mobile distractions) only to thinking distance.
L3: Correctly assigns vehicle/road factors (wet or icy surface, worn tyres/brakes, heavy load) only to braking distance.

parts.prompt: Using kinematics and the work-energy theorem, derive how thinking distance and braking distance depend on speed v, and explain clearly which human, vehicle, and road factors affect each component separately. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Stopping distance sums linear thinking distance vt and quadratic braking distance v squared over 2a determined by reaction time and road friction. Total stopping distance is d_stop = d_think + d_brake. During reaction time t_r the car moves at constant speed v, so d_think = v t_r (proportional to v). Under constant braking force F, work done against friction equals initial kinetic energy: F d_brake = ½mv², giving d_brake = mv²/(2F) = v²/(2a) (proportional to v²). Doubling speed doubles thinking distance but quadruples braking distance. Driver fatigue, alcohol, drugs, and distractions lengthen t_r (thinking distance only), whereas wet/icy roads, worn tyres, defective brakes, and greater vehicle mass increase braking distance.
workingSteps: Define stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
Derive d_think = vt_r (∝ v) and d_brake = mv²/(2F) = v²/(2a) (∝ v²) from work-energy theorem.
Classify factors affecting thinking distance vs factors affecting braking distance.

items.stem: A group of students uses Searle's dual-wire apparatus with a Vernier scale. They want to measure the elastic stiffness and Young modulus of a copper wire.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Wear safety goggles in case the taut wire snaps and place a sand tray or cushioned pad directly beneath the hanging slotted masses, keeping feet clear. Hang a long thin test wire alongside an identical reference wire carrying a small constant mass from the same rigid beam so ceiling sag and thermal expansion cancel equally. Check micrometer zero error, then use the ratchet to measure wire diameter in perpendicular directions at least three positions along the wire; average d and compute A = πd²/4. Measure original length L from clamp to Vernier marker with a metre ruler after applying a small initial load to remove kinks. Add known masses incrementally (F = mg, g = 9.81 m s⁻²), recording Vernier extension e at eye level, then record extensions while unloading to verify the elastic limit was not exceeded. Plot F against e, draw a best-fit line through the linear elastic region, determine gradient from > 50% span, and evaluate E = (L / A) × gradient.

markScheme.criterion: States safety precautions: wear safety goggles for snapping wire and place a sand tray/cushion under slotted masses.
Explains that the identical reference wire compensates both ceiling-beam sag and thermal expansion.
Measures diameter using a zero-checked micrometer with ratchet at >= 3 places in perpendicular directions to find A = πd²/4.
Applies a small initial straightening load, measures original length L with a metre ruler, and records incremental Vernier extensions e for loads F = mg.
Takes unloading readings to confirm the wire returns to original readings (elastic limit not exceeded).
Plots F against e (or stress against strain) and extracts E = (L / A) × gradient from a best-fit straight line.

parts.prompt: Explain how the students should set up the apparatus safely, measure wire dimensions and extensions accurately, check elastic behaviour, and determine the Young modulus graphically. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Wear safety goggles and place a sand tray beneath the slotted masses; an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while perpendicular micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty; measure unstretched length L with a metre ruler, apply incremental loads F = mg while reading Vernier extensions during both loading and unloading, plot F against e, and obtain E = (L/A) × gradient.
workingSteps: Level 1: Safety goggles + sand tray beneath slotted masses; long thin test wire and identical reference wire.
Level 2: Micrometer with ratchet (zero-error checked) at >= 3 perpendicular pairs for d -> A = πd²/4; ruler for L; initial straightening load + Vernier extension readings.
Level 3: Repeat readings during unloading to confirm elastic limit, plot F vs e (straight line through origin), compute E = L × gradient / A.

items.stem: A thin hollow hoop of mass m = 1.6 kg and radius r = 0.15 m (I = mr²) rolls from rest without slipping down a 30° incline through a vertical height of h = 2.4 m. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) a = 2.45 m s⁻². (b) α = 16.3 rad s⁻². (c) v = 4.85 m s⁻¹. (d) μ_s = 0.289. (e) the solid sphere reaches the bottom first because it has the smallest moment of inertia factor, so a greater proportion of gravitational potential energy becomes translational kinetic energy rather than rotational kinetic energy.

markScheme.criterion: Applies mg sin θ − F_f = ma and F_f r = mr²(a/r) with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Obtains a = 2.45 m s⁻².
Applies α = a/r to obtain 16.3 rad s⁻².
Applies mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω² to obtain v = 4.85 m s⁻¹.
Sets F_f ≤ μ_s F_N with F_f = ½mg sin θ and F_N = mg cos θ.
Obtains minimum μ_s = ½ tan 30° = 0.289.
States solid sphere arrives first due to its smaller moment of inertia factor.
Links smaller rotational KE share to larger translational KE and higher speed.

items.stem: A ball is launched from floor level across a flat room at 30 m s⁻¹ and 56° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the floor.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 30 sin 56° = 24.9 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 30 cos 56° = 16.8 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.81 = 5.07 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 85.1 m. Target = 85.1 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 85.1 m (B).

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: A heavy block of mass 7 kg is attached to a rubber rope of natural length 2 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.85 m in 0.34 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the spring constant of the rope.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 2 + 0.85 = 2.85 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 542 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 460 N. Target = 542 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (2 + 0.85) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 542 N m⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: A small metal sphere of mass 0.8 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.2 m on a light wire. The wire breaks if the tension exceeds 38 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the sphere at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((38/0.8) − 9.81) × 1.2] = 6.73 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 6.73 m s⁻¹ (A).

options.distractorRationale: Adds g instead of subtracting g when rearranging T_max − mg = mv²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 1.8 m and mass 5 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 6.5 kg hangs so its centre of gravity acts 1.5 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at 44° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the tension T in the angled support wire.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about hinge O: T sin 44° × 1.8 = (5 × 0.9 + 6.5 × 1.5) × 9.81 = 139.8 N m. Hence T sin 44° = 77.66 N and T = 111.8 N ≈ 112 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos 44° = 80.42 N ≈ 80.4 N. Vertical balance: R_y = (5 + 6.5) × 9.81 − 77.66 = 35.15 N ≈ 35.2 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 112 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = mgL sin θ.
Obtains 299 J.
Subtracts ½mv² from ΔE_p.
Obtains 153 J.
Applies W_f = μ(mg cos θ)L.
Obtains 0.271.

items.stem: In Searle's Young modulus investigation (RP4), a student tests a metal alloy wire of unstretched length $(2.60 \pm 0.002)$ m. Micrometer diameter readings in perpendicular directions at three places average to 0.34 mm, 0.32 mm, and 0.33 mm (each $\pm 0.01$ mm). A graph of load $F$ against extension $e$ is a straight line through the origin of gradient 6.9 N mm⁻¹ ($\pm 1.6\%$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $A = \pi d^2/4 = 8.55 × 10⁻⁸ m²$. (b) $E = L(\mathrm{grad})/A = 210 GPa$. (c) $\%\Delta E = 7.74\%$. (d) an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while perpendicular micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Averages three diameters and converts mm to m in $A = \pi d^2/4$.
Cross-sectional area $A = 8.55 × 10⁻⁸ m²$.
Converts gradient to N m⁻¹ and substitutes into $E = (L/A)\,\mathrm{grad}$.
Young modulus $E = 210 GPa$.
Combines $\%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad}$.
Percentage uncertainty in $E = 7.74\%$.
Identical reference wire compensates both support sag and temperature expansion.
Perpendicular micrometer readings at >= 3 positions detect non-uniformity/oval cross-section.

items.stem: A steel ball of mass 1.3 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.5 m on a light string. At the lowest point, its speed is 4.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.3 × 4.5² / 0.5 = 52.6 N, so T = 52.6 + 1.3 × 9.81 = 65.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 65.4 N (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: Under what exact physical condition is the total angular momentum of a multi-disc clutch assembly conserved during engagement?
items.workedSolution: Internal friction torques act equally and oppositely on the two plates, so total angular momentum is conserved provided no resultant external torque acts on the system.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that no resultant external torque acts on the system.

options.distractorRationale: Angular momentum is conserved regardless of the initial speeds provided external torque is zero.

items.stem: Engineers are redesigning a heavy cast-iron KERS flywheel for a racing car. They want to store more energy per kilogram while keeping energy losses low when running freely.
items.workedSolution: From $E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$, concentrating mass at the rim raises $I$, while strong, low-density composites resist bursting stress so $\omega_{\max}$ increases dramatically. An evacuated casing and magnetic bearings minimise windage and friction losses while high-strength rim permits greater angular speed, supported by containment shielding for safety.

markScheme.criterion: States that stored energy $E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ grows linearly with $I$ and quadratically with $\omega$.

items.stem: Wheel A and Wheel B have the same total mass and outer diameter. Wheel A is a solid uniform disc, whereas Wheel B has most of its mass in a heavy outer rim joined by thin spokes. Which statement explains why Wheel B is harder to accelerate rotationally?
items.workedSolution: Because $I = \sum m r^2$, each mass element contributes in proportion to $r^2$: concentrating mass at a larger radius from the rotation axis increases moment of inertia.

items.stem: A gas-fired power station shown in the Sankey diagram receives $640\text{ MW}$ of chemical power from fuel. It delivers $240\text{ MW}$ of electrical output, loses $280\text{ MW}$ in exhaust gases, and loses the rest to cooling water. Calculate the overall efficiency $\eta$ of the station.
items.workedSolution: $\eta = \frac{P_{\text{output}}}{P_{\text{input}}} \times 100\% = \frac{240}{640} \times 100\% = 37.5\%$.

items.stem: What physical quantity is directly equal to the area enclosed between a non-uniform angular acceleration–time ($\alpha$–$t$) graph and the time axis?
items.workedSolution: Since $\alpha = \Delta\omega / \Delta t$, integrating gives area beneath angular acceleration-time graph equals change in angular velocity.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that area beneath angular acceleration-time graph equals change in angular velocity.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a non-uniform metal hatch of length L = 1.8 m and mass 24 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.83 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 42° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) T = 146.1 N ≈ 146 N. (b) the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium. (c)(i) R_x = 97.75 N, R_y = 126.9 N, so R = 160.2 N ≈ 160 N. (c)(ii) α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 52.39° ≈ 52.4° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Στ = 0 about O using T cos(angle to vertical) × L = m g x_G.
Obtains T = 146.1 N (146 N) matching 1.5 × 10² N.
Identifies horizontal component of angled cable tension directed toward the wall.
States hinge must exert an equal opposite horizontal force away from the wall for ΣF_x = 0.
Computes R_x = 97.75 N and R_y = 126.9 N and applies Pythagoras.
Resultant hinge reaction magnitude R = 160 N.
Uses tan α = R_y / R_x with both hinge components.
Direction α = 52.4° above the horizontal.

Equate moments about O: T cos 42° × 1.8 = 24 × 9.81 × 0.83.

parts.expectedAnswer: For horizontal equilibrium, the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium.
workingSteps: Identify that the inclined cable pulls horizontally toward the wall.
Conclude from zero horizontal resultant force that the hinge must push horizontally away from the wall.

Determine the angle above the horizontal at which this resultant hinge force R acts.

items.stem: A metal cylinder of mass 9 kg is attached to an elastic rope of natural length 1.8 m. It falls freely from rest at the fixed support to point A, where the rope becomes taut. It then stretches the rope by 1.1 m over 0.12 s before stopping at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 5.94 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (9 × 5.94) / 0.12 = 445 N.
Obtains 534 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 465 N.

items.stem: A small lorry of mass 1800 kg accelerates along a level road while a small plumb bob hangs from its ceiling at 34° to the vertical. Later, the lorry climbs a straight 14° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 95 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.7. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 18 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 470 N toward the stop sign. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg => a = g tan θ.
Obtains 6.62 m s⁻².
Applies μ_s mg = m v_max² / R.
Obtains 25.5 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts resistive work F_res(πR) from initial kinetic energy ½mu².
Obtains 13.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By resolving forces on the bob, calculate the horizontal acceleration when the string hangs at 34° to the vertical.
Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular road without sliding.
Calculate the speed of the lorry when it reaches the stop sign at the end of the semicircular bend.

items.stem: A lead bob of mass 2.8 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.8 m attached to a light steel cable. The maximum tension the cable can hold without breaking is 77 N. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Writes T_max − mg = m v_max² / r at the lowest point.
Obtains 5.64 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By considering the forces acting on the bob at the lowest point, calculate the maximum speed at the bottom so the cable does not break.

items.stem: A brass ball of mass 2.5 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.4 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a wax block of mass 5.5 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the speed of the joined objects immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 5.24 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 73.6 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 1.64 m s⁻¹. Target = 1.64 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 1.64 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: A heavy lantern hangs at rest from two angled cables, as shown on the left. The right-hand diagram shows the vectors for weight W and cable tensions T₁ and T₂. What geometric condition must hold for translational equilibrium?
items.workedSolution: Placing W, T₂, and T₁ head-to-tail in a closed loop geometrically enforces ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 at the same time. Therefore the correct statement is: Using a scale vector drawing, three coplanar forces acting at a point are in equilibrium if and only if their vectors form a closed triangle head-to-tail giving zero resultant force.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: three coplanar forces acting at a point are in equilibrium if and only if their vectors form a closed triangle head-to-tail giving zero resultant force.

options.distractorRationale: To cancel the resultant of two forces, the third force must have equal magnitude and opposite direction, closing the triangle head-to-tail.

items.stem: A sandbag of mass 9.5 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 1.8 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.95 m in 0.28 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum tension in the cord at the lowest point B.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 1.8 + 0.95 = 2.75 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 567 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 539 N. Target = 539 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (1.8 + 0.95) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 539 N (A).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a dockside crane has total length L = 22 m and mass 400 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 6 m from rear end A. A 4400 kg concrete counterweight sits 4.8 m to the left of P (1.2 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 3 m to the right of P (9 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 15 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) M_cw = 2.072 × 10⁵ N m ≈ 2.07 × 10⁵ N m. (b) Equating clockwise and anticlockwise moments about P gives m_max = 1328 kg ≈ 1.33 × 10³ kg. (c) Vertical force balance yields R = 6.012 × 10⁴ N ≈ 6.01 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses M = m g d with counterweight mass and lever arm from P.
Counterweight moment = 2.07 × 10⁵ N m.
Subtracts boom self-weight moment from counterweight moment and divides by g × load lever arm.
Maximum safe load mass = 1.33 × 10³ kg.
Applies vertical force balance summing counterweight, boom, and load weights.
Upward mast reaction R = 6.01 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: On a frictionless horizontal surface, block X of mass 5.2 kg moves right at 12 m s⁻¹ and collides with stationary block Y of mass 1.6 kg. Immediately after impact, block Y moves right at 10.92 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of block X immediately after the collision.

items.stem: A steel sphere is released from rest just below the surface of a deep column of oil. The experiment is then repeated using a much larger steel sphere in water.
items.workedSolution: At terminal velocity viscous drag plus upthrust equals weight so resultant force and acceleration are zero. At release v = 0 so viscous drag is zero and net downward force W − U gives maximum initial acceleration. As speed rises, Stokes drag 6πηrv increases linearly with v, decreasing resultant force W − U − F and acceleration until F + U = W and acceleration reaches zero at constant terminal velocity. For a large sphere in low-viscosity water, speed grows high enough to trigger turbulent wake eddies where streamlines cross and drag no longer follows F = 6πηrv.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Identifies three vertical forces: constant weight W downwards, constant upthrust U upwards, and speed-dependent drag F upwards.
L1: States that at release v = 0 so F = 0 and initial resultant force W − U produces maximum acceleration.
L2: Explains that as v increases, drag F = 6πηrv grows, reducing resultant force and acceleration.
L2: States terminal velocity occurs when F + U = W so resultant force and acceleration are zero.
L3: Explains that a larger sphere in low-viscosity water accelerates to high speed producing turbulent flow with eddies.
L3: Concludes Stokes' law fails in turbulent flow because drag scales nonlinearly (approximately with v²) instead of 6πηrv.

parts.prompt: Describe and explain how the forces and acceleration of the small sphere evolve from release until terminal velocity, and explain why Stokes' law breaks down for the much larger sphere falling through low-viscosity water. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: At terminal velocity viscous drag plus upthrust equals weight so resultant force and acceleration are zero. At release v = 0 so viscous drag is zero and net downward force W − U gives maximum initial acceleration. As speed rises, Stokes drag 6πηrv increases linearly with v, decreasing resultant force W − U − F and acceleration until F + U = W and acceleration reaches zero at constant terminal velocity. For a large sphere in low-viscosity water, speed grows high enough to trigger turbulent wake eddies where streamlines cross and drag no longer follows F = 6πηrv.
workingSteps: Analyse forces at t = 0 (W down, U up, drag = 0, maximum initial acceleration).
Trace rising drag F = 6πηrv reducing net downward force and acceleration asymptotically to zero.
Contrast laminar flow with turbulent eddies in water where Stokes' law fails.

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 1.6 kg moves right at 6 m s⁻¹ and strikes stationary trolley Y of mass 4.5 kg. Immediately after impact, trolley Y moves right at 2.59 m s⁻¹ and trolley X rebounds to the left. Calculate the kinetic energy lost in this rebound collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward positive, (1.6)(6) = (1.6)v_X + (4.5)(2.59) gives v_X = -1.28 m s⁻¹ (1.28 m s⁻¹ to the left). Scalar final kinetic energies add: K_f = ½(1.6)(1.28)² + ½(4.5)(2.59)² = 16.4 J. Energy lost = 28.8 J − K_f = 12.4 J. Target = 12.4 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds rebound speed 1.28 m s⁻¹ and sums scalar kinetic energies to obtain 12.4 J (B).

items.stem: A small ball is projected from level ground with an initial speed of 21 m s⁻¹ at 55° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.
items.workedSolution: (a) v_apex = 21 × cos 55°. Answer: 12.0 m s⁻¹. (b) u_y = 21 × sin 55° = 17.2 m s⁻¹. h_max = u_y² / (2 × 9.8). Answer: 15.1 m. (c) T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 3.51 s. R = 12.0 × T. Answer: 42.3 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes v_y = 0 at apex so v_apex = u cos θ.
Obtains 12.0 m s⁻¹.
Applies h_max = (u sin θ)² / (2g).
Obtains 15.1 m.
Evaluates R = u_x × (2u_y / g).
Obtains 42.3 m.

items.stem: A small steel ball of mass 2 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.6 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a block of clay of mass 2.4 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height above the lowest point reached by the joined objects.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 5.60 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 2.55 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.331 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 17.1 J. Target = 0.331 m.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 0.331 m (D).

items.stem: In a statics experiment, a metal beam AB has length L = 5 m and mass 12 kg. Its centre of gravity G lies 2.5 m from end A. It is balanced horizontally on a pivot P at 1.5 m from end A by placing a 14 kg block to the left of P. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) The moment of a force is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. (b) Moment balance about P gives d = 0.8571 m left of P, so distance from end B is 4.357 m ≈ 4.36 m.

markScheme.criterion: Force multiplied by distance from pivot.
Perpendicular distance to the line of action.
Correct moment balance about P yielding lever arm d = 0.8571 m.
Converts cleanly to distance from end B = 4.36 m.

parts.prompt: Determine the distance from end B at which the calibration block must be placed so that the beam balances horizontally.
workingSteps: Clockwise moment of beam weight about P = 12 × 9.81 × 1.000.
Equate with anticlockwise moment of block: d = (12 × 1.000) / 14 = 0.8571 m to the left of P.
Distance from end B = (5 − 1.5) + 0.8571 = 4.357 m ≈ 4.36 m.

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 12 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 3.2 m. It falls freely from rest at the fixed support to point A, where the cord becomes taut. It then stretches the cord by 0.9 m over 0.27 s before stopping at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 7.92 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (12 × 7.92) / 0.27 = 352 N.
Obtains 470 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 1.07 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Two identical 0.250 kg air-table discs make a glancing collision. Disc A travels along $+x$ at 8.00 m s⁻¹, strikes stationary disc B, and leaves at 4.00 m s⁻¹ at 60.0° above the $+x$ axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) p₂ = 1.73 kg m s⁻¹. (b) θ₂ = 30.0°. (c) E_k,after = 8.00 J. (d) elastic collision.

markScheme.criterion: Computes p₀, p₁ₓ = m₁v₁cosθ₁, and p₁ᵧ = m₁v₁sinθ₁.
Applies x and y momentum conservation to find p₂ₓ and p₂ᵧ.
Combines components via Pythagoras to obtain p₂ = 1.73 kg m s⁻¹.
Calculates recoil angle θ₂ = 30.0°.
Applies E_k = p²/(2m) to both pucks after impact.
Sums kinetic energies to obtain 8.00 J.
Compares against initial E_k = 8.00 J and classifies as elastic collision.

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 4 kg moves to the right at 10 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with trolley Y of mass 3.6 kg moving to the left at 4 m s⁻¹ (arrow on Y not shown). Immediately after impact, trolley Y moves to the right at 5 m s⁻¹. Take motion to the right as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) p_before = 4 × 10 + 3.6 × (−4) = 25.6 kg m s⁻¹. Answer: 25.6 kg m s⁻¹ to the right. (b) v_X = (25.6 − 3.6 × 5) / 4 = 1.90 m s⁻¹. Answer: 1.90 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m_X u_X − m_Y |u_Y| with correct signs.
Obtains 25.6 kg m s⁻¹ to the right.

Obtains 1.90 m s⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform scaffold plank of total length L = 6.8 m and mass 40 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is at the left end, and support B is 4.6 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 2.2 m. A technician of mass 86 kg initially stands 2.7 m from the left end of the plank. items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B give F₁ = 450.8 N ≈ 451 N. (b) Vertical equilibrium gives F₂ = 785.2 N ≈ 785 N. (c) the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases. (d) Setting F₁ = 0 about B yields d_tip = 0.5581 m ≈ 0.558 m.

markScheme.criterion: Takes moments about B summing plank and technician anticlockwise moments.
Support A reaction F₁ = 451 N.
Support B reaction F₂ = 785 N via vertical force balance.
States that the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.
Sets F₁ = 0 and equates clockwise overhang moment to restoring plank moment about B.

items.stem: A small stone is thrown from flat ground at 34 m s⁻¹ and 26° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the total time of flight before returning to the ground.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 34 sin 26° = 14.9 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 34 cos 26° = 30.6 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 3.04 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 93.0 m. Target = 3.04 s.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 3.04 s (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes time to reach the apex u sin θ / g rather than full time of flight.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Swaps sin θ and cos θ when resolving vertical launch speed.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses total speed u instead of vertical component u sin θ.

items.stem: A van of mass 1300 kg accelerates along a level road while a small brass bob hangs from its ceiling at 26° to the vertical. Later, the van climbs a straight 14° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 45 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.5. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 20 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 560 N toward the stop line. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg => a = g tan θ.
Obtains 4.78 m s⁻².
Applies μ_s mg = m v_max² / R.
Obtains 14.8 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts resistive work F_res(πR) from initial kinetic energy ½mu².
Obtains 16.7 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By resolving forces on the bob, calculate the horizontal acceleration when the string hangs at 26° to the vertical.
Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular road without sliding.
Calculate the speed of the van when it reaches the stop line at the end of the semicircular bend.

items.stem: A $76.0\text{ kg}$ weather probe falls vertically through the lower atmosphere ($g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$) before opening a small parachute. Its motion follows the two-stage velocity–time graph shown. At point P, the upward air drag is $450\text{ N}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $W = 745.6\text{ N}$, $F = 295.6\text{ N}$, $a = 3.89 m s⁻²$. (b) Drag grows with speed until equal to weight at terminal velocity and opening the parachute creates an upward resultant force; SUVAT is invalid and total distance equals area under the $v\text{–}t$ curve.

markScheme.criterion: Calculate weight $W = 76.0 \times 9.81 = 746\text{ N}$.
Find downward resultant $F = W - 450 = 296\text{ N}$ and divide by $76.0\text{ kg}$.
Acceleration $= 3.89 m s⁻²$.
L1 (Area 1): As speed grows, upward drag increases, decreasing downward resultant force (mg − D) and acceleration (N2L).
L1 (Area 1): At Q, drag equals constant weight -> zero resultant force -> constant terminal speed (N1L).
L2 (Area 2): Opening drogue parachute raises drag well above weight, producing an upward resultant force and downward deceleration (N2L).
L2 (Area 2): As speed falls, drag decreases until drag equals weight again at a lower constant terminal speed S.
L3 (Area 3): Explains direction stays downwards because deceleration reduces positive downward speed toward vT2 rather than reversing it.
L3 (Area 3): Notes SUVAT equations cannot be used (non-uniform acceleration); distance fallen is found from area under the v–t curve.

parts.prompt: Calculate the downward acceleration of the probe at point P.
workingSteps: Downward resultant force $F = W - D = 296 N$.

parts.prompt: Explain using Newton's laws why the probe's acceleration falls to zero at Q, why opening the drogue parachute at R reduces its speed without reversing its direction of motion, and how to find total distance fallen from the graph.
parts.expectedAnswer: Drag grows with speed until equal to weight at terminal velocity and opening the parachute creates an upward resultant force. During descent from release through P, increasing air drag cuts the downward resultant force $mg - D$ until at Q drag equals weight, giving zero resultant force and constant terminal speed (N1L). Deploying the drogue canopy at R sharply increases area and upward drag above weight, giving an upward resultant force and deceleration (N2L) that slows the downward velocity—it never reverses direction because drag falls back to $mg$ while velocity is still downwards, establishing a lower terminal speed at S. Because acceleration is non-uniform, SUVAT equations are invalid and total distance fallen is found from the area under the $v\text{–}t$ graph.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Drag increases with speed -> downward resultant drops -> at Q drag = weight -> zero acceleration (N1L).
Area 2 (L2): Drogue opens -> drag >> weight -> upward resultant decelerates downward motion -> drag drops until D = mg at lower terminal speed S.
Area 3 (L3): Velocity stays downward (deceleration != upward motion) and distance equals area under v-t curve (SUVAT invalid).

items.stem: A brass block of mass 5.5 kg slides from rest down a wooden slope of length 7.5 m inclined at 22° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 4.45 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. If the block is instead released from rest halfway down the slope, calculate its speed at the bottom.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 22° − ½mv² = 97.1 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 7.5 = 13.0 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.15 m s⁻¹. Target = 3.15 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 3.15 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: A metal block of mass 10.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a straight incline of length 8 m, inclined at 24° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 4.39 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy dissipated against friction during the slide.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 24° = 335 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(10.5)(4.39)² = 101 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 234 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 24°)L, μ = 0.311. Target = 234 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 24° accurately to obtain 234 J (C).

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 15 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough wooden ramp. The slope has length 4.5 m and is inclined at 26° to the horizontal. It slides against a constant friction force and reaches the bottom at 3.11 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mgL sin θ − ½mv².
Obtains 217 J.
Divides dissipated energy from (a) by ramp length L.
Obtains 48.3 N.
Recognizes unchanged acceleration and applies v² ∝ s => v_new = v / √2.
Obtains 2.20 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 2.7 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.7 m on a strong string. At the lowest point, its speed is 6 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 2.7 × 6² / 0.7 = 139 N, so T = 139 + 2.7 × 9.8 = 165 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 165 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A uniform concrete drainage channel of length L = 2.80 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a semi-annular cross-section of outer diameter D = 20.0 cm and inner diameter d = 12.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2400 kg m⁻³. It is uniform along its length, so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. An electric winch motor of electrical input power 420 W and efficiency 75% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.01005 m², V = A L = 0.02815 m³, m = ρ V = 67.56 kg ≈ 67.6 kg. (b) W = 662.7 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 331.4 N ≈ 331 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.400 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 927.8 J ≈ 928 J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.75 × 420 = 315.0 W, so t = 927.8 / 315.0 = 2.945 s ≈ 2.95 s. (e) density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

markScheme.criterion: Computes semi-annular cross-section A = (π/8)(D² − d²) = 0.01005 m² with cm → m conversion.
Calculates V = A L = 0.02815 m³ and substitutes m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 67.56 kg rounding clearly to 67.6 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 2.80 = m g × 1.400.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 331 N (4 s.f. 331.4 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.400 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 928 J (4 s.f. 927.8 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 315.0 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 2.95 s (4 s.f. 2.945 s).
States valid physical assumption: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 2.4 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.7 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 1.92 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy lost during the collision.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 5.77 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 3.21 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.525 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 17.8 J. Target = 17.8 J.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 17.8 J (B).

items.stem: A non-uniform reinforced concrete beam of length L = 3.20 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a rectangular cross-section of width w = 22.0 cm and thickness h = 12.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2420 kg m⁻³. Its centre of gravity G lies at distance x = 1.41 m from end A. An overhead crane motor of electrical input power 720 W and efficiency 80% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.02640 m², V = A L = 0.08448 m³, m = ρ V = 204.4 kg ≈ 204 kg. (b) W = 2006 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 882.5 N ≈ 882 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.408 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 2824 J ≈ 2.82 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.80 × 720 = 576.0 W, so t = 2824 / 576.0 = 4.903 s ≈ 4.90 s. (e) electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates cross-section A = 0.02640 m², volume V = 0.08448 m³, and applies m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 204.4 kg confirming 204 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 3.20 = m g × 1.408.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 882 N (4 s.f. 882.5 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.408 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 2.82 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 2824 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 576.0 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 4.90 s (4 s.f. 4.903 s).
Identifies electrical heating in motor windings and mechanical friction in hoist gears.
Links losses to thermal energy dissipated to the surroundings (electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings).

items.stem: In Required Practical 3 using two light gates, a student plots $2h/t$ against $t$ and finds a straight line of gradient 9.92 m s⁻² and vertical intercept 3.16 m s⁻¹. Calculate the percentage difference between this measured value of $g$ and the accepted value $9.81$ m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: From $h = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^2$, rearranging gives $2h/t = gt + 2u$. Thus $g = 9.92$ m s⁻², $u = 3.16 / 2 = 1.58 m s⁻¹$, and percentage difference $= |9.92 - 9.81|/9.81 \times 100\% = 1.12\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates pctDiffG $= 1.12\%$.

items.stem: In an electromagnet-and-trapdoor free-fall experiment (RP3), a steel sphere falls from rest through height $h = 1.45$ m. Because residual magnetism delays release by 11 ms, the electronic timer records 0.5547 s. What apparent value of $g$ is calculated from $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$?
items.workedSolution: $g_{\mathrm{apparent}} = 2h / t^2 = 2(1.45) / (0.5547)^2 = 9.42 m s⁻²$, systematically below 9.81 m s⁻² because the timer started before the ball detached.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates $g = 9.42 m s⁻²$.

items.stem: Two Hookean springs have known spring constants k₁ and k₂. They can be joined in series or in parallel to hold a load F within their elastic limits.
items.workedSolution: Series springs share force with additive extensions reducing stiffness whereas parallel springs share extension with additive forces increasing stiffness. In series, neglecting spring weight, both springs experience the same tension F while total extension adds: x_s = x₁ + x₂ = F/k₁ + F/k₂, giving 1/k_s = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂. In parallel, a rigid horizontal crossbar enforces identical extension x_p while tensions add: F = F₁ + F₂ = (k₁ + k₂)x_p, giving k_p = k₁ + k₂. Since k_p > k_s, for fixed load F the series arrangement stretches further (x_s > x_p) and stores more strain energy (E = ½Fx). Experimentally, measure extension with a clamped vertical metre rule and optical pin/set square to prevent parallax, check unloading to stay below the elastic limit, and extract k_s and k_p from F–x gradients.

markScheme.criterion: L1: States Hooke's law F = kx within the limit of proportionality for each spring.
L1: Identifies equal tension F and additive extensions x_s = x₁ + x₂ in series to derive 1/k_s = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂.
L2: Identifies equal extension x_p and additive forces F = F₁ + F₂ in parallel to derive k_p = k₁ + k₂.
L2: Proves parallel stiffness always exceeds series stiffness so series extension x_s > x_p for fixed load F.
L3: Uses E = ½Fx to show series combination stores greater elastic strain energy under the same load F.
L3: Describes vertical ruler + pointer/set-square parallax control, elastic-limit check on unloading, and F–x graph gradient analysis.

parts.prompt: Derive the effective spring constant for both series and parallel combinations from Hooke's law, compare their extensions and stored elastic strain energies under identical load F, and outline how to verify both equations accurately in the laboratory. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Series springs share force with additive extensions reducing stiffness whereas parallel springs share extension with additive forces increasing stiffness. In series, neglecting spring weight, both springs experience the same tension F while total extension adds: x_s = x₁ + x₂ = F/k₁ + F/k₂, giving 1/k_s = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂. In parallel, a rigid horizontal crossbar enforces identical extension x_p while tensions add: F = F₁ + F₂ = (k₁ + k₂)x_p, giving k_p = k₁ + k₂. Since k_p > k_s, for fixed load F the series arrangement stretches further (x_s > x_p) and stores more strain energy (E = ½Fx). Experimentally, measure extension with a clamped vertical metre rule and optical pin/set square to prevent parallax, check unloading to stay below the elastic limit, and extract k_s and k_p from F–x gradients.
workingSteps: Derive 1/k_s = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂ using equal tension and additive extensions.
Derive k_p = k₁ + k₂ using equal extension and additive tensions.
Compare x and E = ½Fx at fixed F, and describe parallax-free graphical F–x verification.

items.stem: The graph plots thinking distance, braking distance, and total stopping distance against initial speed $v$. Assume a constant reaction time and a constant braking force. Which statement correctly describes how these distances depend on speed?
items.workedSolution: During reaction time the car moves at constant speed (d_think = vt_r ∝ v); during braking F d_brake = ½mv² gives d_brake ∝ v². Therefore the correct statement is: Thinking distance is directly proportional to speed whereas braking distance is proportional to speed squared at constant braking force.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: thinking distance is directly proportional to speed whereas braking distance is proportional to speed squared at constant braking force.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the torque τ of a constant force F acting on a rigid body pivoted at O?
items.workedSolution: Torque is defined as τ = Fr sin θ, where r sin θ is the perpendicular lever arm from the pivot to the line of action of F. Therefore the correct statement is: About any chosen axis O, torque equals force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, producing zero torque when the line of action passes through the pivot.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: torque equals force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, producing zero torque when the line of action passes through the pivot.

items.stem: A football is kicked from a level sports field at 18 m s⁻¹ and 62° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the speed of the projectile at the highest point of its path.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 62° = 8.45 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 62°)² / (2g) = 12.9 m. Target = 8.45 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 62° at apex to obtain 8.45 m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the projectile stops completely for an instant at its highest point, forgetting its constant horizontal velocity u cos θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses u sin θ instead of u cos θ for the speed at the apex.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumes speed remains equal to launch speed u throughout the flight.

Obtains 21.2 m s⁻¹.
Applies T = 2u_y / g.
Obtains 4.33 s.
Multiplies u cos θ by flight time T.
Obtains 136 m.

The rope stretches by a maximum extension of 0.85 m in 0.28 s before the cylinder stops at the lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Uses free-fall relation v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 8.86 m s⁻¹.
Equates mg(L + x) = ½kx² over the complete vertical drop.
Obtains 1.05 × 10³ N m⁻¹.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a non-uniform rod of length L = 3.6 m and mass 22 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light vertical wires at A and B. The wires are 2.9 m apart. Its centre of gravity G lies 2.09 m to the right of A and 0.81 m to the left of B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Without carrying out a full calculation, which statement correctly compares the tensions in the two wires?
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about the centre of gravity G gives T₁ d_A = T₂ d_B, so the wire with the smaller distance to G carries the larger tension: wire B carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire B.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly concludes that wire B carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire B.

options.text: In horizontal equilibrium, wire B carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire B.

options.label: B
options.text: Wire A carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is farther from wire A.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the inverse lever-arm relation; the support closer to G bears the larger share of weight.

options.label: C

options.distractorRationale: Horizontal equilibrium requires zero net moment, which forces unequal tensions when G is off-centre.

options.label: D

options.distractorRationale: Moment balance directly couples the tension ratio to the distances of G from each wire.

items.stem: A brass bob of mass 2.2 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 2 m on a light nylon cord. The cord breaks if the tension exceeds 95 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the bob at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((95/2.2) − 9.81) × 2] = 8.17 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 8.17 m s⁻¹ (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds g instead of subtracting g when rearranging T_max − mg = mv²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a control wheel bar has length d = 0.48 m. Two equal and opposite parallel forces of magnitude F = 150 N act perpendicularly at its ends. What is the combined mechanical effect of this couple acting alone on the free bar?
items.workedSolution: A rigid body acted on only by this couple experiences zero resultant force but a non-zero resultant torque causing rotational motion.

markScheme.criterion: A rigid body acted on only by this couple experiences zero resultant force but a non-zero resultant torque causing rotational motion.

items.stem: A sled of weight 1360 N slides at a constant speed down a snowy slope. The slope has length 25 m and vertical height 7 m. Calculate the magnitude of the resistive force opposing motion along the slope.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed ΔE_k = 0. Potential energy lost = W h = 1360 × 7 = 9.52 × 10³ J. Parallel equilibrium gives F_res = W sin θ = W h / L = 381 N. Target = 381 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses sin θ = 7/25 and zero net force to obtain 381 N (D).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 1.8 m and mass 4 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 9.5 kg hangs so its centre of gravity acts 1.4 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at 54° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about O give T = 113.8 N ≈ 114 N. (b) Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos θ = 66.92 N ≈ 66.9 N. (c) Vertical balance: R_y = W_total − T sin θ = 40.33 N ≈ 40.3 N.

markScheme.criterion: Writes full moment balance about hinge O including both rod and sign moments with T sin θ.
Evaluates T = 113.8 N (114 N) showing agreement with 1.1 × 10² N.
Applies horizontal equilibrium R_x = T cos θ.
R_x = 66.9 N away from the wall.
Applies vertical equilibrium R_y = W_total − T sin θ.
R_y = 40.3 N upwards.

items.stem: A metal block of mass 14 kg is released from rest at the top of a straight incline of length 11.5 m, inclined at 28° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 8.44 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the coefficient of kinetic friction μ (defined by F_f = μ R) between the block and the incline.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 28° = 741 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(14)(8.44)² = 499 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 243 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 28°)L, μ = 0.174. Target = 0.174.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 28° accurately to obtain 0.174 (C).

items.stem: In Required Practical 4, a metal alloy wire has length $(2.60 \pm 0.002)$ m. Perpendicular micrometer readings give mean diameters 0.34 mm, 0.32 mm, and 0.33 mm (uncertainty $\pm 0.01$ mm). The $F$ against $e$ graph has percentage uncertainty 1.6% in its gradient. Calculate the total percentage uncertainty in the Young modulus $E$.
items.workedSolution: Mean diameter $d = 0.33$ mm gives $A = \pi d^2/4 = 8.55 × 10⁻⁸ m²$. $E = L \times \mathrm{grad} / A = 210 GPa$. Percentage uncertainty $\%\Delta E = \%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad} = 0.0769 + 2(3.03) + 1.6 = 7.74\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates pctUncE $= 7.74\%$.

items.stem: A spinning space probe with extended sensor arms has moment of inertia 32.0 kg m² and spins at 1.80 rad s⁻¹ with zero external torque. Internal motors pull the arms inward, reducing the moment of inertia to 12.0 kg m².
items.workedSolution: (a) $\omega_2 = 4.80 rad s⁻¹$. (b) Work done $= \frac{1}{2}I_2\omega_2^2 - \frac{1}{2}I_1\omega_1^2 = 86.4 J$. (c) Internal radial forces do positive work pulling masses inward so rotational kinetic energy increases.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$.
Obtains $\omega_2 = 4.80 rad s⁻¹$.
Calculates initial rotational KE $\frac{1}{2}I_1\omega_1^2$.
Calculates final rotational KE $\frac{1}{2}I_2\omega_2^2$ and finds difference.
Obtains internal work $= 86.4 J$.
Explains that internal radial forces produce zero torque about the spin axis.
States that internal radial forces do positive work pulling the pods inward.

items.stem: A parcel of weight 450 N slides down a straight slope at a constant speed of 2.5 m s⁻¹. The ramp is 10 m long and drops by 2.5 m vertically. Calculate the magnitude of the friction force acting up the ramp.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed, friction balances downslope weight: F_f = W(h/L) = 450 × (2.5/10) = 113 N. Rate of thermal energy generation P = F_f v = 281 W. Target = 113 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_f = Wh/L and P = F_f v to obtain 113 N (B).

items.stem: A small smooth steel sphere is released from rest into a tall cylinder of viscous oil and reaches constant terminal velocity. Which force relationship describes the sphere at terminal velocity?
items.workedSolution: As speed increases, F_d = 6πηrv rises until F_b + F_d = F_g, giving zero net force and constant terminal speed. Therefore the correct statement is: At terminal velocity upward buoyancy Fb and upward viscous drag Fd balance downward gravitational weight Fg so acceleration is zero.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: at terminal velocity upward buoyancy Fb and upward viscous drag Fd balance downward gravitational weight Fg so acceleration is zero.

options.label: A
options.text: Upward viscous drag Fd alone balances downward weight Fg because buoyancy vanishes once the sphere moves.
options.distractorRationale: Archimedes buoyancy Fb = ρVg depends on displaced volume and remains active whether the sphere is moving or stationary.

options.label: B
options.text: Downward weight Fg strictly exceeds the sum of buoyancy Fb and viscous drag Fd to keep the sphere moving downwards.
options.distractorRationale: Constant velocity implies zero resultant force; no net downward force is required to sustain steady motion.

options.label: C
options.text: Upward buoyancy Fb grows linearly with speed until it equals gravitational weight Fg while drag remains negligible.
options.distractorRationale: Buoyancy is constant for a sphere completely below the surface; it is Stokes viscous drag Fd = 6πηrv that grows linearly with speed.

options.label: D
options.text: At terminal velocity upward buoyancy Fb and upward viscous drag Fd balance downward gravitational weight Fg so acceleration is zero.

items.stem: The diagram shows the rotor of a heavy mechanical brake wheel. Its central hub has moment of inertia 2.40 kg m² and carries 4 rim masses of 2.50 kg each at radius 0.480 m. Over 9.00 s, its rotational speed changes uniformly from 16.0 rev s⁻¹ to 4.00 rev s⁻¹ against a constant bearing friction torque of 3.20 N m.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I = 4.70 kg m²$. (b) $|\alpha| = \frac{2\pi|f_2 - f_1|}{t} = 8.38 rad s⁻²$. (c) Applied torque $T_{\mathrm{app}} = 36.2 N m$. (d) Peak power $P_{\max} = T_{\mathrm{app}}\omega_{\max} = 3.64 × 10³ W$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $I = I_{\mathrm{hub}} + \sum m r^2$ with squared radius.
Obtains $I = 4.70 kg m²$.
Converts $\text{rev s}^{-1}$ to $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ via $2\pi$ and divides change by $t$.
Obtains $|\alpha| = 8.38 rad s⁻²$.
Combines $I|\alpha|$ with bearing friction torque in the correct sense.
Obtains applied torque $= 36.2 N m$.
Applies $P = T\omega$ at the highest angular speed.
Obtains maximum power $= 3.64 × 10³ W$.

items.stem: A wind-tunnel fan of moment of inertia $I = 2.40\text{ kg m}^2$ speeds non-uniformly from $10.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ to $70.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ over $t_1 = 6.00\text{ s}$ along $\omega(t) = 10.0 + 60.0\left[2(t/6.00) - (t/6.00)^2\right]$. At $t = 3.00\text{ s}$, the tangent rises by $30.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ across a $3.00\text{ s}$ horizontal run.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\alpha = 30.0 / 3.00 = 10.0 rad s⁻²$. (b) $T = 2.40 \times 10.0 = 24.0 N m$. (c) decreasing gradient shows net torque falling as resistive drag torque increases toward driving torque.

markScheme.criterion: Uses tangent gradient $\Delta\omega / \Delta t = 30.0 / 3.00$.
Correct angular acceleration 10.0 rad s⁻².
Substitutes into $T = I\alpha$.
Correct net torque 24.0 N m.
Notes resistive drag torque increases as $\omega$ rises.
Explains decreasing gradient shows net torque falling as resistive drag torque increases toward driving torque.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a heavy non-uniform trapdoor of length L = 2 m and mass 20 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.84 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 36° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the angle above the horizontal at which the resultant reaction force R from hinge O acts.
items.workedSolution: Moments about O: T cos 36° × 2 = 20 × 9.81 × 0.84 ⇒ T = 101.9 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T sin 36° = 59.87 N. Vertical balance: R_y = 20 × 9.81 − T cos 36° = 113.8 N. Resultant R = √(R_x² + R_y²) = 128.6 N ≈ 129 N, at angle α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 62.25° ≈ 62.3° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 62.3°.

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 10 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 3.6 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the cord becomes taut, and then stretches it by 0.7 m in 0.18 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward force exerted by the cord between A and B.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.8 × 3.6) = 8.40 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.18 + 10(9.8) = 565 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 565 N (A).

items.stem: A van of mass 1200 kg accelerates along a level road while a small brass bob hangs from its ceiling at 26° to the vertical. Later, the van climbs a straight 14° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 45 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.5. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 21 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 530 N toward the stop line. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 26°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 26° = ma and T cos 26° = mg => a = g tan 26° = 4.78 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.5 × 9.81 × 45) = 14.9 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1200)(21)² / 530 = 499 m. Target = 4.78 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 4.78 m s⁻² (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: A lead bob of mass 3 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.6 m attached to a light steel cable. The maximum tension the cable can hold without breaking is 83 N. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Writes T_max − mg = m v_max² / r at the lowest point.
Obtains 5.35 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By considering the forces acting on the bob at the lowest point, calculate the maximum speed at the bottom so the cable does not break.

items.stem: A small steel ball of mass 1.7 kg hangs on a light string of length 2.2 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a block of clay of mass 1.7 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string just before the ball strikes the clay block.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 6.57 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 50.0 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 3.28 m s⁻¹. Target = 50.0 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 50.0 N (A).

items.stem: A signal canister is fired at 22 m s⁻¹ at 35° above the horizontal from the top of a 40 m vertical cliff above the sea. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) t = 4.42 s. (b) range = 79.6 m. (c) v = 35.6 m s⁻¹. (d) air resistance opposes motion continuously, reducing both maximum height and horizontal range while producing an asymmetric path with a steeper downward descent.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves u_y = 22 sin 35° and forms 4.905t² − 12.62t − 40 = 0.
Solves quadratic for positive root t = 4.42 s.
Multiplies u_x = 22 cos 35° by flight time.
Obtains range = 79.6 m.
Calculates impact speed v = 35.6 m s⁻¹.
States both maximum height and horizontal range decrease.
Notes the trajectory becomes asymmetric with a steeper final descent.

items.stem: A metal block of mass 10 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 2.4 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.85 m in 0.24 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the spring constant of the cord.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 2.4 + 0.85 = 3.25 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 882 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 749 N. Target = 882 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (2.4 + 0.85) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 882 N m⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a dockside crane has total length L = 23 m and mass 1000 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 6 m from rear end A. A 2800 kg concrete counterweight sits 4.2 m to the left of P (1.8 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 4.5 m to the right of P (10.5 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 14.5 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum safe load mass at the hook for rotational equilibrium about P.
items.workedSolution: Anticlockwise counterweight moment about P: M_cw = 2800 × 9.81 × 4.2 = 1.154 × 10⁵ N m. Clockwise boom moment: M_boom = 1000 × 9.81 × 4.5 = 4.415 × 10⁴ N m. Remaining clockwise moment available for load: W_max × 14.5 = 7.122 × 10⁴ N m ⇒ W_max = 4912 N ≈ 4.91 × 10³ N, m_max = W_max / 9.81 = 500.7 kg ≈ 501 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct maximum safe load mass = 501 kg.

items.stem: A ball is launched from floor level across a flat room at 45 m s⁻¹ and 33° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the speed of the projectile at the highest point of its path.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 33° = 37.7 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 33°)² / (2g) = 30.6 m. Target = 37.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 33° at apex to obtain 37.7 m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the projectile stops completely for an instant at its highest point, forgetting its constant horizontal velocity u cos θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses u sin θ instead of u cos θ for the speed at the apex.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumes speed remains equal to launch speed u throughout the flight.

items.stem: A brass ball of mass 0.6 kg hangs from a light string of length 1.4 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the lowest point, it collides with and sticks to a wax block of mass 1.2 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mgL = ½mu² => u = √(2gL).
Obtains 5.24 m s⁻¹.
Finds v = mu/(m+M) from momentum conservation and evaluates ½mu² − ½(m+M)v².
Obtains 5.49 J.
Applies h = v² / (2g).
Obtains 0.156 m.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform steel bar AB has total length L = 4.8 m and mass 19 kg. Its centre of gravity G is at its midpoint, 2.4 m from end A. It rests horizontally on a sharp pivot P at 1.34 m from end A. A counterbalance block of unknown mass sits 0.34 m from end A. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the upward reaction force R exerted by pivot P on the balanced beam.
items.workedSolution: Take moments about pivot P. Lever arm of beam CG is d_G = 2.4 − 1.34 = 1.060 m. Lever arm of counterbalance is d_load = 1.34 − 0.34 = 1.000 m. Balancing moments: m_load g d_load = m_beam g d_G ⇒ m_load = (19 × 1.060) / 1.000 = 20.14 kg ≈ 20.1 kg. Vertical equilibrium gives R = (m_beam + m_load)g = (19 + 20.14) × 9.81 = 384.0 N ≈ 384 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct upward pivot reaction R = 384 N.

items.stem: A sandbag of mass 2 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 4 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the cord becomes taut, and then stretches it by 1.4 m in 0.18 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward force exerted by the cord between A and B.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.81 × 4) = 8.86 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.18 + 2(9.81) = 118 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 118 N (A).

items.stem: When analysing an isolated oblique collision recorded on a stroboscopic video, how do elastic and inelastic collisions compare?
items.workedSolution: Vector momentum is conserved in every isolated collision; checking Σp²/(2m) before and after identifies whether kinetic energy was conserved. Therefore the correct statement is: Both elastic and inelastic collisions conserve total vector momentum whereas only an elastic collision conserves total kinetic energy.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: both elastic and inelastic collisions conserve total vector momentum whereas only an elastic collision conserves total kinetic energy.

options.label: A
options.text: Both elastic and inelastic collisions conserve total vector momentum whereas only an elastic collision conserves total kinetic energy.

options.label: B
options.text: An elastic collision conserves kinetic energy without conserving momentum whereas an inelastic collision conserves only momentum.
options.distractorRationale: All isolated collisions obey Newton's third law and conserve total vector momentum.

options.label: C
options.text: Total energy is destroyed in an inelastic collision while momentum doubles to compensate.
options.distractorRationale: Total energy is always conserved; in an inelastic collision kinetic energy transfers into thermal or sound stores.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither kinetic energy nor vector momentum is conserved whenever particles deflect in two dimensions.
options.distractorRationale: Vector momentum is always conserved in an isolated two-dimensional collision.

items.stem: On a smooth level track, cart X of mass 3 kg moves to the right at 9 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with cart Y of mass 4.2 kg moving to the left at 5.5 m s⁻¹ (arrow not shown). Immediately after the collision, cart Y moves right at 4 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of cart X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward as positive: p_before = (3)(9) + (4.2)(−5.5) = 3.90 kg m s⁻¹. From p_before = (3)v_X + (4.2)(4), v_X = -4.30 m s⁻¹, which is 4.30 m s⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: Uses signed head-on momentum p_before = 3.90 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 4.30 m s⁻¹ to the left (B).

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform wooden plank of total length L = 4.8 m and mass 48 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is at the left end, and support B is 3.4 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 1.4 m. A technician of mass 60 kg initially stands 1.5 m from the left end of the plank. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the upward reaction force F₁ exerted by support A.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: F₁ × 3.4 = (48 × 1.000 + 60 × 1.900) × 9.81 ⇒ F₁ = 467.4 N ≈ 467 N. At tipping (F₁ = 0): m_load × d_tip = m_beam × (x_B − x_G) ⇒ d_tip = (48 × 1.000) / 60 = 0.8000 m ≈ 0.800 m. At the very tip (overhang 1.4 m): m_end = (48 × 1.000) / 1.4 = 34.29 kg ≈ 34.3 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct solver-verified answer = 467 N.

items.stem: A steel ball is fired from a spring launcher on level ground at 26 m s⁻¹ and 56° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the ground.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 26 sin 56° = 21.6 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 26 cos 56° = 14.5 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 4.40 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 64.0 m. Target = 64.0 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 64.0 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies horizontal speed by ascent time u sin θ / g instead of full flight time 2u sin θ / g.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cos θ for sin θ in the flight-time expression.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: A van of mass 1400 kg accelerates along a level road while a small brass bob hangs from its ceiling at 18° to the vertical. Later, the van climbs a straight 14° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 50 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.7. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 16 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 500 N toward the stop line. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 18°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 18° = ma and T cos 18° = mg => a = g tan 18° = 3.18 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.7 × 9.8 × 50) = 18.5 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1400)(16)² / 500 = 358 m. Target = 3.18 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 3.18 m s⁻² (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: On the skydiver's velocity–time graph, the curve flattens into a horizontal plateau at point Q. Which force condition explains this horizontal section?
items.workedSolution: At terminal velocity Q, upward drag equals downward weight so resultant force is zero and velocity is constant (Newton's first law). Therefore option C is correct: upward drag equals downward weight so resultant force is zero and velocity is constant.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: upward drag equals downward weight so resultant force is zero and velocity is constant.

items.stem: A rubber block of mass 11.5 kg slides from rest down a rough concrete slope of length 4.5 m inclined at 38° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 4.79 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. If the block is instead released from rest halfway down the slope, calculate its speed at the bottom.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 38° − ½mv² = 181 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 4.5 = 40.1 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.39 m s⁻¹. Target = 3.39 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 3.39 m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: A stone block of mass 14.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough wooden slope of length 8.5 m, inclined at 32° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 6.3 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy dissipated against friction during the slide.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 32° = 640 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(14.5)(6.3)² = 288 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 352 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 32°)L, μ = 0.344. Target = 352 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 32° accurately to obtain 352 J (A).
