items.stem: A lead bob of mass 0.7 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.7 m on a light steel cable. At the lowest point, its speed is 6.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the cable at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 0.7 × 6.5² / 1.7 = 17.4 N, so T = 17.4 + 0.7 × 9.8 = 24.3 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 24.3 N (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A uniform limestone channel of length L = 3.00 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a semi-annular cross-section of outer diameter D = 25.0 cm and inner diameter d = 15.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2480 kg m⁻³. It is uniform along its length, so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. A compact crane motor of electrical input power 620 W and efficiency 82% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.01571 m², V = A L = 0.04712 m³, m = ρ V = 116.9 kg ≈ 117 kg. (b) W = 1146 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 573.2 N ≈ 573 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.500 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 1720 J ≈ 1.72 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.82 × 620 = 508.4 W, so t = 1720 / 508.4 = 3.383 s ≈ 3.38 s. (e) density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

markScheme.criterion: Computes semi-annular cross-section A = (π/8)(D² − d²) = 0.01571 m² with cm → m conversion.
Calculates V = A L = 0.04712 m³ and substitutes m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 116.9 kg rounding clearly to 117 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 3.00 = m g × 1.500.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 573 N (4 s.f. 573.2 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.500 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 1.72 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 1720 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 508.4 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 3.38 s (4 s.f. 3.383 s).
States valid physical assumption: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

items.stem: A small steel ball of mass 2.2 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.5 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a block of clay of mass 1.76 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height above the lowest point reached by the joined objects.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 5.42 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 3.01 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.463 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 14.4 J. Target = 0.463 m.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 0.463 m (C).

items.stem: A uniform stone drainage channel of length L = 2.60 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a semi-annular cross-section of outer diameter D = 22.0 cm and inner diameter d = 12.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2780 kg m⁻³. It is uniform along its length, so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. A mobile crane motor of electrical input power 580 W and efficiency 80% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.01335 m², V = A L = 0.03471 m³, m = ρ V = 96.51 kg ≈ 96.5 kg. (b) W = 946.7 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 473.4 N ≈ 473 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.300 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 1231 J ≈ 1.23 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.80 × 580 = 464.0 W, so t = 1231 / 464.0 = 2.652 s ≈ 2.65 s. (e) electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates cross-section A = 0.01335 m², volume V = 0.03471 m³, and applies m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 96.51 kg confirming 96.5 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 2.60 = m g × 1.300.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 473 N (4 s.f. 473.4 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.300 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 1.23 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 1231 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 464.0 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 2.65 s (4 s.f. 2.652 s).
Identifies electrical heating in motor windings and mechanical friction in hoist gears.
Links losses to thermal energy dissipated to the surroundings (electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings).

items.stem: In Required Practical 3, a student drops a dense steel sphere through two light gates and plots $2h/t$ against $t$. The best-fit straight line has gradient 9.74 m s⁻² (with percentage uncertainty 2.1%) and vertical intercept 2.28 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $u = 2.28/2 = 1.14 m s⁻¹$. (b) $\Delta g = 0.205 m s⁻²$. (c) Percentage difference $= 0.714\%$ (smaller than the 2.1% experimental uncertainty, so result is consistent with 9.81 m s⁻²). (d) use a plumb line to align the metre ruler vertically and plot two h over t against t so the gradient equals gravitational field strength independently of initial speed.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies vertical intercept equals $2u$.
Initial speed $u = 1.14 m s⁻¹$.
Multiplies measured $g$ by fractional uncertainty.
Absolute uncertainty $\Delta g = 0.205 m s⁻²$.
Computes $|g_{\mathrm{meas}} - 9.81|/9.81 \times 100\%$.
Percentage difference $= 0.714\%$.
Uses a plumb line / set square against bench to ensure ruler is completely vertical.
Shows $2h/t = gt + 2u$ keeps gradient equal to $g$ regardless of initial speed $u$.

parts.prompt: Determine the speed $u$ of the sphere as it crossed the upper light gate.
Calculate the absolute uncertainty in the measured value of $g$.
Calculate the percentage difference between the measured $g$ and accepted value $9.81$ m s⁻².
Explain how the ruler is aligned vertically and why plotting $2h/t$ against $t$ removes error from the unknown release height above Gate 1.
parts.expectedAnswer: use a plumb line to align the metre ruler vertically and plot two h over t against t so the gradient equals gravitational field strength independently of initial speed
workingSteps: Align clamped metre ruler against a plumb line (reject bare 'pendulum').
2h/t = gt + 2u separates unknown u into the vertical intercept while gradient stays g.

items.stem: In the electromagnet-and-trapdoor arrangement of Required Practical 3, plotting drop height $h$ against $t^2$ produces a straight line of gradient 4.84 m s⁻². In an individual drop from $h = 1.45$ m, the digital timer records 0.5547 s because residual magnetism delays release by 11 ms.
items.workedSolution: (a) $g = 2 \times 4.84 = 9.68 m s⁻²$. (b) Percentage difference $= 1.33\%$. (c) Single drop gives $g = 9.42 m s⁻²$. (d) residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $g = 2 \times \mathrm{gradient}$.
Measured $g = 9.68 m s⁻²$.
Divides absolute discrepancy by accepted $9.81$ m s⁻².
Percentage difference $= 1.33\%$.
Substitutes into $g = 2h/t^2$.
Apparent $g = 9.42 m s⁻²$.
Residual magnetism delays release so recorded $t$ is systematically too large.
Suggests reducing electromagnet current / inserting paper spacer / using two light gates.

Calculate the percentage difference between this graph value and $9.81$ m s⁻².
Calculate the apparent value of $g$ obtained from the single drop at $h = 1.45$ m.
Explain why residual magnetism produces a systematic underestimate of $g$ and suggest one way to minimise it.
parts.expectedAnswer: residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g; minimise by reducing electromagnet current to the minimum needed to hold the sphere or inserting a thin sheet of paper.
workingSteps: Timer starts when current switches off, before sphere detaches -> t too large -> 2h/t² too small.
Use minimum holding current / paper spacer / switch to two light gates.

items.stem: Two springs $k_1$ and $k_2$ are tested first in series and then in parallel under the same hanging weight $F$. Which comparison between the two arrangements is always true?
items.workedSolution: Because k_p = k₁ + k₂ > k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂) = k_s for all positive k₁, k₂, the parallel combination is always stiffer and extends less. Therefore the correct statement is: Combining two springs in parallel always produces a stiffer system with smaller extension than connecting the same springs in series.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: combining two springs in parallel always produces a stiffer system with smaller extension than connecting the same springs in series.

options.label: A
options.text: Combining two springs in parallel always produces a stiffer system with smaller extension than connecting the same springs in series.

options.label: B
options.text: Connecting two springs in series always produces a stiffer combination with smaller extension than connecting them in parallel.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses springs with electrical resistors; parallel springs add stiffness (k₁ + k₂) while series springs reduce stiffness.

options.label: C
options.text: Both series and parallel arrangements extend by the exact same distance because the hanging load F is identical.
options.distractorRationale: Series extension is F/k₁ + F/k₂, which is always larger than parallel extension F/(k₁ + k₂).

options.label: D
options.text: The parallel system stores more elastic strain energy than the series system under the same hanging load F.
options.distractorRationale: Since E = ½Fx and F is identical, the larger series extension stores more elastic energy than the parallel system.

items.stem: A 1500 kg family estate car travels at 24.0 m s⁻¹ along a level highway. Seeing a hazard ahead, the driver reacts in 0.750 s and brakes uniformly at 6.00 m s⁻² to a complete halt.
items.workedSolution: (a) d_think = 18.0 m. (b) d_stop = 66.0 m. (c) F_b = 9.00 × 10³ N. (d) work done by the braking force equals initial kinetic energy so braking distance equals mv squared divided by 2F.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates thinking distance 18.0 m.
Computes braking distance v²/(2a) = 48.0 m.
Sums to total stopping distance 66.0 m.
Applies F = ma (or F d_brake = ½mv²).
Obtains braking force 9.00 × 10³ N.
Equates work done by braking force F d_brake to kinetic energy ½mv².
Deduces d_brake = mv²/(2F) ∝ v² (work done by the braking force equals initial kinetic energy so braking distance equals mv squared divided by 2F).

items.stem: A heavy block of mass 8.5 kg is attached to a rubber rope of natural length 1.8 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 1.35 m in 0.32 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum tension in the rope at the lowest point B.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 1.8 + 1.35 = 3.15 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 288 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 389 N. Target = 389 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (1.8 + 1.35) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 389 N (B).

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 1.2 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.8 m on a strong string. The string breaks if the tension exceeds 33 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the ball at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((33/1.2) − 9.81) × 0.8] = 3.76 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 1.6 m and mass 11 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 6.5 kg hangs so its centre of gravity acts 1.3 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at 44° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the vertical upward component of force exerted on the rod by hinge O.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about hinge O: T sin 44° × 1.6 = (11 × 0.8 + 6.5 × 1.3) × 9.81 = 169.2 N m. Hence T sin 44° = 105.8 N and T = 152.3 N ≈ 152 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos 44° = 109.5 N ≈ 110 N. Vertical balance: R_y = (11 + 6.5) × 9.81 − 105.8 = 65.91 N ≈ 65.9 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 65.9 N.

items.stem: A wooden crate of mass 10 kg is released from rest at the top of a steel ramp. The slope is 11.5 m long and inclined at 36° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 8.41 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = mgL sin θ.
Obtains 663 J.
Subtracts ½mv² from ΔE_p.
Obtains 309 J.
Applies W_f = μ(mg cos θ)L.
Obtains 0.339.

items.stem: In Searle's Young modulus investigation (RP4), a student tests a steel wire of unstretched length $(2.40 \pm 0.002)$ m. Micrometer diameter readings in perpendicular directions at three places average to 0.42 mm, 0.44 mm, and 0.43 mm (each $\pm 0.01$ mm). A graph of load $F$ against extension $e$ is a straight line through the origin of gradient 12.1 N mm⁻¹ ($\pm 2.0\%$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $A = \pi d^2/4 = 1.45 × 10⁻⁷ m²$. (b) $E = L(\mathrm{grad})/A = 200 GPa$. (c) $\%\Delta E = 6.73\%$. (d) an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while perpendicular micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Averages three diameters and converts mm to m in $A = \pi d^2/4$.
Cross-sectional area $A = 1.45 × 10⁻⁷ m²$.
Converts gradient to N m⁻¹ and substitutes into $E = (L/A)\,\mathrm{grad}$.
Young modulus $E = 200 GPa$.
Combines $\%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad}$.
Percentage uncertainty in $E = 6.73\%$.
Identical reference wire compensates both support sag and temperature expansion.
Perpendicular micrometer readings at >= 3 positions detect non-uniformity/oval cross-section.

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 1.1 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.6 m on a strong string. At the lowest point, its speed is 7 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.1 × 7² / 1.6 = 33.7 N, so T = 33.7 + 1.1 × 9.81 = 44.5 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 44.5 N (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: Two clutch discs rotate in opposite directions on the same frictionless shaft. Disc 1 has $I_1 = 1.20\text{ kg m}^2$ at $+40.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$, and Disc 2 has $I_2 = 1.80\text{ kg m}^2$ at $-10.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$. They engage and reach a common angular speed. How much rotational kinetic energy is lost as thermal energy?
items.workedSolution: Initial angular momentum $L = 1.20(40.0) + 1.80(-10.0) = 30.0\text{ N m s}$, giving $\omega_{\mathrm{f}} = \frac{30.0}{3.00} = 10.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$. Initial KE $= \frac{1}{2}(1.20)(40^2) + \frac{1}{2}(1.80)(10^2) = 1050\text{ J}$; final KE $= \frac{1}{2}(3.00)(10^2) = 150\text{ J}$. Energy dissipated $= 900 J$.

markScheme.criterion: Thermal energy dissipated equals 900 J.

items.stem: A single-cylinder four-stroke diesel generator needs a heavy steel flywheel on its crankshaft. An electric induction motor of the same mean power output does not. The turning-moment graph shows how the diesel engine's torque varies with crankshaft angle.
items.workedSolution: A four-stroke engine produces driving torque on only one of its four strokes while an electric motor gives steady torque. On the turning-moment diagram, the flywheel absorbs excess energy when engine torque exceeds mean load and releases energy during zero-torque strokes. Since $\Delta E = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_{\max}^2 - \omega_{\min}^2) = I\bar{\omega}\Delta\omega$, a large moment of inertia $I$ keeps speed fluctuation $\Delta\omega$ small, balanced against slower deliberate acceleration.

markScheme.criterion: States that a four-stroke engine produces driving torque during only one stroke in four whereas an electric motor provides nearly steady torque.
Notes that torque falls to zero or negative during induction, compression, and exhaust strokes.
Explains from the graph that excess energy above the mean-load line accelerates the flywheel and increases its rotational kinetic energy.
Explains that when engine torque is below the mean load, the flywheel decelerates and supplies energy to keep the shaft turning through compression.
Applies $\Delta E = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_{\max}^2 - \omega_{\min}^2)$ to show that larger moment of inertia $I$ gives a smaller speed fluctuation $\Delta\omega$.
Identifies a valid practical design trade-off such as slower deliberate acceleration or extra mass/bearing load from a very large flywheel.

parts.prompt: Explain why the diesel engine needs a flywheel to maintain steady speed under constant load while the electric motor does not, referencing the turning-moment diagram and the role of moment of inertia in limiting speed fluctuations.
parts.expectedAnswer: A four-stroke diesel cylinder delivers positive driving torque during only one of its four strokes, with negative or near-zero torque during induction, compression, and exhaust, whereas an electric motor supplies nearly continuous torque. On the turning-moment diagram, the flywheel absorbs excess energy when engine torque exceeds mean load and releases energy during zero-torque strokes so the crankshaft continues turning smoothly through compression. Because cyclic energy exchange equals half times moment of inertia times the difference in squared angular speeds, increasing the moment of inertia reduces the angular speed fluctuation for a given energy pulse, although excessive inertia slows deliberate throttle response.
workingSteps: L1: Contrast the single power stroke per two revolutions of a four-stroke engine with the nearly steady torque of an electric motor.
L1: Identify that engine torque falls below the mean load (and goes negative during compression) for most of the cycle.
L2: Link positive shaded areas above the mean-load line to excess work stored as rotational kinetic energy while the flywheel accelerates.
L2: Link regions below the mean-load line to kinetic energy released by the flywheel to drive the load and compress gas.
L3: Use $\Delta E = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_{\max}^2 - \omega_{\min}^2) = I\omega_{\mathrm{mean}}\Delta\omega$ to explain why large $I$ keeps $\Delta\omega$ small.
L3: Note the engineering trade-off that a larger moment of inertia also reduces responsiveness when changing speed deliberately.

items.stem: A foam ball is thrown upwards at an angle through air and reaches the highest point of its path. Which statement correctly describes its resultant acceleration at this highest point?
items.workedSolution: Combining downward weight mg with perpendicular backward horizontal drag gives a resultant force exceeding mg and angled backwards below horizontal. Therefore the correct statement is: At the highest point vertical velocity is zero while horizontal velocity remains non-zero so resultant acceleration exceeds g and tilts opposite to horizontal motion.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: at the highest point vertical velocity is zero while horizontal velocity remains non-zero so resultant acceleration exceeds g and tilts opposite to horizontal motion.

Calculate the tension $T_2$ in the cord angled at $50.0^\circ$ to the horizontal.
Explain why the upward tension in the vertical support wire and the downward weight $F_{\text{g}}$ of the sculpture do not form a Newton third-law pair, stating what defines such a pair.
parts.expectedAnswer: They act on the same sculpture and have different types, whereas a Newton third-law force pair consists of two forces of the same type equal in magnitude and opposite in direction acting on two different bodies.
workingSteps: a Newton third-law force pair consists of two forces of the same type equal in magnitude and opposite in direction acting on two different bodies.

items.stem: A heavy rotating drum experiences a constant bearing friction torque while speeding up and while braking. How does this friction torque combine with the external applied torque in each stage?
items.workedSolution: Because friction always opposes motion, bearing friction opposes rotation and acts alongside a braking torque or against a driving torque: $T_{\mathrm{drive}} - T_{\mathrm{f}} = I\alpha$ during acceleration and $T_{\mathrm{brake}} + T_{\mathrm{f}} = I|\alpha|$ during braking.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that bearing friction opposes rotation and acts alongside a braking torque or against a driving torque.

options.label: A
options.text: Bearing friction opposes rotation and acts alongside a braking torque or against a driving torque.

options.label: B
options.text: Bearing friction always adds to the applied torque so it assists spin-up and opposes braking.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the direction of friction, which always opposes relative motion.

options.label: C
options.text: Bearing friction acts only during braking and becomes zero once a motor drives the axle.
options.distractorRationale: Assumes bearing friction disappears when driven externally.

options.label: D
options.text: Bearing friction cancels out of the rotational equation whenever angular acceleration is uniform.
options.distractorRationale: Neglects dissipative torque in $T_{\mathrm{net}} = I\alpha$.

items.stem: A spring of constant $k = 1600\text{ N m}^{-1}$ compressed by $\Delta x = 0.250\text{ m}$ launches a $2.00\text{ kg}$ block along a rough track and up a vertical rise $h = 1.50\text{ m}$ ($g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$). If $6.60\text{ J}$ is dissipated against resistive forces during the climb, what is the block's speed at the top?
items.workedSolution: Stored elastic energy $E_{\text{H}} = \frac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^2 = 50.0 J$. Gravitational PE gain $\Delta E_{\text{p}} = mgh = 2.00(9.8)(1.50) = 29.4 J$. Remaining $E_{\text{k}} = 50.0 - 29.4 - 6.60 = 14.0 J$, giving $v = \sqrt{2E_{\text{k}}/m} = 3.74 m s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $E_{\text{H}} = \Delta E_{\text{p}} + E_{\text{k}} + W_{\text{loss}}$ at $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to obtain $v = 3.74 m s⁻¹$.

items.stem: Starting from rest, a turntable follows the concave-down curve shown reaching $\omega = 60.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ at $t = 6.00\text{ s}$ (area under the curved section $= 240\text{ rad}$), then spins steadily at $60.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ until $t = 10.0\text{ s}$. Calculate the total angular displacement $\theta$ over the full $10.0\text{ s}$.
items.workedSolution: Cruise area from $6.00\text{ s}$ to $10.0\text{ s}$ is $60.0 \times 4.00 = 240\text{ rad}$. Total $\theta = 240 + 240 = 480 rad$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 480 rad.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a non-uniform access door of length L = 1.8 m and mass 12 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.72 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 30° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) T = 54.37 N ≈ 54.4 N. (b) the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium. (c)(i) R_x = 27.19 N, R_y = 70.63 N, so R = 75.68 N ≈ 75.7 N. (c)(ii) α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 68.95° ≈ 68.9° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Στ = 0 about O using T cos(angle to vertical) × L = m g x_G.
Obtains T = 54.37 N (54.4 N) matching 54 N.
Identifies horizontal component of angled cable tension directed toward the wall.
States hinge must exert an equal opposite horizontal force away from the wall for ΣF_x = 0.
Computes R_x = 27.19 N and R_y = 70.63 N and applies Pythagoras.
Resultant hinge reaction magnitude R = 75.7 N.
Uses tan α = R_y / R_x with both hinge components.
Direction α = 68.9° above the horizontal.

parts.prompt: By taking moments about hinge O, show clearly that the tension T in the cable is approximately 54 N.
workingSteps: Vertical component of cable tension is T cos 30°.
Equate moments about O: T cos 30° × 1.8 = 12 × 9.81 × 0.72.

parts.prompt: Explain why hinge O must exert a horizontal component of force on the door, and state its direction.
parts.expectedAnswer: For horizontal equilibrium, the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium.
workingSteps: Identify that the inclined cable pulls horizontally toward the wall.
Conclude from zero horizontal resultant force that the hinge must push horizontally away from the wall.

Determine the angle above the horizontal at which this resultant hinge force R acts.

items.stem: A steel ball of mass 9 kg is attached to a rubber cord of natural length 1.8 m. It falls freely from rest at the fixed support to point A, where the cord becomes taut. It then stretches the cord by 1.1 m over 0.21 s before stopping at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 5.94 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (9 × 5.94) / 0.21 = 255 N.
Obtains 343 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 465 N.

items.stem: A delivery van of mass 1400 kg accelerates along a level road while a small pendulum bob hangs from its ceiling at 30° to the vertical. Later, the van climbs a straight 12° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 85 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.8. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 18 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 530 N toward the checkpoint. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg => a = g tan θ.
Obtains 5.66 m s⁻².
Applies μ_s mg = m v_max² / R.
Obtains 25.8 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts resistive work F_res(πR) from initial kinetic energy ½mu².
Obtains 11.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By resolving forces on the bob, calculate the horizontal acceleration when the string hangs at 30° to the vertical.
Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular road without sliding.
Calculate the speed of the van when it reaches the checkpoint at the end of the semicircular bend.

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 2.8 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.4 m attached to a strong string. The maximum tension the string can hold without breaking is 66 N. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Writes T_max − mg = m v_max² / r at the lowest point.
Obtains 4.39 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By considering the forces acting on the ball at the lowest point, calculate the maximum speed at the bottom so the string does not break.

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 0.9 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.6 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 1.62 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string just before the bob strikes the putty.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 5.60 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 26.5 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 2.00 m s⁻¹. Target = 26.5 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 26.5 N (C).

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 7 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 2 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.55 m in 0.26 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the spring constant of the cord.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 2 + 0.55 = 2.55 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 1.16 × 10³ N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 636 N. Target = 1.16 × 10³ N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (2 + 0.55) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 1.16 × 10³ N m⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a lifting crane has total length L = 25 m and mass 550 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 4.5 m from rear end A. A 3000 kg concrete counterweight sits 2.7 m to the left of P (1.8 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 3 m to the right of P (7.5 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 19.5 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) M_cw = 7.946 × 10⁴ N m ≈ 7.95 × 10⁴ N m. (b) Equating clockwise and anticlockwise moments about P gives m_max = 330.8 kg ≈ 331 kg. (c) Vertical force balance yields R = 3.807 × 10⁴ N ≈ 3.81 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses M = m g d with counterweight mass and lever arm from P.
Counterweight moment = 7.95 × 10⁴ N m.
Subtracts boom self-weight moment from counterweight moment and divides by g × load lever arm.
Maximum safe load mass = 331 kg.
Applies vertical force balance summing counterweight, boom, and load weights.
Upward mast reaction R = 3.81 × 10⁴ N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the anticlockwise moment exerted by the concrete counterweight about pivot P.
workingSteps: Moment M_cw = W_cw × 2.7 = 7.946 × 10⁴ N m ≈ 7.95 × 10⁴ N m.

parts.prompt: Taking into account the weight of the boom, determine the maximum load mass that can be lifted at the hoist hook so the net moment about P is zero.
workingSteps: Clockwise moment of boom = 550 × 9.81 × 3 = 1.619 × 10⁴ N m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total upward reaction force exerted by the vertical mast pivot P when this maximum load is suspended in equilibrium.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium: R = (m_cw + m_boom + m_max) g.

items.stem: On a smooth level track, cart X of mass 3.6 kg moves right at 12 m s⁻¹ and collides with stationary cart Y of mass 2.8 kg. Immediately after impact, cart Y moves right at 10.08 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of cart X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Momentum conservation: (3.6)(12) = (3.6)v_X + (2.8)(10.08), giving v_X = 4.16 m s⁻¹. K_i = 259 J and K_f = 173 J, so ΔK_lost = K_i − K_f = 85.8 J. Target = 4.16 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves linear momentum and evaluates kinetic energy budget to obtain 4.16 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: A steel ball bearing of radius 2.20 mm and density 7800 kg m⁻³ falls vertically through a tall measuring cylinder of glycerol (density 1260 kg m⁻³, viscosity 1.35 Pa s) under laminar flow ($g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$).
items.workedSolution: (a) U = 0.551 mN. (b) F = 2.86 mN. (c) v = 0.0511 m s⁻¹. (d) increasing liquid temperature weakens intermolecular cohesion so liquid viscosity decreases and terminal speed increases.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates sphere volume V = (4/3)πr³ with r in metres.
Obtains upthrust U = 0.551 mN.
Computes weight W and applies equilibrium F = W − U.
Obtains terminal drag F = 2.86 mN.
Rearranges Stokes' law v = F / (6πηr).
Obtains terminal speed v = 0.0511 m s⁻¹.
States higher temperature lowers liquid viscosity due to reduced intermolecular cohesion.
Concludes terminal velocity increases (increasing liquid temperature weakens intermolecular cohesion so liquid viscosity decreases and terminal speed increases).

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 2 kg moves right at 9 m s⁻¹ and strikes stationary trolley Y of mass 6.8 kg. Immediately after impact, trolley Y moves right at 3.87 m s⁻¹ and trolley X rebounds to the left. Calculate the total kinetic energy of the two objects immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward positive, (2)(9) = (2)v_X + (6.8)(3.87) gives v_X = -4.16 m s⁻¹ (4.16 m s⁻¹ to the left). Scalar final kinetic energies add: K_f = ½(2)(4.16)² + ½(6.8)(3.87)² = 68.2 J. Energy lost = 81.0 J − K_f = 12.8 J. Target = 68.2 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds rebound speed 4.16 m s⁻¹ and sums scalar kinetic energies to obtain 68.2 J (D).

items.stem: A small ball is projected from level ground with an initial speed of 21 m s⁻¹ at 24° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.
items.workedSolution: (a) v_apex = 21 × cos 24°. Answer: 19.2 m s⁻¹. (b) u_y = 21 × sin 24° = 8.54 m s⁻¹. h_max = u_y² / (2 × 9.8). Answer: 3.72 m. (c) T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 1.74 s. R = 19.2 × T. Answer: 33.4 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes v_y = 0 at apex so v_apex = u cos θ.
Obtains 19.2 m s⁻¹.
Applies h_max = (u sin θ)² / (2g).
Obtains 3.72 m.
Evaluates R = u_x × (2u_y / g).
Obtains 33.4 m.

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 1 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.5 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 1.2 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy lost during the collision.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 5.42 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 2.47 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.310 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 8.03 J. Target = 8.03 J.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 8.03 J (C).

items.stem: In a statics experiment, a steel bar AB has length L = 4.8 m and mass 8 kg. Its centre of gravity G lies 2.78 m from end A. It is balanced horizontally on a pivot P at 1.34 m from end A by placing a 14 kg block to the left of P. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) The moment of a force is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. (b) Moment balance about P gives d = 0.8229 m left of P, so distance from end B is 4.283 m ≈ 4.28 m.

markScheme.criterion: Force multiplied by distance from pivot.
Perpendicular distance to the line of action.
Correct moment balance about P yielding lever arm d = 0.8229 m.
Converts cleanly to distance from end B = 4.28 m.

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 10 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 2.6 m. It falls freely from rest at the fixed support to point A, where the cord becomes taut. It then stretches the cord by 0.6 m over 0.33 s before stopping at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 7.14 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (10 × 7.14) / 0.33 = 216 N.
Obtains 315 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 1.05 × 10³ N.

items.stem: On a frictionless horizontal surface, block X of mass 3.5 kg moves to the right at 12 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with block Y of mass 3.6 kg moving to the left at 3 m s⁻¹ (arrow on Y not shown). Immediately after impact, block Y moves to the right at 2 m s⁻¹. Take motion to the right as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) p_before = 3.5 × 12 + 3.6 × (−3) = 31.2 kg m s⁻¹. Answer: 31.2 kg m s⁻¹ to the right. (b) v_X = (31.2 − 3.6 × 2) / 3.5 = 6.86 m s⁻¹. Answer: 6.86 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m_X u_X − m_Y |u_Y| with correct signs.
Obtains 31.2 kg m s⁻¹ to the right.
Solves p_before = m_X v_X + m_Y v_Y for v_X.
Obtains 6.86 m s⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: A golf ball is hit from flat ground at 44 m s⁻¹ and 52° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the ground.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 44 sin 52° = 34.7 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 44 cos 52° = 27.1 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 7.08 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 192 m. Target = 192 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 192 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies horizontal speed by ascent time u sin θ / g instead of full flight time 2u sin θ / g.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cos θ for sin θ in the flight-time expression.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: A van of mass 1800 kg accelerates along a level road while a small brass bob hangs from its ceiling at 30° to the vertical. Later, the van climbs a straight 12° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 55 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.85. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 20 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 410 N toward the stop line. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 30°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 30° = ma and T cos 30° = mg => a = g tan 30° = 5.66 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.85 × 9.8 × 55) = 21.4 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1800)(20)² / 410 = 878 m. Target = 5.66 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 5.66 m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: A metal box of mass 6.5 kg slides from rest down a straight ramp of length 8.5 m inclined at 34° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 5.31 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. If the box is instead released from rest halfway down the ramp, calculate its speed at the bottom.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 34° − ½mv² = 211 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 8.5 = 24.9 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.75 m s⁻¹. Target = 3.75 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 3.75 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: A plastic box of mass 9 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough ramp of length 11 m, inclined at 32° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 7.8 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the coefficient of dynamic friction μ_d between the box and the ramp.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 32° = 514 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(9)(7.8)² = 274 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 240 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 32°)L, μ = 0.292. Target = 0.292.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 32° accurately to obtain 0.292 (A).

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 1.7 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.9 m on a strong string. At the lowest point, its speed is 4.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.7 × 4.5² / 0.9 = 38.2 N, so T = 38.2 + 1.7 × 9.8 = 54.9 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 54.9 N (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A uniform concrete cable trough of length L = 2.50 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a semi-annular cross-section of outer diameter D = 26.0 cm and inner diameter d = 16.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2150 kg m⁻³. It is uniform along its length, so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. An electric hoist of electrical input power 480 W and efficiency 76% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.01649 m², V = A L = 0.04123 m³, m = ρ V = 88.65 kg ≈ 88.7 kg. (b) W = 869.7 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 434.8 N ≈ 435 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.250 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 1087 J ≈ 1.09 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.76 × 480 = 364.8 W, so t = 1087 / 364.8 = 2.980 s ≈ 2.98 s. (e) density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

markScheme.criterion: Computes semi-annular cross-section A = (π/8)(D² − d²) = 0.01649 m² with cm → m conversion.
Calculates V = A L = 0.04123 m³ and substitutes m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 88.65 kg rounding clearly to 88.7 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 2.50 = m g × 1.250.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 435 N (4 s.f. 434.8 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.250 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 1.09 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 1087 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 364.8 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 2.98 s (4 s.f. 2.980 s).
States valid physical assumption: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 1 kg hangs on a light string of length 2.4 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 1.2 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height above the lowest point reached by the joined objects.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 6.86 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 3.12 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.496 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 12.8 J. Target = 0.496 m.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 0.496 m (B).

items.stem: A non-uniform wooden beam of length L = 2.60 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a rectangular cross-section of width w = 26.0 cm and thickness h = 16.0 cm, with average density ρ = 1150 kg m⁻³. Its centre of gravity G lies at distance x = 1.09 m from end A. A battery-powered winch of electrical input power 340 W and efficiency 74% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.04160 m², V = A L = 0.1082 m³, m = ρ V = 124.4 kg ≈ 124 kg. (b) W = 1220 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 512.5 N ≈ 512 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.092 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 1332 J ≈ 1.33 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.74 × 340 = 251.6 W, so t = 1332 / 251.6 = 5.296 s ≈ 5.30 s. (e) electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates cross-section A = 0.04160 m², volume V = 0.1082 m³, and applies m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 124.4 kg confirming 124 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 2.60 = m g × 1.092.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 512 N (4 s.f. 512.5 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.092 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 1.33 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 1332 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 251.6 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 5.30 s (4 s.f. 5.296 s).
Identifies electrical heating in motor windings and mechanical friction in hoist gears.
Links losses to thermal energy dissipated to the surroundings (electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings).

By taking moments about end A, calculate the minimum vertical upward force F applied at end B required to just lift end B off the ground. [2]

workingSteps: Vertical rise of centre of gravity G is Δh = x = 1.092 m

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum time taken for the 340 W hoist motor operating at 74% efficiency to stand the component upright. [2]
workingSteps: Useful output power P_out = η P_in = 0.74 × 340 = 251.6 W

parts.expectedAnswer: electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings.

options.label: B
options.text: Use a plumb line to align the metre ruler vertically and plot two h over t against t so the gradient equals gravitational field strength independently of initial speed.

options.label: C
options.text: Eyeball the stand vertically and assume the sphere enters Gate 1 with zero velocity.
options.distractorRationale: Visual estimation leaves tilt error, and the sphere already has speed u > 0 at Gate 1.

options.label: D
options.text: Plot h/t² against h because it eliminates gravitational acceleration from the vertical intercept.
options.distractorRationale: h = ut + ½gt² linearizes cleanly as 2h/t = gt + 2u (or h/t = ½gt + u).

items.stem: A student using an electromagnet and trapdoor consistently obtains $g = 9.42$ m s⁻² across repeated trials with a dense steel sphere. Which systematic error best explains this result?
items.workedSolution: RP3 evaluation: Residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g.

markScheme.criterion: Residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g.

items.stem: Two light Hookean springs with constants $k_1$ and $k_2$ are joined end-to-end in series, as shown on the left. They support a load $F$. Which reasoning gives the combined spring constant $k_s$?
items.workedSolution: In series each light spring carries tension F, so x = x₁ + x₂ = F/k₁ + F/k₂ ⇒ 1/k_s = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂. Therefore the correct statement is: Springs in series experience the same tension while their extensions add giving reciprocal effective stiffness 1 over k1 plus 1 over k2.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: springs in series experience the same tension while their extensions add giving reciprocal effective stiffness 1 over k1 plus 1 over k2.

options.text: Springs in series share the same extension while the load splits equally between them, giving kₛ = k₁ + k₂.

options.distractorRationale: Neglecting spring mass, static equilibrium requires every link in series to carry the full tension F.

options.label: C
options.text: Tension doubles across the second spring so extensions cancel and kₛ = 2(k₁ + k₂).
options.distractorRationale: Both springs carry tension F and their extensions add: x = F/k₁ + F/k₂.

items.stem: Heavy rain wets an asphalt motorway while an alert driver maintains the same cruise speed. How do the car's thinking distance and braking distance respond?
items.workedSolution: Road condition and tyre tread determine frictional braking force (braking distance), whereas driver alertness determines reaction time (thinking distance). Therefore the correct statement is: Wet or icy roads and worn tyres reduce friction and braking force and so increase braking distance without changing thinking distance.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: wet or icy roads and worn tyres reduce friction and braking force and so increase braking distance without changing thinking distance.

options.label: A
options.text: Wet roads double the driver's physiological reaction time while leaving maximum tyre braking force unaffected.

options.text: Both thinking distance and braking distance decrease because water drag slows the vehicle rapidly.
options.distractorRationale: Water lowers static friction between tyres and tarmac, greatly increasing braking distance.

options.label: C
options.text: Wet or icy roads and worn tyres reduce friction and braking force thereby increasing braking distance without changing thinking distance.

options.text: Neither thinking distance nor braking distance changes if the vehicle's mass stays constant.
options.distractorRationale: Reduced road friction lowers braking force F_b and deceleration a, increasing d_brake = v²/(2a).

items.stem: Two masses slide on a light frictionless horizontal rod rotating about a central vertical axis. An internal cord pulls both masses radially inward toward the axis. How do angular momentum L, angular speed ω, and rotational kinetic energy E_k change?
items.workedSolution: Because τ_ext = 0, L = Iω is constant; reducing I raises ω = L/I and raises E_k = L²/(2I) via positive internal work done against the radial inertia of the masses. Therefore the correct statement is: During this inward radial pull, with zero net external torque angular momentum remains constant, so decreasing the moment of inertia increases both angular speed and rotational kinetic energy because internal forces do positive work.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: with zero net external torque angular momentum remains constant, so decreasing the moment of inertia increases both angular speed and rotational kinetic energy because internal forces do positive work.

options.label: A
options.text: During this inward radial pull, with zero net external torque angular momentum remains constant, so decreasing the moment of inertia increases both angular speed and rotational kinetic energy because internal forces do positive work.

options.label: B
options.text: During this inward radial pull, both angular momentum L and rotational kinetic energy E_k remain strictly constant while angular speed ω decreases.
options.distractorRationale: Decreasing I requires ω = L/I to increase and E_k = L²/(2I) to increase as internal tension does positive work pulling the masses inward.

options.label: C
options.text: During this inward radial pull, angular momentum L increases because the inward cord exerts a large external torque about the rotation axis.
options.distractorRationale: A purely radial internal force passes through the rotation axis (sin θ = 0) and produces zero external torque, so L is conserved.

options.label: D
options.text: During this inward radial pull, angular speed ω stays constant while rotational kinetic energy drops proportionally to the smaller moment of inertia.
options.distractorRationale: Violates conservation of angular momentum L = Iω when net external torque is zero.

items.stem: A small stone is thrown from flat ground at 18 m s⁻¹ and 55° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height reached above the ground.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 55° = 10.3 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 55°)² / (2g) = 11.1 m. Target = 11.1 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 55° at apex to obtain 11.1 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Converts all initial kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy, forgetting non-zero horizontal speed u cos θ at the apex.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses horizontal component u cos θ instead of vertical component u sin θ in h = u_y² / (2g).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of two in the denominator of h_max = u_y² / (2g).

items.stem: A tennis ball is fired from a launcher on a level pitch at a speed of 38 m s⁻¹ and an angle of 22° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates u_y = u sin θ.
Obtains 14.2 m s⁻¹.
Applies T = 2u_y / g.
Obtains 2.90 s.
Multiplies u cos θ by flight time T.
Obtains 102 m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the initial vertical component of velocity.
Determine the total time of flight before returning to the pitch.
Calculate the horizontal range of the trajectory.

items.stem: A metal cylinder of mass 4.5 kg is attached to an elastic rope of natural length 2.2 m. It falls from rest at the fixed upper support, and the rope obeys Hooke's law once it becomes taut at point A. The rope stretches by a maximum extension of 0.75 m in 0.16 s before the cylinder stops at the lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Uses free-fall relation v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 6.57 m s⁻¹.
Equates mg(L + x) = ½kx² over the complete vertical drop.
Obtains 463 N m⁻¹.
Evaluates a_B = (kx − mg) / m.
Obtains 67.4 m s⁻².

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a horizontal metal bar of length L = 4.4 m and mass 32 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light wires at A and B. The wires are 3.8 m apart, and wire A is inclined at 50° above the horizontal bar. Its centre of gravity G lies 2.43 m to the right of A and 1.37 m to the left of B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the tension T₂ in wire B.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: T₁_y × 3.8 = 32 × 9.81 × 1.37 ⇒ T₁_y = 113.2 N, T₂_y = 200.7 N. With wire A at 50°, T₁ = T₁_y / sin 50° = 147.7 N ≈ 148 N, horizontal component H = T₁ cos 50° = 94.97 N, and T₂ = √(H² + T₂_y²) = 222.1 N ≈ 222 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct wire tension = 222 N.

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 1.6 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 2.2 m on a strong string. The string breaks if the tension exceeds 63 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the ball at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((63/1.6) − 9.81) × 2.2] = 8.06 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 8.06 m s⁻¹ (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds g instead of subtracting g when rearranging T_max − mg = mv²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a control wheel bar has length d = 0.4 m. Two equal and opposite parallel forces of magnitude F = 18 N act perpendicularly at its ends. What is the magnitude of the torque of this couple?
items.workedSolution: Torque of a couple = F × perpendicular separation = 18 × 0.4 = 7.200 N m ≈ 7.20 N m.

markScheme.criterion: Correct couple torque = 7.20 N m.

items.stem: A heavy box of weight 1360 N slides at a constant speed down a straight ramp. The slope has length 11 m and vertical height 3.1 m. Calculate the gravitational potential energy lost over the full length of the slope.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed ΔE_k = 0. Potential energy lost = W h = 1360 × 3.1 = 4.22 × 10³ J. Parallel equilibrium gives F_res = W sin θ = W h / L = 383 N. Target = 4.22 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Uses sin θ = 3.1/11 and zero net force to obtain 4.22 × 10³ J (C).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 2.8 m and mass 7 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 10 kg hangs so its centre of gravity acts 2.5 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at 46° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about O give T = 169.5 N ≈ 169 N. (b) Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos θ = 117.7 N ≈ 118 N. (c) Vertical balance: R_y = W_total − T sin θ = 44.85 N ≈ 44.8 N.

markScheme.criterion: Writes full moment balance about hinge O including both rod and sign moments with T sin θ.
Evaluates T = 169.5 N (169 N) showing agreement with 1.7 × 10² N.
Applies horizontal equilibrium R_x = T cos θ.
R_x = 118 N away from the wall.
Applies vertical equilibrium R_y = W_total − T sin θ.
R_y = 44.8 N upwards.

parts.prompt: By taking moments about hinge O, show clearly that the tension T in the angled wire is approximately 1.7 × 10² N.
workingSteps: Clockwise moment about O = (7 × 1.4 + 10 × 2.5) × 9.81 = 341.4 N m.
T = 169.5 N ≈ 169 N, which rounds to 1.7 × 10² N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the horizontal component of the force exerted by hinge O on the rod.
workingSteps: Horizontal equilibrium: R_x = T cos 46° = 169.5 × cos 46° = 117.7 N ≈ 118 N away from the wall.

parts.prompt: Calculate the vertical component of the force exerted by hinge O on the rod.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium: R_y = W − T sin 46° = 44.85 N ≈ 44.8 N upwards.

items.stem: A metal block of mass 4.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a straight incline of length 4.5 m, inclined at 32° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 4.79 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy dissipated against friction during the slide.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 32° = 105 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(4.5)(4.79)² = 51.6 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 53.6 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 32°)L, μ = 0.318. Target = 53.6 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 32° accurately to obtain 53.6 J (C).

items.stem: During Required Practical 4 on a hard-drawn steel wire of length $L = 2.40$ m, three micrometer diameter pairs average to 0.42 mm, 0.44 mm, and 0.43 mm. The linear elastic graph of force $F$ against extension $e$ has gradient 12.1 N mm⁻¹. Determine the Young modulus $E$ in GPa.
items.workedSolution: Mean diameter $d = 0.43$ mm gives $A = \pi d^2/4 = 1.45 × 10⁻⁷ m²$. $E = L \times \mathrm{grad} / A = 200 GPa$. Percentage uncertainty $\%\Delta E = \%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad} = 0.0833 + 2(2.33) + 2 = 6.73\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates youngModulusGPa $= 200 GPa$.

items.stem: A brass bob of mass 0.7 kg is attached to a light nylon cord of length 0.8 m. It moves in a vertical circle and passes through the lowest point at 7 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_c = mv² / r.
Obtains 42.9 N.
Applies T − mg = F_c => T = F_c + mg.
Obtains 49.7 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant centripetal force on the bob at the lowest point.
Hence calculate the tension in the cord at the lowest point.

items.stem: Two clutch discs share a frictionless vertical shaft. One has moment of inertia $I_1 = 0.750 kg m²$ spinning at 48.0 rad s⁻¹, and the other has $I_2 = 1.25 kg m²$ initially at rest. The discs engage and reach a common angular speed after slipping for 0.600 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\omega_{\mathrm{f}} = 18.0 rad s⁻¹$. (b) Mean clutch torque $= \frac{I_2|\omega_{\mathrm{f}} - \omega_2|}{\Delta t} = 37.5 N m$. (c) Energy dissipated $= 540 J$ as heat from sliding friction.

markScheme.criterion: Applies conservation of angular momentum $(I_1 + I_2)\omega_{\mathrm{f}} = I_1\omega_1 + I_2\omega_2$.
Obtains $\omega_{\mathrm{f}} = 18.0 rad s⁻¹$.
Applies angular impulse $T\Delta t = \Delta(I_2\omega_2)$.
Obtains mean torque $= 37.5 N m$.
Computes both initial and final total rotational kinetic energy.
Obtains energy loss $= 540 J$.
States that energy is dissipated as thermal energy due to friction while the plates slip.

Divide by $\Delta t = 0.600 s$ to obtain $T = 37.5 N m$.

Energy lost $= 540 J$, dissipated as thermal energy by sliding friction between the clutch surfaces.

items.stem: A 980 kg electric bus carries a KERS flywheel of moment of inertia 2.50 kg m². It climbs a 180 m slope rising 19.0 m vertically against 195 N mean drag, and the flywheel speed must stay at or above 180 rad s⁻¹. Take $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Calculate the minimum initial angular speed of the flywheel at the bottom.
items.workedSolution: Total climb energy $E = 980(9.81)(19.0) + 195(180) = 2.18 × 10⁵ J$. From $\frac{1}{2}I(\omega_{\max}^2 - \omega_{\min}^2) = E$, $\omega_{\max} = \sqrt{180^2 + \frac{2E}{2.50}} = 455 rad s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Minimum initial angular speed equals 455 rad s⁻¹.

options.distractorRationale: Assumes the flywheel slows all the way to rest instead of retaining $180\text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds $\omega_{\min}$ outside the square root instead of inside $\sqrt{\omega_{\min}^2 + 2E/I}$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Introduces an erroneous factor of one-half during rearrangement.

items.stem: A metal block of weight 1150 N slides down a rough slope at a constant speed of 6.5 m s⁻¹. The ramp is 22 m long and drops by 11 m vertically. Calculate the magnitude of the friction force acting up the ramp.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed, friction balances downslope weight: F_f = W(h/L) = 1150 × (11/22) = 575 N. Rate of thermal energy generation P = F_f v = 3.74 × 10³ W. Target = 575 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_f = Wh/L and P = F_f v to obtain 575 N (D).

items.stem: A golf ball is struck from level ground at speed $28.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an elevation angle of $40.0^\circ$ above the horizontal ($g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$). The figure contrasts its ideal vacuum trajectory with its real trajectory in air.
items.workedSolution: (a) $H = 16.5 m$. (b) $t = 3.67 s$, $R = 78.8 m$. (c) fluid resistance opposes the instantaneous velocity so the horizontal velocity component decreases continuously throughout flight. (d) at the highest point vertical velocity is zero while horizontal velocity remains non-zero so resultant acceleration exceeds g and tilts opposite to horizontal motion.

markScheme.criterion: Finds u_y = 28.0 sin 40.0° and applies H = u_y²/(2g) with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Obtains vacuum apex height H = 16.5 m.
Calculates total flight time t = 2u_y/g = 3.67 s.
Multiplies horizontal speed u_x = 28.0 cos 40.0° by flight time.
Obtains vacuum range R = 78.8 m.
States horizontal drag decelerates the ball continuously throughout flight.

Links reduced horizontal velocity on descent to shorter range and steeper descent (fluid resistance opposes the instantaneous velocity so the horizontal velocity component decreases continuously throughout flight).
Identifies non-zero horizontal drag acting backwards perpendicular to downward weight at the apex.

Concludes resultant acceleration exceeds g and tilts backwards (at the highest point vertical velocity is zero while horizontal velocity remains non-zero so resultant acceleration exceeds g and tilts opposite to horizontal motion).

items.stem: A small smooth sphere of radius $2.00\text{ mm}$ and density $7800\text{ kg m}^{-3}$ falls slowly in laminar flow through oil of density $1200\text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and viscosity $\eta = 1.50\text{ Pa s}$ ($g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$). Using $F_{\text{b}} = \rho V g$ and $F_{\text{d}} = 6\pi\eta r v$, what is its terminal speed?
items.workedSolution: Balancing $F_{\text{d}} + F_{\text{b}} = F_{\text{g}}$ gives $v = \frac{2r^2(\rho_{\text{s}} - \rho_{\text{f}})g}{9\eta} = \frac{2(2.00 \times 10^{-3})^2(6600)(9.8)}{9(1.50)} = 38.3 mm s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $F_{\text{d}} + F_{\text{b}} = F_{\text{g}}$ at $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to obtain $38.3 mm s⁻¹$.

items.stem: The diagram shows the rotor of a workshop pottery wheel. Its central hub has moment of inertia 0.650 kg m² and carries 4 rim masses of 1.25 kg each at radius 0.400 m. Over 8.00 s, its rotational speed changes uniformly from 3.00 rev s⁻¹ to 11.0 rev s⁻¹ against a constant bearing friction torque of 1.40 N m.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I = 1.45 kg m²$. (b) $|\alpha| = \frac{2\pi|f_2 - f_1|}{t} = 6.28 rad s⁻²$. (c) Applied torque $T_{\mathrm{app}} = 10.5 N m$. (d) Peak power $P_{\max} = T_{\mathrm{app}}\omega_{\max} = 726 W$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $I = I_{\mathrm{hub}} + \sum m r^2$ with squared radius.
Obtains $I = 1.45 kg m²$.
Converts $\text{rev s}^{-1}$ to $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ via $2\pi$ and divides change by $t$.
Obtains $|\alpha| = 6.28 rad s⁻²$.
Combines $I|\alpha|$ with bearing friction torque in the correct sense.
Obtains applied torque $= 10.5 N m$.
Applies $P = T\omega$ at the highest angular speed.
Obtains maximum power $= 726 W$.

items.stem: A coastal generating station burns liquid fuel oil of specific energy $44.0\text{ MJ kg}^{-1}$ and density $850\text{ kg m}^{-3}$. Its Sankey diagram shows $500\text{ MW}$ fuel input, $190\text{ MW}$ electrical output, and $210\text{ MW}$ exhaust heat loss.
items.workedSolution: (a) volumetric energy density is energy per unit volume in joules per cubic metre whereas specific energy is energy per unit mass in joules per kilogram. (b) Energy density $= 37.4 GJ m⁻³$. (c) $\eta = 38.0\%$. (d) $\Delta m/\Delta t = 11.4 kg s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Defines volumetric energy density as energy per unit volume (J m⁻³).

Defines specific energy as energy per unit mass (J kg⁻¹) (volumetric energy density is energy per unit volume in joules per cubic metre whereas specific energy is energy per unit mass in joules per kilogram).
Multiplies specific energy by density ρ = 850 kg m⁻³.
Obtains 37.4 GJ m⁻³.
Applies η = P_output / P_input.
Obtains efficiency 38.0%.
Recognizes input power = (Δm/Δt) × specific energy.
Substitutes 500 MW and 44.0 MJ kg⁻¹ consistently.
Obtains mass rate 11.4 kg s⁻¹.

items.stem: A winch drum of moment of inertia $I = 4.50\text{ kg m}^2$ lifts a load in a laboratory experiment ($g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$). Starting from rest, its $\alpha$–$t$ graph forms a triangle peaking at $16.0\text{ rad s}^{-2}$ and returning to zero at $t = 6.00\text{ s}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $T_{\text{peak}} = 4.50 \times 16.0 = 72.0 N m$. (b) $\Delta\omega = 48.0\text{ rad s}^{-1} \Rightarrow \text{impulse} = 216 N m s$. (c) torque parallels force moment of inertia parallels mass and I omega parallels linear momentum.

Correct angular impulse 216 N m s.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a non-uniform metal hatch of length L = 2.4 m and mass 22 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.86 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 30° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the magnitude of the resultant reaction force R exerted on the door by hinge O.
items.workedSolution: Moments about O: T cos 30° × 2.4 = 22 × 9.81 × 0.86 ⇒ T = 89.30 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T sin 30° = 44.65 N. Vertical balance: R_y = 22 × 9.81 − T cos 30° = 138.5 N. Resultant R = √(R_x² + R_y²) = 145.5 N ≈ 146 N, at angle α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 72.13° ≈ 72.1° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 146 N.

items.stem: A metal block of mass 3 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 2.6 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the cord becomes taut, and then stretches it by 1.1 m in 0.15 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward tension in the cord during this 0.15 s interval.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.8 × 2.6) = 7.14 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.15 + 3(9.8) = 172 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 172 N (D).

items.stem: A delivery van of mass 1600 kg accelerates along a level road while a small pendulum bob hangs from its ceiling at 34° to the vertical. Later, the van climbs a straight 8° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 80 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.8. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 18 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 350 N toward the checkpoint. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 34°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 34° = ma and T cos 34° = mg => a = g tan 34° = 6.62 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.8 × 9.81 × 80) = 25.1 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1600)(18)² / 350 = 741 m. Target = 6.62 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 6.62 m s⁻² (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

markScheme.criterion: Writes T_max − mg = m v_max² / r at the lowest point.
Obtains 4.61 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By considering the forces acting on the bob at the lowest point, calculate the maximum speed at the bottom so the cord does not break.

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 0.3 kg hangs on a light string of length 1 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 0.66 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the speed of the joined objects immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 4.43 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 8.83 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 1.38 m s⁻¹. Target = 1.38 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 1.38 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: A probe descends through air following the curved v–t graph shown, approaching terminal velocity v_T = 32 m s⁻¹. At t = 2.0 s, its velocity is 12.59 m s⁻¹, and the tangent drawn at t = 2.0 s passes through (0.0 s, 2.89 m s⁻¹) and (6.0 s, 32.00 m s⁻¹).
items.workedSolution: (a) 4.85 m s⁻². (b) 6.30 m s⁻². (c) instantaneous acceleration equals the gradient of the tangent drawn to the curved velocity-time graph at that instant, rather than the chord from the origin.

markScheme.criterion: Applies gradient Δv/Δt to the tangent points.
Obtains instantaneous a = 4.85 m s⁻².
Divides Δv = 12.59 m s⁻¹ by Δt = 2.0 s.
Obtains average a = 6.30 m s⁻².
States drag increases with speed, reducing resultant force and slope of the v–t curve.
Links instantaneous acceleration to tangent gradient rather than origin chord.

items.stem: A metal block of mass 5.5 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 3 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 1.15 m in 0.14 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum tension in the cord at the lowest point B.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 3 + 1.15 = 4.15 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 338 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 389 N. Target = 389 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (3 + 1.15) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 389 N (A).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a tower crane has total length L = 25 m and mass 950 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 5 m from rear end A. A 4000 kg concrete counterweight sits 3.6 m to the left of P (1.4 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 3 m to the right of P (8 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 19.5 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum safe load mass at the hook for rotational equilibrium about P.
items.workedSolution: Anticlockwise counterweight moment about P: M_cw = 4000 × 9.81 × 3.6 = 1.413 × 10⁵ N m. Clockwise boom moment: M_boom = 950 × 9.81 × 3 = 2.796 × 10⁴ N m. Remaining clockwise moment available for load: W_max × 19.5 = 1.133 × 10⁵ N m ⇒ W_max = 5811 N ≈ 5.81 × 10³ N, m_max = W_max / 9.81 = 592.3 kg ≈ 592 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct maximum safe load mass = 592 kg.

Obtains 7.21 J.

items.stem: On a frictionless horizontal surface, block X of mass 0.8 kg moves to the right at 7 m s⁻¹. It collides with stationary block Y of mass 2.6 kg. Immediately after the collision, block Y moves to the right at 2.67 m s⁻¹. Take motion to the right as positive.

Obtains 1.68 m s⁻¹ to the left.
Adds positive scalar kinetic energies ½m_X v_X² + ½m_Y v_Y².
Obtains 10.4 J.
Evaluates K_i − K_f.
Obtains 9.21 J.

items.stem: A small stone is thrown from flat ground at 27 m s⁻¹ and 55° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height reached above the ground.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 55° = 15.5 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 55°)² / (2g) = 25.0 m. Target = 25.0 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 55° at apex to obtain 25.0 m (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Converts all initial kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy, forgetting non-zero horizontal speed u cos θ at the apex.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses horizontal component u cos θ instead of vertical component u sin θ in h = u_y² / (2g).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of two in the denominator of h_max = u_y² / (2g).

items.stem: A brass ball of mass 1 kg hangs from a light string of length 2.2 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the lowest point, it collides with and sticks to a wax block of mass 1.2 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mgL = ½mu² => u = √(2gL).
Obtains 6.57 m s⁻¹.
Finds v = mu/(m+M) from momentum conservation and evaluates ½mu² − ½(m+M)v².
Obtains 11.8 J.
Applies h = v² / (2g).
Obtains 0.455 m.

items.stem: In a statics experiment, a steel bar AB has length L = 3.2 m and mass 18 kg. Its centre of gravity G lies 2.05 m from end A. It is balanced horizontally on a pivot P at 1.02 m from end A by placing a 26 kg block to the left of P. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate how far from end B the 26 kg block must be placed for horizontal equilibrium.
items.workedSolution: Distance of CG from pivot P: d_G = 2.05 − 1.02 = 1.030 m. Taking moments about P: 26 × d = 18 × 1.030 ⇒ d = 0.7131 m left of P. Position from end A is x_A = 1.02 − 0.7131 = 0.3069 m. Therefore distance from end B is L − x_A = 3.2 − 0.3069 = 2.893 m ≈ 2.89 m.

markScheme.criterion: Correct distance from end B = 2.89 m.

items.stem: A sandbag of mass 12 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 2 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the cord becomes taut, and then stretches it by 1.2 m in 0.21 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward tension in the cord during this 0.21 s interval.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.81 × 2) = 6.26 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.21 + 12(9.81) = 476 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 476 N (C).

items.stem: A moving snooker ball makes a glancing, frictionless elastic collision with an identical stationary ball. Using both vector momentum conservation and $E_k = p^2/(2m)$, what geometric outcome must hold?
items.workedSolution: Equal masses m yield p₀²/(2m) = p₁²/(2m) + p₂²/(2m) ⇒ p₀² = p₁² + p₂², which by Pythagoras forces a 90° angle between p₁ and p₂. Therefore the correct statement is: An oblique elastic collision between identical spheres with one initially at rest sends them apart at ninety degrees.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: an oblique elastic collision between identical spheres with one initially at rest sends them apart at ninety degrees.

options.label: B
options.text: The angle between their post-collision paths is always strictly less than forty-five degrees.

options.label: C
options.text: The two identical spheres always separate symmetrically at sixty degrees on each side of the original line.

items.stem: On a smooth level track, cart X of mass 4 kg moves to the right at 11 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with cart Y of mass 2.4 kg moving to the left at 5 m s⁻¹ (arrow not shown). Immediately after the collision, cart Y moves right at 3 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of cart X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward as positive: p_before = (4)(11) + (2.4)(−5) = 32.0 kg m s⁻¹. From p_before = (4)v_X + (2.4)(3), v_X = 6.20 m s⁻¹, which is 6.20 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Uses signed head-on momentum p_before = 32.0 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 6.20 m s⁻¹ to the right (B).

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform diving board of total length L = 7 m and mass 28 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is 0.8 m from the left end, and support B is 4.2 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 2 m. A technician of mass 58 kg initially stands 3.5 m from the left end of the plank. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². The technician steps off and a toolbox is placed at the outer overhanging tip. Calculate the maximum toolbox mass the plank can support without tipping.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: F₁ × 4.2 = (28 × 1.500 + 58 × 1.500) × 9.81 ⇒ F₁ = 301.3 N ≈ 301 N. At tipping (F₁ = 0): m_load × d_tip = m_beam × (x_B − x_G) ⇒ d_tip = (28 × 1.500) / 58 = 0.7241 m ≈ 0.724 m. At the very tip (overhang 2 m): m_end = (28 × 1.500) / 2 = 21.00 kg ≈ 21.0 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct solver-verified answer = 21.0 kg.

items.stem: A ball is launched from floor level across a flat room at 32 m s⁻¹ and 22° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the total time of flight before returning to the floor.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 32 sin 22° = 12.0 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 32 cos 22° = 29.7 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 2.45 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 72.6 m. Target = 2.45 s.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 2.45 s (C).
