options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Swaps sin θ and cos θ when resolving vertical launch speed.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses total speed u instead of vertical component u sin θ.

items.stem: A minibus of mass 1800 kg accelerates along a level road while a small metal bob hangs from its ceiling at 18° to the vertical. Later, the minibus climbs a straight 14° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 45 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.55. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 15 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 410 N toward the exit. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 18°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 18° = ma and T cos 18° = mg => a = g tan 18° = 3.18 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.55 × 9.8 × 45) = 15.6 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1800)(15)² / 410 = 494 m. Target = 3.18 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 3.18 m s⁻² (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: Shortly after opening a parachute, an $85.0\text{ kg}$ skydiver experiences an upward air resistance of $1340\text{ N}$. Taking $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$, calculate the magnitude of the skydiver's upward deceleration.
items.workedSolution: Weight $W = 85.0 \times 9.81 = 833.9\text{ N}$; upward resultant force $F = 1340 - 833.9 = 506.1\text{ N}$; deceleration $a = F/m = 5.95 m s⁻²$. Option B (5.95 m s⁻²) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Upward deceleration $= 5.95 m s⁻²$ (5.95 m s⁻², option B).

items.stem: A parcel of mass 2.5 kg slides from rest down a rough ramp of length 5.5 m inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 4.77 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. If the parcel is instead released from rest halfway down the ramp, calculate its speed at the bottom.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 30° − ½mv² = 39.0 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 5.5 = 7.09 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.37 m s⁻¹. Target = 3.37 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 3.37 m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: A plastic box of mass 4.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough ramp of length 5 m, inclined at 40° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 4.37 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy dissipated against friction during the slide.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 40° = 142 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(4.5)(4.37)² = 43.0 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 98.8 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 40°)L, μ = 0.585. Target = 98.8 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 40° accurately to obtain 98.8 J (C).

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 1.7 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.3 m on a strong string. At the lowest point, its speed is 9.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.7 × 9.5² / 1.3 = 118 N, so T = 118 + 1.7 × 9.8 = 135 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 135 N (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A uniform concrete tie beam of length L = 3.40 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a rectangular cross-section of width w = 25.0 cm and thickness h = 12.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2520 kg m⁻³. It is uniform along its length, so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. An electric hoist motor of electrical input power 820 W and efficiency 85% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.03000 m², V = A L = 0.1020 m³, m = ρ V = 257.0 kg ≈ 257 kg. (b) W = 2522 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 1261 N ≈ 1.26 × 10³ N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.700 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 4287 J ≈ 4.29 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.85 × 820 = 697.0 W, so t = 4287 / 697.0 = 6.150 s ≈ 6.15 s. (e) electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates cross-section A = 0.03000 m², volume V = 0.1020 m³, and applies m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 257.0 kg confirming 257 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 3.40 = m g × 1.700.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 1.26 × 10³ N (4 s.f. 1261 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.700 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 4.29 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 4287 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 697.0 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 6.15 s (4 s.f. 6.150 s).
Identifies electrical heating in motor windings and mechanical friction in hoist gears.
Links losses to thermal energy dissipated to the surroundings (electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings).

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 0.8 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.4 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 0.96 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy lost during the collision.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 5.24 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 2.38 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.289 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 5.99 J. Target = 5.99 J.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 5.99 J (A).

items.stem: A non-uniform concrete kerb beam of length L = 3.00 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a rectangular cross-section of width w = 20.0 cm and thickness h = 15.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2450 kg m⁻³. Its centre of gravity G lies at distance x = 1.29 m from end A. An electric lifting winch of electrical input power 640 W and efficiency 77% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.03000 m², V = A L = 0.09000 m³, m = ρ V = 220.5 kg ≈ 221 kg. (b) W = 2163 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 930.1 N ≈ 930 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.290 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 2790 J ≈ 2.79 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.77 × 640 = 492.8 W, so t = 2790 / 492.8 = 5.662 s ≈ 5.66 s. (e) density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

markScheme.criterion: Computes cross-section A = w h = 0.03000 m² with cm → m conversion.
Calculates V = A L = 0.09000 m³ and substitutes m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 220.5 kg rounding clearly to 221 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 3.00 = m g × 1.290.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 930 N (4 s.f. 930.1 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.290 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 2.79 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 2790 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 492.8 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 5.66 s (4 s.f. 5.662 s).
States valid physical assumption: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

items.stem: Why is dropping a sphere through two light gates superior to dropping from a hand-held release onto a single trapdoor in RP3?
items.workedSolution: RP3 evaluation: Starting timing electronically at Gate 1 avoids release-delay errors, while students use a plumb line to align the metre ruler vertically and plot two h over t against t so the gradient equals gravitational field strength independently of initial speed.

markScheme.criterion: Starting timing electronically at Gate 1 avoids release-delay errors, while students use a plumb line to align the metre ruler vertically and plot two h over t against t so the gradient equals gravitational field strength independently of initial speed.

options.label: A
options.text: Starting timing electronically at Gate 1 avoids release-delay errors, while students use a plumb line to align the metre ruler vertically and plot two h over t against t so the gradient equals gravitational field strength independently of initial speed.

options.label: B
options.text: Two light gates guarantee the sphere's initial speed at Gate 1 is exactly zero.
options.distractorRationale: The sphere already has speed u > 0 at Gate 1; the 2h/t vs t graph absorbs u into the vertical intercept 2u.

options.label: C
options.text: Light gates eliminate the need to measure vertical height h between the gates.
options.distractorRationale: Accurate vertical measurement of h with a clamped metre ruler and plumb line remains essential.

options.label: D
options.text: Light gates make air resistance zero even for light expanded-polystyrene spheres.
options.distractorRationale: Electronic timing removes release/reaction errors, not aerodynamic drag.

items.stem: Required Practical 3 uses a small, dense steel sphere instead of a large hollow plastic ball. Why is this choice made, and what systematic error acts like air drag in the electromagnet setup?
items.workedSolution: RP3 evaluation: High weight-to-drag ratio keeps air resistance negligible; alongside air drag, residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g.

markScheme.criterion: High weight-to-drag ratio keeps air resistance negligible; alongside air drag, residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g.

options.text: A denser sphere falls faster solely because gravitational field strength g increases with mass.
options.distractorRationale: In vacuum all masses accelerate at g = 9.81 m s⁻²; density merely makes air drag negligible compared to weight.

options.label: B
options.text: A larger hollow ball reduces drag because its greater surface area stabilises the wake.
options.distractorRationale: Larger cross-sectional area increases drag while smaller mass lowers weight, increasing deceleration.

options.label: C
options.text: Air resistance causes an overestimate of g because the sphere takes longer to hit the trapdoor.
options.distractorRationale: Longer fall time t reduces 2h/t², causing an underestimate of g.

options.label: D
options.text: High weight-to-drag ratio keeps air resistance negligible; alongside air drag, residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g.

markScheme.criterion: Finds k_s = 24.0 N m⁻¹ and total extension 500 mm.

items.stem: A uniform solid cylinder of mass m = 2.5 kg and radius r = 0.12 m has moment of inertia I = ½mr². It is released from rest and rolls without slipping down a slope at θ = 25° through a vertical drop of h = 1.8 m. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) I = 0.0180 kg m². (b) v = 4.85 m s⁻¹. (c) E_k,rot = 14.7 J. (d) a = 2.76 m s⁻², F_f = 3.45 N. (e) static friction acts up the incline to supply the torque required for angular acceleration while doing zero net work because the contact point is instantaneously at rest.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates I = ½mr² = 0.0180 kg m².
Applies mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω² with ω = v/r and g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Obtains bottom speed v = 4.85 m s⁻¹.
Applies E_k,rot = ½Iω² (or 1/3 mgh).
Obtains rotational KE = 14.7 J.
Calculates a = (2/3)g sin 25° = 2.76 m s⁻².
Applies τ = F_f r = Iα to obtain F_f = 3.45 N.
States static friction acts up the incline to exert the accelerating torque.
Explains the contact point has zero instantaneous velocity so friction does zero net work.

items.stem: A ball is launched from floor level across a flat room with an initial speed of 27 m s⁻¹ at 37° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes v_y = 0 at apex so v_apex = u cos θ.
Obtains 21.6 m s⁻¹.
Applies h_max = (u sin θ)² / (2g).
Obtains 13.5 m.
Evaluates R = u_x × (2u_y / g).
Obtains 71.4 m.

items.stem: A tennis ball is fired from a launcher on a level pitch at 18 m s⁻¹ and 60° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the pitch.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 18 sin 60° = 15.6 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 18 cos 60° = 9.00 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.81 = 3.18 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 28.6 m. Target = 28.6 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 28.6 m (C).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cos θ for sin θ in the flight-time expression.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: A metal block of mass 6.5 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 3.4 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 1.35 m in 0.16 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum tension in the cord at the lowest point B.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 3.4 + 1.35 = 4.75 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 332 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 449 N. Target = 449 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (3.4 + 1.35) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 449 N (A).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a horizontal beam of length L = 3.2 m and mass 14 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light vertical wires at A and B. The wires are 2.4 m apart. Its centre of gravity G lies 0.72 m to the right of A and 1.68 m to the left of B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B yield T₁ = 96.14 N ≈ 96.1 N. (b) Force balance gives T₂ = 41.20 N ≈ 41.2 N. (c) wire A carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire A.

markScheme.criterion: Applies moment balance about attachment B.
Applies ΣF_y = 0 to obtain T₂.
Identifies the wire closer to G as carrying greater tension.
Justifies using equal opposite moments about G with shorter lever arm.

parts.prompt: By taking moments about attachment B, calculate the tension T₁ in wire A.
workingSteps: Since wire A is vertical, T₁ = 96.14 N ≈ 96.1 N.

parts.prompt: Using vertical force equilibrium, determine the tension T₂ in wire B.
State which wire carries the greater tension and justify your answer qualitatively in terms of moments about the centre of gravity.
parts.expectedAnswer: In equilibrium, wire A carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire A.
workingSteps: Take moments about the centre of gravity so the weight has zero moment.
Show that the wire with the shorter perpendicular distance to G must exert the larger tension to balance moments.

items.stem: A small metal sphere of mass 1.4 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.2 m on a light wire. The wire breaks if the tension exceeds 33 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the sphere at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((33/1.4) − 9.81) × 1.2] = 4.06 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 4.06 m s⁻¹ (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds g instead of subtracting g when rearranging T_max − mg = mv²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a brass lever has length d = 0.68 m. Two equal and opposite parallel forces of magnitude F = 62 N act perpendicularly at its ends.
items.workedSolution: A rigid body is in equilibrium when it has zero resultant force and zero resultant moment about any point.

markScheme.criterion: Zero resultant force (translational equilibrium).
Zero resultant moment about any point (rotational equilibrium).

items.stem: A metal block of weight 680 N slides at a constant velocity down a rough slope. It travels 28 m along the slope through a vertical drop of 14.6 m.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p = W h (not W L).
Obtains 9.93 × 10³ J.
Uses constant speed (ΔE_k = 0) so F_res L = ΔE_p.
Obtains 355 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the loss of gravitational potential energy over the full descent.
Hence determine the mean resistive force acting up the slope.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 2.8 m and mass 8 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 4.5 kg hangs so its centre of gravity acts 2.4 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at 54° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal component of force exerted on the rod by hinge O.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about hinge O: T sin 54° × 2.8 = (8 × 1.4 + 4.5 × 2.4) × 9.81 = 215.8 N m. Hence T sin 54° = 77.08 N and T = 95.27 N ≈ 95.3 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos 54° = 56.00 N ≈ 56.0 N. Vertical balance: R_y = (8 + 4.5) × 9.81 − 77.08 = 45.55 N ≈ 45.5 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 56.0 N.

items.stem: A stone block of mass 8 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough wooden slope. The slope is 10 m long and inclined at 36° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 5.91 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = mgL sin θ.
Obtains 461 J.
Subtracts ½mv² from ΔE_p.
Obtains 322 J.
Applies W_f = μ(mg cos θ)L.
Obtains 0.506.

items.stem: In Searle's Young modulus investigation (RP4), a student tests a brass wire of unstretched length $(1.90 \pm 0.001)$ m. Micrometer diameter readings in perpendicular directions at three places average to 0.36 mm, 0.38 mm, and 0.37 mm (each $\pm 0.01$ mm). A graph of load $F$ against extension $e$ is a straight line through the origin of gradient 5.7 N mm⁻¹ ($\pm 2.4\%$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $A = \pi d^2/4 = 1.08 × 10⁻⁷ m²$. (b) $E = L(\mathrm{grad})/A = 101 GPa$. (c) $\%\Delta E = 7.86\%$. (d) an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while perpendicular micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Averages three diameters and converts mm to m in $A = \pi d^2/4$.
Cross-sectional area $A = 1.08 × 10⁻⁷ m²$.
Converts gradient to N m⁻¹ and substitutes into $E = (L/A)\,\mathrm{grad}$.
Young modulus $E = 101 GPa$.
Combines $\%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad}$.
Percentage uncertainty in $E = 7.86\%$.
Identical reference wire compensates both support sag and temperature expansion.
Perpendicular micrometer readings at >= 3 positions detect non-uniformity/oval cross-section.

Determine the Young modulus $E$ of the wire in GPa.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $E$.
Explain the purpose of the reference wire and why perpendicular micrometer readings are taken at three places.
parts.expectedAnswer: an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while perpendicular micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty
workingSteps: Identical reference wire cancels ceiling sag and thermal expansion equally on both scales.
Perpendicular readings at 3 positions check circularity and reduce random error in d².

items.stem: A lead bob of mass 0.9 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.3 m on a light steel cable. At the lowest point, its speed is 9 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the cable at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 0.9 × 9² / 1.3 = 56.1 N, so T = 56.1 + 0.9 × 9.81 = 64.9 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 64.9 N (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A spinning satellite in deep space pulls its extended side masses inward. Its angular momentum stays constant, yet its rotational kinetic energy increases. What supplies this extra rotational kinetic energy?
items.workedSolution: Since $E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{L^2}{2I}$ rises when $I$ decreases at constant $L$, internal radial forces do positive work pulling masses inward so rotational kinetic energy increases.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that internal radial forces do positive work pulling masses inward so rotational kinetic energy increases.

items.stem: Engineers evaluate a composite flywheel of moment of inertia 5.40 kg m² operating between 180 rad s⁻¹ and 156 rad s⁻¹ inside a backup generator set of total mass 1.05 × 10³ kg. On a test incline of road length 160 m rising 11.0 m vertically, the mean resistive drag force is 175 N. Take $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = 2.18 × 10⁴ J$. (b) $\Delta E_{\mathrm{p}} = 1.13 × 10⁵ J$. (c) Subtracting drag work 2.80 × 10⁴ J and dividing by $mg$ gives $h_{\max} = 0 m$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_{\max}^2 - \omega_{\min}^2)$.
Obtains 2.18 × 10⁴ J.
Uses $mgh$ with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Obtains 1.13 × 10⁵ J.
Computes drag work $F_{\mathrm{d}}s$ and subtracts from flywheel energy release.
Equates remaining energy to $mg h_{\max}$.
Obtains $h_{\max} = 0 m$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy released by the flywheel as it slows across its operating speed range.
Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy during the test incline.
workingSteps: Use $\Delta E_{\mathrm{p}} = m g \Delta h$ with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

parts.prompt: Assuming zero transmission losses and constant resistive work along the same road length, determine the maximum vertical height this flywheel energy release could lift the vehicle.
workingSteps: Work against drag $W_{\mathrm{d}} = F_{\mathrm{d}} s = 2.80 × 10⁴ J$.
Remaining energy for height gain $mgh_{\max} = \Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} - W_{\mathrm{d}}$.

items.stem: A sled of weight 1400 N slides down a snowy slope at a constant speed of 6.5 m s⁻¹. The ramp has length 22 m along the slope and a vertical drop of 11 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses F_f = W sin θ = W h / L at constant velocity.
Obtains 700 N.
Applies P = F_f v.
Obtains 4.55 × 10³ W.

items.stem: For the curved velocity–time graph of a falling parcel, point P lies at $t = 4.00\text{ s}$ where $v = 22.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The straight tangent line drawn at P crosses the vertical velocity axis ($t = 0$) at $v = 7.65\text{ m s}^{-1}$. What is the parcel's instantaneous acceleration at $t = 4.00\text{ s}$?
items.workedSolution: The tangent passes through $(0, 7.65\text{ m s}^{-1})$ and $(4.00\text{ s}, 22.0\text{ m s}^{-1})$, so $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{22.0 - 7.65}{4.00 - 0} = 3.59 m s⁻²$.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates tangent gradient $(22.0 - 7.65)/4.00 = 3.59 m s⁻²$.

items.stem: A high-pressure cleaning nozzle directs a horizontal jet of water at $15.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and mass flow rate $8.00\text{ kg s}^{-1}$ perpendicularly onto a flat vertical concrete wall.
items.workedSolution: (a) Newton second law in the form resultant force equals rate of change of momentum applies directly to systems whose mass is changing. (b) $F = 120 N$. (c) $F_{\text{rev}} = 240 N$. (d) $P = 900 W$.

markScheme.criterion: States F = ma requires constant mass.
Explains F = Δp/Δt accommodates continuous mass flow (Newton second law in the form resultant force equals rate of change of momentum applies directly to systems whose mass is changing).
Applies F = (Δm/Δt)Δv with Δv = 15.0 m s⁻¹.
Obtains F = 120 N.
Recognizes velocity reversal doubles momentum change Δv = 2v.
Obtains rebound force 240 N.
Applies P = ½(Δm/Δt)v².
Obtains kinetic power 900 W.

items.stem: Aircraft engineers compare aviation kerosene and liquid hydrogen using both specific energy and volumetric energy density. Which statement accurately distinguishes these two quantities?
items.workedSolution: Energy density (E/V, in J m⁻³) determines fuel-tank volume, while specific energy (E/m, in J kg⁻¹) determines fuel mass; they are linked by ρ. Therefore the correct statement is: Volumetric energy density is energy per unit volume in joules per cubic metre whereas specific energy is energy per unit mass in joules per kilogram.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: volumetric energy density is energy per unit volume in joules per cubic metre whereas specific energy is energy per unit mass in joules per kilogram.

options.distractorRationale: Swaps the SI definitions of volumetric energy density (J m⁻³) and specific energy (J kg⁻¹).

options.label: B
options.text: Both volumetric energy density and specific energy measure power output per unit mass in watts per kilogram.
options.distractorRationale: Both quantify stored energy per unit volume or mass, not rate of transfer (power).

options.label: C
options.text: Volumetric energy density is energy per unit volume in joules per cubic metre whereas specific energy is energy per unit mass in joules per kilogram.

options.label: D
options.text: Volumetric energy density equals specific energy divided by fuel density rather than multiplied by fuel density.
options.distractorRationale: Since E/V = (E/m)(m/V), volumetric energy density equals specific energy multiplied by density ρ.

items.stem: A motor shaft accelerates non-uniformly from $\omega_0 = 10.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ to steady speed $\omega_{\text{p}} = 70.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ over $t_1 = 6.00\text{ s}$ along the smooth curve $\omega(t) = 10.0 + 60.0\left[2(t/6.00) - (t/6.00)^2\right]$. A tangent drawn at $t = 2.00\text{ s}$ rises by $\Delta\omega = 40.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ over $\Delta t = 3.00\text{ s}$. What is the instantaneous angular acceleration at $t = 2.00\text{ s}$?
items.workedSolution: Instantaneous angular acceleration equals the gradient of the tangent to the $\omega$–$t$ curve: $\alpha = \frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t} = \frac{40.0}{3.00} = 13.3 rad s⁻²$ (matching $\frac{2(60.0)}{6.00}(1 - 2.00/6.00) = 13.3 rad s⁻²$).

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 13.3 rad s⁻².

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a heavy non-uniform trapdoor of length L = 1.8 m and mass 30 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.83 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 24° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) T = 148.5 N ≈ 149 N. (b) the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium. (c)(i) R_x = 60.42 N, R_y = 158.6 N, so R = 169.7 N ≈ 170 N. (c)(ii) α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 69.14° ≈ 69.1° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Στ = 0 about O using T cos(angle to vertical) × L = m g x_G.
Obtains T = 148.5 N (149 N) matching 1.5 × 10² N.
Identifies horizontal component of angled cable tension directed toward the wall.
States hinge must exert an equal opposite horizontal force away from the wall for ΣF_x = 0.
Computes R_x = 60.42 N and R_y = 158.6 N and applies Pythagoras.
Resultant hinge reaction magnitude R = 170 N.
Uses tan α = R_y / R_x with both hinge components.
Direction α = 69.1° above the horizontal.

parts.prompt: By taking moments about hinge O, show clearly that the tension T in the cable is approximately 1.5 × 10² N.
workingSteps: Vertical component of cable tension is T cos 24°.
Equate moments about O: T cos 24° × 1.8 = 30 × 9.81 × 0.83.

parts.prompt: Explain why hinge O must exert a horizontal component of force on the door, and state its direction.
parts.expectedAnswer: For horizontal equilibrium, the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium.
workingSteps: Identify that the inclined cable pulls horizontally toward the wall.
Conclude from zero horizontal resultant force that the hinge must push horizontally away from the wall.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant reaction force R exerted by hinge O on the door.
Determine the angle above the horizontal at which this resultant hinge force R acts.

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 11 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 3 m. It falls freely from rest at the fixed support to point A, where the cord becomes taut. It then stretches the cord by 1 m over 0.3 s before stopping at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.
items.workedSolution: (a) v_A = √(2 × 9.8 × 3). Answer: 7.67 m s⁻¹. (b) Mean resultant upward force = (11 × 7.67) / 0.3 = 281 N. F_mean = 281 + 11 × 9.8. Answer: 389 N. (c) T_B = 2 × 11 × 9.8 × (3 + 1) / 1. Answer: 862 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 7.67 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (11 × 7.67) / 0.3 = 281 N.
Obtains 389 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 862 N.

items.stem: A small lorry of mass 1600 kg accelerates along a level road while a small plumb bob hangs from its ceiling at 26° to the vertical. Later, the lorry climbs a straight 8° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 80 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.8. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 15 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 500 N toward the stop sign. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg => a = g tan θ.
Obtains 4.78 m s⁻².
Applies μ_s mg = m v_max² / R.
Obtains 25.1 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts resistive work F_res(πR) from initial kinetic energy ½mu².
Obtains 8.24 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By resolving forces on the bob, calculate the horizontal acceleration when the string hangs at 26° to the vertical.
Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular road without sliding.
Calculate the speed of the lorry when it reaches the stop sign at the end of the semicircular bend.

items.stem: A lead bob of mass 1.4 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.6 m attached to a light steel cable. The maximum tension the cable can hold without breaking is 39 N. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Writes T_max − mg = m v_max² / r at the lowest point.
Obtains 3.29 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By considering the forces acting on the bob at the lowest point, calculate the maximum speed at the bottom so the cable does not break.

items.stem: A brass ball of mass 2.3 kg hangs on a light string of length 0.8 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a wax block of mass 5.06 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string just before the ball strikes the block.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 3.96 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 67.7 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 1.24 m s⁻¹. Target = 67.7 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 67.7 N (B).

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 9.5 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 2.8 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 1.05 m in 0.14 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the spring constant of the cord.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 2.8 + 1.05 = 3.85 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 650 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 683 N. Target = 650 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (2.8 + 1.05) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 650 N m⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a dockside crane has total length L = 22 m and mass 1200 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 5.5 m from rear end A. A 3800 kg concrete counterweight sits 4.1 m to the left of P (1.4 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 4 m to the right of P (9.5 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 14 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) M_cw = 1.528 × 10⁵ N m ≈ 1.53 × 10⁵ N m. (b) Equating clockwise and anticlockwise moments about P gives m_max = 770.0 kg ≈ 770 kg. (c) Vertical force balance yields R = 5.660 × 10⁴ N ≈ 5.66 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses M = m g d with counterweight mass and lever arm from P.
Counterweight moment = 1.53 × 10⁵ N m.
Subtracts boom self-weight moment from counterweight moment and divides by g × load lever arm.
Maximum safe load mass = 770 kg.
Applies vertical force balance summing counterweight, boom, and load weights.
Upward mast reaction R = 5.66 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: On a smooth level track, cart X of mass 5.2 kg moves right at 14 m s⁻¹ and collides with stationary cart Y of mass 1.2 kg. Immediately after impact, cart Y moves right at 14.4 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of cart X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Momentum conservation: (5.2)(14) = (5.2)v_X + (1.2)(14.4), giving v_X = 10.7 m s⁻¹. K_i = 510 J and K_f = 421 J, so ΔK_lost = K_i − K_f = 88.8 J. Target = 10.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves linear momentum and evaluates kinetic energy budget to obtain 10.7 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: A student measures the viscosity η of a clear liquid in the laboratory. They use small steel ball bearings of several different diameters.
items.workedSolution: Measuring terminal velocity between markers below the surface balances weight against upthrust and Stokes drag to determine fluid viscosity. Measure ball diameter d in perpendicular directions using a micrometer (r = d/2), determine densities ρ_s and ρ_f via balance and volume, and release each sphere gently along the centre of a wide tall cylinder. Time descent between two rubber markers placed well below the meniscus (verify equal intervals across three markers so terminal speed is reached). Plot v against r²: the straight-line gradient equals 2(ρ_s − ρ_f)g/(9η), yielding η while keeping liquid temperature constant.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Measures sphere diameter at multiple orientations with a micrometer to find radius r = d/2.
L1: Places upper timing band well below liquid surface (and checks equal times across markers) to ensure terminal velocity.
L2: Releases spheres centrally in a wide cylinder to avoid wall drag and maintain slow laminar flow.
L2: Applies terminal force equilibrium W = U + 6πηrv to derive v = 2r²(ρ_s − ρ_f)g / (9η).
L3: Plots v against r² for multiple sphere sizes and extracts η from the gradient 2(ρ_s − ρ_f)g / (9η).
L3: Records and controls liquid temperature because liquid viscosity drops markedly as temperature rises.

parts.expectedAnswer: Measuring terminal velocity between markers below the surface balances weight against upthrust and Stokes drag to determine fluid viscosity. Measure ball diameter d in perpendicular directions using a micrometer (r = d/2), determine densities ρ_s and ρ_f via balance and volume, and release each sphere gently along the centre of a wide tall cylinder. Time descent between two rubber markers placed well below the meniscus (verify equal intervals across three markers so terminal speed is reached). Plot v against r²: the straight-line gradient equals 2(ρ_s − ρ_f)g/(9η), yielding η while keeping liquid temperature constant.
workingSteps: Detail micrometer measurement of r and density measurements of sphere and fluid.
Specify wide cylinder, timing markers below the surface, parallax reduction, and repeated timings.
Show terminal balance W = U + 6πηrv ⇒ v = [2(ρ_s − ρ_f)g/(9η)] r², plot v vs r², and control temperature.

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 2 kg moves right at 9 m s⁻¹ and strikes stationary trolley Y of mass 6.4 kg. Immediately after impact, trolley Y moves right at 3.62 m s⁻¹ and trolley X rebounds to the left. Calculate the kinetic energy lost in this rebound collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward positive, (2)(9) = (2)v_X + (6.4)(3.62) gives v_X = -2.58 m s⁻¹ (2.58 m s⁻¹ to the left). Scalar final kinetic energies add: K_f = ½(2)(2.58)² + ½(6.4)(3.62)² = 48.6 J. Energy lost = 81.0 J − K_f = 32.4 J. Target = 32.4 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds rebound speed 2.58 m s⁻¹ and sums scalar kinetic energies to obtain 32.4 J (D).

items.stem: A steel ball is fired from a spring launcher on level ground with an initial speed of 33 m s⁻¹ at 55° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.
items.workedSolution: (a) v_apex = 33 × cos 55°. Answer: 18.9 m s⁻¹. (b) u_y = 33 × sin 55° = 27.0 m s⁻¹. h_max = u_y² / (2 × 9.8). Answer: 37.3 m. (c) T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 5.52 s. R = 18.9 × T. Answer: 104 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes v_y = 0 at apex so v_apex = u cos θ.
Obtains 18.9 m s⁻¹.
Applies h_max = (u sin θ)² / (2g).
Obtains 37.3 m.
Evaluates R = u_x × (2u_y / g).
Obtains 104 m.

items.stem: A small steel ball of mass 0.8 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.5 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a block of clay of mass 2 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height above the lowest point reached by the joined objects.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 5.42 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 1.55 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.122 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 8.41 J. Target = 0.122 m.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 0.122 m (B).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform wooden plank AB has total length L = 4.6 m and mass 13 kg. Its centre of gravity G is at its midpoint, 2.3 m from end A. It rests horizontally on a sharp pivot P at 1.84 m from end A. A counterbalance block of unknown mass sits 0.46 m from end A. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) The moment of a force about a pivot is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. (b) Taking moments about P: m_load g (1.380) = (13) g (0.4600), giving m_load = 4.333 kg ≈ 4.33 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Product of force and distance from the pivot.
Specifies perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
Equates opposing moments about P using d_G = 0.4600 m and d_load = 1.380 m.
Obtains balancing mass m = 4.33 kg (4 s.f. 4.333 kg).

items.stem: A metal block of mass 5 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 2.6 m. It falls freely from rest at the fixed support to point A, where the cord becomes taut. It then stretches the cord by 1.2 m over 0.18 s before stopping at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 7.14 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (5 × 7.14) / 0.18 = 198 N.
Obtains 247 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 311 N.

items.stem: In a scattering experiment, a moving particle makes an elastic glancing collision with an identical stationary target particle. In radioactive alpha decay, a stationary heavy nucleus splits into an alpha particle and a heavy daughter nucleus.
items.workedSolution: An oblique elastic collision between identical spheres with one initially at rest sends them apart at ninety degrees. For identical masses m, vector momentum conservation forms a closed triangle p₀ = p₁ + p₂ while elastic kinetic energy conservation gives p₀²/(2m) = p₁²/(2m) + p₂²/(2m), simplifying to p₀² = p₁² + p₂². By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, p₁ and p₂ must be perpendicular (θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°). In decay from rest, equal and opposite momenta |p_α| = |p_daughter| make E_k = p²/(2m) inversely proportional to mass, so the much lighter alpha particle takes nearly all the kinetic energy.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Writes vector momentum conservation p₀ = p₁ + p₂ forming a closed vector triangle.
L1: States kinetic energy is conserved in an elastic collision and uses E_k = p²/(2m).
L2: Cancels common factor 1/(2m) for equal masses to derive p₀² = p₁² + p₂².
L2: Applies Pythagoras' theorem to prove the angle between p₁ and p₂ is exactly 90°.
L3: Applies momentum conservation from rest in alpha decay to show |p_α| = |p_daughter|.
L3: Uses E_k = p²/(2m) at equal p to deduce E_k ∝ 1/m, explaining why the much lighter alpha particle gets most kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Using vector momentum conservation and E_k = p²/(2m), prove why identical particles separate at 90° in an elastic glancing collision, and explain why the lighter alpha particle carries almost all the kinetic energy in alpha decay. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: An oblique elastic collision between identical spheres with one initially at rest sends them apart at ninety degrees. For identical masses m, vector momentum conservation forms a closed triangle p₀ = p₁ + p₂ while elastic kinetic energy conservation gives p₀²/(2m) = p₁²/(2m) + p₂²/(2m), simplifying to p₀² = p₁² + p₂². By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, p₁ and p₂ must be perpendicular (θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°). In decay from rest, equal and opposite momenta |p_α| = |p_daughter| make E_k = p²/(2m) inversely proportional to mass, so the much lighter alpha particle takes nearly all the kinetic energy.
workingSteps: Write vector momentum triangle p₀ = p₁ + p₂ for equal masses m.
Apply E_k = p²/(2m) for an elastic collision to deduce p₀² = p₁² + p₂² and invoke Pythagoras for 90° separation.
Apply equal-magnitude recoil momenta in decay to show E_k ∝ 1/m favours the lighter fragment.

items.stem: On a frictionless horizontal surface, block X of mass 2.5 kg moves to the right at 10 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with block Y of mass 2.4 kg moving to the left at 6 m s⁻¹ (arrow on Y not shown). Immediately after impact, block Y moves to the right at 3 m s⁻¹. Take motion to the right as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) p_before = 2.5 × 10 + 2.4 × (−6) = 10.6 kg m s⁻¹. Answer: 10.6 kg m s⁻¹ to the right. (b) v_X = (10.6 − 2.4 × 3) / 2.5 = 1.36 m s⁻¹. Answer: 1.36 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m_X u_X − m_Y |u_Y| with correct signs.
Obtains 10.6 kg m s⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform diving board of total length L = 5.2 m and mass 48 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is 0.4 m from the left end, and support B is 2.8 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 2 m. A technician of mass 66 kg initially stands 1.3 m from the left end of the plank. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B give F₁ = 540.3 N ≈ 540 N. (b) Vertical equilibrium gives F₂ = 578.1 N ≈ 578 N. (c) the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases. (d) Setting F₁ = 0 about B yields d_tip = 0.4364 m ≈ 0.436 m.

markScheme.criterion: Takes moments about B summing plank and technician anticlockwise moments.
Support A reaction F₁ = 540 N.
Support B reaction F₂ = 578 N via vertical force balance.
States that the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.
Sets F₁ = 0 and equates clockwise overhang moment to restoring plank moment about B.
Tipping distance past B = 0.436 m.

State qualitatively how the reaction forces at supports A and B change as the technician walks slowly toward the right-hand overhang.
parts.expectedAnswer: As the technician moves toward the overhang, the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.

items.stem: A ball is launched from floor level across a flat room at 14 m s⁻¹ and 34° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the floor.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 14 sin 34° = 7.83 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 14 cos 34° = 11.6 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 1.60 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 18.5 m. Target = 18.5 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 18.5 m (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies horizontal speed by ascent time u sin θ / g instead of full flight time 2u sin θ / g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cos θ for sin θ in the flight-time expression.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: A car of mass 1300 kg accelerates along a level road while a small steel bob hangs from its ceiling at 18° to the vertical. Later, the car climbs a straight 10° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 60 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.6. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 21 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 620 N toward the finish line. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular bend of radius 60 m without skidding.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 18° = ma and T cos 18° = mg => a = g tan 18° = 3.18 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.6 × 9.8 × 60) = 18.8 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1300)(21)² / 620 = 462 m. Target = 18.8 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 18.8 m s⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the static friction coefficient μ_s in μ_s mg = mv²/R.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides by μ_s instead of multiplying by μ_s.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes v² = μ_s g R without taking the square root.

items.stem: The velocity–time graph shows the vertical fall of a skydiver after jumping from a stationary balloon at the origin. The skydiver reaches free-fall terminal speed (Q), opens the parachute (R), and lands at a lower terminal speed (S).
items.workedSolution: Level 3 (5–6 marks): Drag grows with speed until equal to weight at terminal velocity and opening the parachute creates an upward resultant force; systematically applies N2L ($F = mg - D = ma$) and N1L ($F = 0$) across release, curved acceleration P, first plateau Q, parachute deceleration R (still moving downwards!), and second lower plateau S.

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): At release (v = 0), drag is zero so resultant force equals weight mg and initial acceleration is g (steepest gradient).
L1 (Area 1): As speed increases (region P), upward air resistance increases, so downward resultant force (mg − D) and acceleration (gradient) decrease (Newton's 2nd law).
L2 (Area 2): At Q, upward drag equals constant downward weight so resultant force is zero.
L2 (Area 2): By Newton's 1st law, acceleration is zero and the skydiver falls at a constant high terminal velocity vT1.
L3 (Area 3): At R, opening the parachute increases surface area so drag greatly exceeds weight, creating an upward resultant force that decelerates the downward motion (N2L).
L3 (Area 3): As speed decreases, drag falls until drag equals weight again at S, establishing a much lower constant terminal velocity vT2.

parts.prompt: Explain the shape of the entire velocity–time graph from release to S using Newton's first and second laws of motion, referring explicitly to weight, air resistance, resultant force, and acceleration at each stage.
parts.expectedAnswer: At release ($t = 0$), speed and air resistance are zero, so the downward resultant force equals weight $mg$ and initial downward acceleration equals $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ (steepest gradient, N2L). Drag grows with speed until equal to weight at terminal velocity and opening the parachute creates an upward resultant force: as speed rises through P, upward drag increases, reducing downward resultant force ($mg - D$) and acceleration so the curve gradient decreases. At Q, upward drag equals constant downward weight, resultant force is zero, and acceleration is zero so the skydiver falls at constant terminal velocity $v_{\text{T1}}$ (N1L). At R, opening the parachute greatly increases surface area and drag so $D \gg mg$, creating a large upward resultant force opposing downward velocity and causing rapid deceleration (N2L). As downward speed drops, drag decreases until $D = mg$ once more at S, giving a lower constant terminal speed $v_{\text{T2}}$.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Initial release (v=0 -> D=0 -> a=g) and rising drag reducing downward resultant force and v-t gradient (N2L).
Area 2 (L2): First terminal velocity Q where drag = weight -> resultant force = 0 -> constant speed (N1L).
Area 3 (L3): Parachute opening R raises area -> D >> mg -> upward resultant force decelerates skydiver -> drag drops until D = mg at lower terminal speed S.

items.stem: A parcel of mass 9.5 kg slides from rest down a rough ramp of length 5 m inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 4.55 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the magnitude of the constant friction force opposing its motion.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 30° − ½mv² = 135 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 5 = 26.9 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.22 m s⁻¹. Target = 26.9 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 26.9 N (A).

items.stem: A metal block of mass 5.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a straight incline of length 10.5 m, inclined at 28° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 7.77 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy dissipated against friction during the slide.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 28° = 266 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(5.5)(7.77)² = 166 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 99.7 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 28°)L, μ = 0.199. Target = 99.7 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 28° accurately to obtain 99.7 J (C).

items.stem: A rubber block of mass 15.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough concrete slope. The slope has length 10 m and is inclined at 22° to the horizontal. It slides against a constant friction force and reaches the bottom at 6.85 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mgL sin θ − ½mv².
Obtains 205 J.
Divides dissipated energy from (a) by ramp length L.
Obtains 20.5 N.
Recognizes unchanged acceleration and applies v² ∝ s => v_new = v / √2.
Obtains 4.84 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 1.3 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.9 m on a strong string. At the lowest point, its speed is 9.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.3 × 9.5² / 1.9 = 61.8 N, so T = 61.8 + 1.3 × 9.8 = 74.5 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 74.5 N (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A uniform concrete beam of length L = 3.50 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a rectangular cross-section of width w = 24.0 cm and thickness h = 11.0 cm, with average density ρ = 2360 kg m⁻³. It is uniform along its length, so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. An electric hoist motor of electrical input power 760 W and efficiency 79% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.02640 m², V = A L = 0.09240 m³, m = ρ V = 218.1 kg ≈ 218 kg. (b) W = 2139 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 1070 N ≈ 1.07 × 10³ N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.750 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 3744 J ≈ 3.74 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.79 × 760 = 600.4 W, so t = 3744 / 600.4 = 6.235 s ≈ 6.24 s. (e) electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates cross-section A = 0.02640 m², volume V = 0.09240 m³, and applies m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 218.1 kg confirming 218 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 3.50 = m g × 1.750.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 1.07 × 10³ N (4 s.f. 1070 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.750 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 3.74 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 3744 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 600.4 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 6.24 s (4 s.f. 6.235 s).
Identifies electrical heating in motor windings and mechanical friction in hoist gears.
Links losses to thermal energy dissipated to the surroundings (electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings).

items.stem: A small steel ball of mass 1.6 kg hangs on a light string of length 0.9 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a block of clay of mass 1.28 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the mechanical energy lost during the collision.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 4.20 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 2.33 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.278 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 6.27 J. Target = 6.27 J.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 6.27 J (C).

items.stem: A tennis ball is fired from a launcher on a level pitch at 27 m s⁻¹ and 24° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height reached above the pitch.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 24° = 24.7 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 24°)² / (2g) = 6.15 m. Target = 6.15 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 24° at apex to obtain 6.15 m (B).

items.stem: A golf ball is hit from flat ground at a speed of 30 m s⁻¹ and an angle of 26° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates u_y = u sin θ.

Applies T = 2u_y / g.
Obtains 2.68 s.
Multiplies u cos θ by flight time T.
Obtains 72.3 m.

items.stem: A metal cylinder of mass 8 kg is attached to an elastic rope of natural length 2.2 m. It falls from rest at the fixed upper support, and the rope obeys Hooke's law once it becomes taut at point A. The rope stretches by a maximum extension of 1.15 m in 0.18 s before the cylinder stops at the lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Uses free-fall relation v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 6.57 m s⁻¹.
Equates mg(L + x) = ½kx² over the complete vertical drop.
Obtains 398 N m⁻¹.
Evaluates a_B = (kx − mg) / m.
Obtains 47.3 m s⁻².

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a horizontal metal bar of length L = 3.8 m and mass 14 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light vertical wires at A and B. The wires are 3.1 m apart. Its centre of gravity G lies 2.23 m to the right of A and 0.87 m to the left of B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the tension T₂ in wire B.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: T₁_y × 3.1 = 14 × 9.81 × 0.87 ⇒ T₁_y = 38.54 N, T₂_y = 98.80 N. For vertical wires, T₁ = 38.54 N ≈ 38.5 N and T₂ = 98.80 N ≈ 98.8 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct wire tension = 98.8 N.

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 0.8 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.4 m on a strong string. The string breaks if the tension exceeds 38 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the ball at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((38/0.8) − 9.81) × 1.4] = 7.26 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 7.26 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a control wheel bar has length d = 0.8 m. Two equal and opposite parallel forces of magnitude F = 50 N act at its ends, each at 50° to the bar. What is the magnitude of the torque of this couple?
items.workedSolution: Perpendicular separation between the parallel lines of action is d_perp = d sin 50° = 0.6128 m. Torque of the couple: T = F d_perp = 50 × 0.6128 = 30.64 N m ≈ 30.6 N m.

markScheme.criterion: Correct couple torque = 30.6 N m.

items.stem: A metal block of weight 120 N slides at a constant speed down a rough slope. The slope has length 9 m and vertical height 4.3 m. Calculate the gravitational potential energy lost over the full length of the slope.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed ΔE_k = 0. Potential energy lost = W h = 120 × 4.3 = 516 J. Parallel equilibrium gives F_res = W sin θ = W h / L = 57.3 N. Target = 516 J.

markScheme.criterion: Uses sin θ = 4.3/9 and zero net force to obtain 516 J (A).

items.stem: A uniform rectangular shelf of length L = 1 m and mass 13 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall along its left edge O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium by an upward vertical force F at its outer edge, 1 m from hinge O. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) F = ½ m g = 63.77 N ≈ 63.8 N. (b) Since R + F = W and R = 63.77 N, for a uniform horizontal flap only three vertical forces act and taking moments about the outer end shows the hinge supports half the weight.

markScheme.criterion: Applies principle of moments about O with CG at midpoint L/2.
States vertical equilibrium or moments about the outer edge.
Concludes the uniform weight is shared equally so hinge reaction equals half the weight.

parts.prompt: Calculate the vertical upward force F needed at the outer edge to hold the flap horizontal.
workingSteps: Take moments about hinge O: F × 1 = 13 × 9.81 × 0.5.

parts.prompt: Explain why the upward reaction force exerted by hinge O on the uniform flap has the same magnitude as F.
parts.expectedAnswer: The hinge reaction matches the outer force because for a uniform horizontal flap only three vertical forces act and taking moments about the outer end shows the hinge supports half the weight.
workingSteps: Note that all forces acting on the uniform horizontal flap are purely vertical.
Show via vertical force balance or moments about the outer edge that the hinge shares the weight equally with the outer lift force.

items.stem: A sled of mass 11 kg is released from rest at the top of a snowy slope of length 10.5 m, inclined at 40° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 9.44 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the coefficient of kinetic friction μ (defined by F_f = μ R) between the sled and the slope.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 40° = 728 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(11)(9.44)² = 490 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 238 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 40°)L, μ = 0.274. Target = 0.274.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 40° accurately to obtain 0.274 (C).

items.stem: During Required Practical 4 on a yellow brass wire of length $L = 1.90$ m, three micrometer diameter pairs average to 0.36 mm, 0.38 mm, and 0.37 mm. The linear elastic graph of force $F$ against extension $e$ has gradient 5.7 N mm⁻¹. Determine the Young modulus $E$ in GPa.
items.workedSolution: Mean diameter $d = 0.37$ mm gives $A = \pi d^2/4 = 1.08 × 10⁻⁷ m²$. $E = L \times \mathrm{grad} / A = 101 GPa$. Percentage uncertainty $\%\Delta E = \%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad} = 0.0526 + 2(2.70) + 2.4 = 7.86\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates youngModulusGPa $= 101 GPa$.

items.stem: A small metal sphere of mass 2.7 kg is attached to a light wire of length 1.3 m. It moves in a vertical circle and passes through the lowest point at 5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_c = mv² / r.
Obtains 51.9 N.
Applies T − mg = F_c => T = F_c + mg.
Obtains 78.4 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant centripetal force on the sphere at the lowest point.
Hence calculate the tension in the wire at the lowest point.

items.stem: Two clutch discs share a frictionless vertical shaft. One has moment of inertia $I_1 = 1.50 kg m²$ spinning at 36.0 rad s⁻¹, and the other has $I_2 = 0.900 kg m²$ spinning at −12.0 rad s⁻¹. The discs engage and reach a common angular speed after slipping for 0.900 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\omega_{\mathrm{f}} = 18.0 rad s⁻¹$. (b) Mean clutch torque $= \frac{I_2|\omega_{\mathrm{f}} - \omega_2|}{\Delta t} = 30.0 N m$. (c) Energy dissipated $= 648 J$ as heat from sliding friction.

markScheme.criterion: Applies conservation of angular momentum $(I_1 + I_2)\omega_{\mathrm{f}} = I_1\omega_1 + I_2\omega_2$.
Obtains $\omega_{\mathrm{f}} = 18.0 rad s⁻¹$.
Applies angular impulse $T\Delta t = \Delta(I_2\omega_2)$.
Obtains mean torque $= 30.0 N m$.
Computes both initial and final total rotational kinetic energy.
Obtains energy loss $= 648 J$.
States that energy is dissipated as thermal energy due to friction while the plates slip.

parts.prompt: Calculate the common angular velocity of the coupled discs.
workingSteps: Conserve angular momentum: $(I_1 + I_2)\omega_{\mathrm{f}} = I_1\omega_1 + I_2\omega_2$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the mean friction torque exerted on Disc 2 during the slipping interval.
workingSteps: Angular impulse on Disc 2 is $I_2|\omega_{\mathrm{f}} - \omega_2| = 27.0 N m s$.
Divide by $\Delta t = 0.900 s$ to obtain $T = 30.0 N m$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the rotational kinetic energy lost during engagement and explain physically what happens to it.
parts.expectedAnswer: 648 J; kinetic energy decreases because thermal energy is dissipated by friction between slipping clutch plates.
workingSteps: Initial KE $= 1.04 × 10³ J$, final KE $= 389 J$.
Energy lost $= 648 J$, dissipated as thermal energy by sliding friction between the clutch surfaces.

items.stem: A single-cylinder generator engine is coupled to a cast-iron flywheel of moment of inertia 4.80 kg m². During each four-stroke cycle its angular speed fluctuates between 172 rad s⁻¹ and 148 rad s⁻¹. What energy is represented by the shaded area above the mean-load torque line on the turning-moment diagram?
items.workedSolution: The shaded energy loop equals the cyclic kinetic energy exchange $\Delta E = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_{\max}^2 - \omega_{\min}^2) = \frac{1}{2}(4.80)(172^2 - 148^2) = 1.84 × 10⁴ J$.

markScheme.criterion: Cyclic flywheel energy exchange equals 1.84 × 10⁴ J.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Squares the speed difference instead of taking the difference of squares.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of one-half in $\frac{1}{2}I(\omega_{\max}^2 - \omega_{\min}^2)$.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes total stored kinetic energy rather than cyclic fluctuation energy.

items.stem: A sled of weight 850 N slides down a snowy slope at a constant speed of 5.5 m s⁻¹. The ramp is 32 m long and drops by 9.6 m vertically. Calculate the magnitude of the friction force acting up the ramp.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed, friction balances downslope weight: F_f = W(h/L) = 850 × (9.6/32) = 255 N. Rate of thermal energy generation P = F_f v = 1.40 × 10³ W. Target = 255 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_f = Wh/L and P = F_f v to obtain 255 N (D).

items.stem: A geology drone releases a marker dart from a canyon rim $42.0\text{ m}$ above the canyon floor at initial speed $18.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ directed $25.0^\circ$ below the horizontal ($g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $t = 2.25 s$. (b) $R = 36.7 m$. (c) Impact angle $= 61.2°$ below horizontal. (d) fluid resistance reduces the maximum height and horizontal range and produces an asymmetric path with a steeper descent.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves initial downward velocity u_y = 18.0 sin 25.0° = 7.61 m s⁻¹.
Substitutes into 42.0 = 7.61t + 4.9t² with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Solves quadratic for positive root t = 2.25 s.
Computes u_x = 18.0 cos 25.0° and multiplies by flight time.
Obtains horizontal range R = 36.7 m.
Finds v_y = u_y + gt and uses tan θ = v_y / u_x.
Obtains impact angle 61.2°.

items.stem: A traffic signal of mass m hangs at rest from two asymmetrical cables shown in the free-body diagram. Which condition must hold for the knot to remain in translational equilibrium?
items.workedSolution: By Newton's first law, translational equilibrium requires ΣF = 0, so both ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 at the same time. Therefore the correct statement is: For a body in translational equilibrium the resultant force is zero so perpendicular force components balance in every direction.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: for a body in translational equilibrium the resultant force is zero so perpendicular force components balance in every direction.

options.label: D
options.text: The resultant horizontal force must equal the weight while vertical forces cancel to zero.
options.distractorRationale: Both horizontal and vertical resultant force components must each equal zero in equilibrium.

items.stem: The diagram shows the rotor of an automated steel-shearing flywheel. Its central hub has moment of inertia 1.10 kg m² and carries 8 rim masses of 0.750 kg each at radius 0.500 m. During a test run lasting 12.0 s, the rotational speed changes uniformly from 5.00 rev s⁻¹ to 17.0 rev s⁻¹ while a constant bearing friction torque of 2.50 N m opposes rotation.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I = 2.60 kg m²$. (b) $|\alpha| = \frac{2\pi|f_2 - f_1|}{t} = 6.28 rad s⁻²$. (c) Applied torque $T_{\mathrm{app}} = 18.8 N m$. (d) Peak power $P_{\max} = T_{\mathrm{app}}\omega_{\max} = 2.01 × 10³ W$.

Obtains $I = 2.60 kg m²$.
Converts $\text{rev s}^{-1}$ to $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ via $2\pi$ and divides change by $t$.
Obtains $|\alpha| = 6.28 rad s⁻²$.
Combines $I|\alpha|$ with bearing friction torque in the correct sense.
Obtains applied torque $= 18.8 N m$.
Applies $P = T\omega$ at the highest angular speed.
Obtains maximum power $= 2.01 × 10³ W$.

items.stem: A rotating shaft has a non-uniform angular acceleration. What physical quantities are given by the tangent gradient and the area under its $\omega$–$t$ graph?
items.workedSolution: Just as for linear $v$–$t$ graphs, the gradient gives instantaneous angular acceleration and area beneath gives angular displacement.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that gradient gives instantaneous angular acceleration and area beneath gives angular displacement.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a non-uniform metal hatch of length L = 2.2 m and mass 28 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.79 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 38° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the magnitude of the resultant reaction force R exerted on the door by hinge O.
items.workedSolution: Moments about O: T cos 38° × 2.2 = 28 × 9.81 × 0.79 ⇒ T = 125.2 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T sin 38° = 77.06 N. Vertical balance: R_y = 28 × 9.81 − T cos 38° = 176.0 N. Resultant R = √(R_x² + R_y²) = 192.2 N ≈ 192 N, at angle α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 66.36° ≈ 66.4° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 192 N.

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 12 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 1.8 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the cord becomes taut, and then stretches it by 1.3 m in 0.18 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward force exerted by the cord between A and B.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.8 × 1.8) = 5.94 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.18 + 12(9.8) = 514 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 514 N (A).

items.stem: A small lorry of mass 1200 kg accelerates along a level road while a small plumb bob hangs from its ceiling at 18° to the vertical. Later, the lorry climbs a straight 10° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 50 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.55. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 16 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 380 N toward the stop sign. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 18°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 18° = ma and T cos 18° = mg => a = g tan 18° = 3.19 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.55 × 9.81 × 50) = 16.4 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1200)(16)² / 380 = 404 m. Target = 3.19 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 3.19 m s⁻² (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

markScheme.criterion: Writes T_max − mg = m v_max² / r at the lowest point.
Obtains 5.44 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A brass ball of mass 0.3 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.8 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a wax block of mass 0.66 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string just before the ball strikes the block.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 5.94 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 8.83 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 1.86 m s⁻¹. Target = 8.83 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 8.83 N (D).

items.stem: Two stationary trolleys of masses m₁ = 1.4 kg and m₂ = 3.5 kg on a frictionless track are pushed apart by an internal spring. Trolley 1 moves left at 2.8 m s⁻¹. Calculate the recoil speed v₂ of trolley 2 to the right.
items.workedSolution: By momentum conservation from rest, m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ → v₂ = (1.4 × 2.8) / 3.5 = 1.12 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates recoil speed v₂ = 1.12 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A metal block of mass 11 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 3 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.45 m in 0.2 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the spring constant of the cord.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 3 + 0.45 = 3.45 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 3.67 × 10³ N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 1.65 × 10³ N. Target = 3.67 × 10³ N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (3 + 0.45) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 3.67 × 10³ N m⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a lifting crane has total length L = 15 m and mass 550 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 4.5 m from rear end A. A 1800 kg concrete counterweight sits 3.3 m to the left of P (1.2 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 4 m to the right of P (8.5 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 10 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum safe load weight at the hook without tipping clockwise about P.
items.workedSolution: Anticlockwise counterweight moment about P: M_cw = 1800 × 9.81 × 3.3 = 5.827 × 10⁴ N m. Clockwise boom moment: M_boom = 550 × 9.81 × 4 = 2.158 × 10⁴ N m. Remaining clockwise moment available for load: W_max × 10 = 3.669 × 10⁴ N m ⇒ W_max = 3669 N ≈ 3.67 × 10³ N, m_max = W_max / 9.81 = 374.0 kg ≈ 374 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct maximum safe load weight = 3.67 × 10³ N.

items.stem: In a statics experiment, a timber beam AB has length L = 4.2 m and mass 19 kg. Its centre of gravity G lies 2.1 m from end A. It is balanced horizontally on a pivot P at 1.34 m from end A by placing a 28 kg block to the left of P. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate how far from end B the 28 kg block must be placed for horizontal equilibrium.
items.workedSolution: Distance of CG from pivot P: d_G = 2.1 − 1.34 = 0.7600 m. Taking moments about P: 28 × d = 19 × 0.7600 ⇒ d = 0.5157 m left of P. Position from end A is x_A = 1.34 − 0.5157 = 0.8243 m. Therefore distance from end B is L − x_A = 4.2 − 0.8243 = 3.376 m ≈ 3.38 m.

markScheme.criterion: Correct distance from end B = 3.38 m.

items.stem: A sandbag of mass 8 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 2 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the cord becomes taut, and then stretches it by 0.5 m in 0.33 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward force exerted by the cord between A and B.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.81 × 2) = 6.26 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.33 + 8(9.81) = 230 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 230 N (A).

items.stem: Following an oblique air-table collision, target glider B of mass 0.800 kg recoils with vector momentum of magnitude $p_2 = 2.51\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$. Using $E_k = p^2/(2m)$, calculate the kinetic energy of glider B.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_k = p²/(2m) to obtain 3.95 J.

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 3 kg moves to the right at 11 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with trolley Y of mass 4.2 kg moving to the left at 3.5 m s⁻¹ (arrow not shown). Immediately after the collision, trolley Y moves right at 3 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of trolley X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward as positive: p_before = (3)(11) + (4.2)(−3.5) = 18.3 kg m s⁻¹. From p_before = (3)v_X + (4.2)(3), v_X = 1.90 m s⁻¹, which is 1.90 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Uses signed head-on momentum p_before = 18.3 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 1.90 m s⁻¹ to the right (C).

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform diving board of total length L = 5.8 m and mass 52 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is 0.8 m from the left end, and support B is 3 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 2 m. A technician of mass 70 kg initially stands 2.3 m from the left end of the plank. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate how far past support B the technician can walk before the plank begins to tip.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: F₁ × 3 = (52 × 0.9000 + 70 × 1.500) × 9.81 ⇒ F₁ = 496.4 N ≈ 496 N. At tipping (F₁ = 0): m_load × d_tip = m_beam × (x_B − x_G) ⇒ d_tip = (52 × 0.9000) / 70 = 0.6686 m ≈ 0.669 m. At the very tip (overhang 2 m): m_end = (52 × 0.9000) / 2 = 23.40 kg ≈ 23.4 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct solver-verified answer = 0.669 m.
