items.stem: A steel ball is fired from a spring launcher on level ground at 36 m s⁻¹ and 38° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the ground.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 36 sin 38° = 22.2 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 36 cos 38° = 28.4 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 4.52 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 128 m. Target = 128 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 128 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies horizontal speed by ascent time u sin θ / g instead of full flight time 2u sin θ / g.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cos θ for sin θ in the flight-time expression.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: A small lorry of mass 1600 kg accelerates along a level road while a small plumb bob hangs from its ceiling at 34° to the vertical. Later, the lorry climbs a straight 10° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 85 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.5. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 22 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 560 N toward the stop sign. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 34°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 34° = ma and T cos 34° = mg => a = g tan 34° = 6.61 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.5 × 9.8 × 85) = 20.4 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1600)(22)² / 560 = 691 m. Target = 6.61 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 6.61 m s⁻² (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: The force–time graph compares two cars of equal mass stopping from the same speed. One has a rigid front and the other has a front crumple zone. Why does the crumple zone reduce injury to passengers?
items.workedSolution: Both curves enclose equal area ($\Delta p = F\Delta t$); same change in momentum over a longer impact time reduces average force on occupants. Therefore option D is correct: same change in momentum over a longer impact time reduces average force on occupants.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: same change in momentum over a longer impact time reduces average force on occupants.

options.text: Because both cars undergo the same impulse, the crumple zone reduces the total change in momentum to zero
options.distractorRationale: Stopping from the same initial speed always requires the exact same momentum change Δp = −mv.

options.label: B
options.text: Because both cars undergo the same impulse, the crumple zone shortens impact time to dissipate kinetic energy faster
options.distractorRationale: Shorter impact time raises peak force F = Δp/Δt, worsening occupant injury.

options.label: C
options.text: Because both cars undergo the same impulse, the shaded area under the crumple-zone curve is much smaller
options.distractorRationale: Area under F–t equals impulse Δp, which is identical for both collisions.

options.label: D
options.text: Because both cars undergo the same impulse, same change in momentum over a longer impact time reduces average force on occupants

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 15.5 kg slides from rest down a rough wooden ramp of length 3 m inclined at 34° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 4.59 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the magnitude of the constant friction force opposing its motion.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 34° − ½mv² = 91.8 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 3 = 30.6 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.25 m s⁻¹. Target = 30.6 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 30.6 N (B).

items.stem: A sled of mass 16 kg is released from rest at the top of a snowy slope of length 3.5 m, inclined at 44° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 3.59 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the coefficient of dynamic friction μ_d between the sled and the slope.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 44° = 381 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(16)(3.59)² = 103 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 278 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 44°)L, μ = 0.705. Target = 0.705.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 44° accurately to obtain 0.705 (A).

Obtains 159 J.

items.stem: A steel ball of mass 3.1 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.7 m on a light string. At the lowest point, its speed is 7.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 3.1 × 7.5² / 1.7 = 103 N, so T = 103 + 3.1 × 9.8 = 133 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 133 N (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A uniform composite beam of length L = 2.90 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a rectangular cross-section of width w = 28.0 cm and thickness h = 14.0 cm, with average density ρ = 1850 kg m⁻³. It is uniform along its length, so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. An electric hoist motor of electrical input power 680 W and efficiency 78% is attached to end B. It lifts end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.03920 m², V = A L = 0.1137 m³, m = ρ V = 210.3 kg ≈ 210 kg. (b) W = 2063 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 1032 N ≈ 1.03 × 10³ N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.450 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 2992 J ≈ 2.99 × 10³ J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.78 × 680 = 530.4 W, so t = 2992 / 530.4 = 5.640 s ≈ 5.64 s. (e) density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

markScheme.criterion: Computes cross-section A = w h = 0.03920 m² with cm → m conversion.
Calculates V = A L = 0.1137 m³ and substitutes m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 210.3 kg rounding clearly to 210 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 2.90 = m g × 1.450.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 1.03 × 10³ N (4 s.f. 1032 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.450 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 2.99 × 10³ J (4 s.f. 2992 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 530.4 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 5.64 s (4 s.f. 5.640 s).
States valid physical assumption: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 1.4 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.4 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 1.12 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height above the lowest point reached by the joined objects.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 5.24 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 2.91 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.432 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 8.54 J. Target = 0.432 m.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 0.432 m (D).

items.stem: A small ball is projected from level ground with an initial speed of 33 m s⁻¹ at 28° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes v_y = 0 at apex so v_apex = u cos θ.
Obtains 29.1 m s⁻¹.
Applies h_max = (u sin θ)² / (2g).
Obtains 12.2 m.
Evaluates R = u_x × (2u_y / g).
Obtains 92.0 m.

Calculate the maximum vertical height reached above the ground.

items.stem: A ball is launched from floor level across a flat room at 34 m s⁻¹ and 38° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the floor.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 34 sin 38° = 20.9 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 34 cos 38° = 26.8 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.81 = 4.27 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 114 m. Target = 114 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 114 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies horizontal speed by ascent time u sin θ / g instead of full flight time 2u sin θ / g.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cos θ for sin θ in the flight-time expression.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: A metal cylinder of mass 6.5 kg is attached to an elastic rope of natural length 4 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.55 m in 0.32 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the spring constant of the rope.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 4 + 0.55 = 4.55 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 1.92 × 10³ N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 1.06 × 10³ N. Target = 1.92 × 10³ N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (4 + 0.55) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 1.92 × 10³ N m⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a horizontal metal bar of length L = 2.6 m and mass 34 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light vertical wires at A and B. The wires are 1.9 m apart. Its centre of gravity G lies 1.18 m to the right of A and 0.72 m to the left of B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B yield T₁ = 126.4 N ≈ 126 N. (b) Force balance gives T₂ = 207.1 N ≈ 207 N. (c) wire B carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire B.

markScheme.criterion: Applies moment balance about attachment B.
Applies ΣF_y = 0 to obtain T₂.
Identifies the wire closer to G as carrying greater tension.
Justifies using equal opposite moments about G with shorter lever arm.

parts.prompt: By taking moments about attachment B, calculate the tension T₁ in wire A.
workingSteps: Since wire A is vertical, T₁ = 126.4 N ≈ 126 N.

parts.prompt: Using vertical force equilibrium, determine the tension T₂ in wire B.
State which wire carries the greater tension and justify your answer qualitatively in terms of moments about the centre of gravity.
parts.expectedAnswer: In equilibrium, wire B carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire B.
workingSteps: Take moments about the centre of gravity so the weight has zero moment.
Show that the wire with the shorter perpendicular distance to G must exert the larger tension to balance moments.

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 2.2 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 2 m on a strong string. The string breaks if the tension exceeds 95 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the ball at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((95/2.2) − 9.81) × 2] = 8.17 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 8.17 m s⁻¹ (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds g instead of subtracting g when rearranging T_max − mg = mv²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a brass lever has length d = 0.44 m. Two equal and opposite parallel forces of magnitude F = 134 N act perpendicularly at its ends.
items.workedSolution: (a) Static equilibrium requires zero resultant force and zero resultant moment about any point. (b) Torque of the couple is T = F d_perp = 58.96 N m ≈ 59.0 N m (note N m, not J).

markScheme.criterion: Zero resultant force.
Zero resultant moment about any point.
Applies T = F d_perp using perpendicular separation.
Torque = 59.0 N m with unit N m.

items.stem: A uniform rectangular shelf of length L = 1.3 m and mass 6 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall along its left edge O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium by an upward vertical force F at its outer edge, 1.3 m from hinge O. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the magnitude of the upward vertical force F.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about wall hinge O: F × L = m g (L / 2) ⇒ F = ½ m g = 0.5 × 6 × 9.81 = 29.43 N ≈ 29.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct vertical holding force F = 29.4 N.

Obtains 0.264.

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 1.9 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.6 m on a strong string. At the lowest point, its speed is 3.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.9 × 3.5² / 0.6 = 38.8 N, so T = 38.8 + 1.9 × 9.81 = 57.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 57.4 N (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: An upper clutch plate of moment of inertia 0.90 kg m² spins freely at 50.0 rad s⁻¹ on a frictionless vertical shaft. It drops directly onto a stationary lower plate of moment of inertia 1.60 kg m² on the same shaft. Calculate their common angular velocity once slipping stops.
items.workedSolution: With no external torque, $(I_1 + I_2)\omega_{\mathrm{f}} = I_1\omega_1$. Thus $\omega_{\mathrm{f}} = \frac{0.90 \times 50.0}{0.90 + 1.60} = 18.0 rad s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Common final angular velocity equals 18.0 rad s⁻¹.

items.stem: Engineers evaluate a composite flywheel of moment of inertia 3.10 kg m² operating between 480 rad s⁻¹ and 160 rad s⁻¹ inside a mountain-shuttle railcar of total mass 1.42 × 10³ kg. On a test incline of road length 260 m rising 18.0 m vertically, the mean resistive drag force is 260 N. Take $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = 3.17 × 10⁵ J$. (b) $\Delta E_{\mathrm{p}} = 2.51 × 10⁵ J$. (c) Subtracting drag work 6.76 × 10⁴ J and dividing by $mg$ gives $h_{\max} = 17.9 m$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_{\max}^2 - \omega_{\min}^2)$.
Obtains 3.17 × 10⁵ J.
Uses $mgh$ with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Obtains 2.51 × 10⁵ J.
Computes drag work $F_{\mathrm{d}}s$ and subtracts from flywheel energy release.
Equates remaining energy to $mg h_{\max}$.
Obtains $h_{\max} = 17.9 m$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy released by the flywheel as it slows across its operating speed range.
Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy during the test incline.
workingSteps: Use $\Delta E_{\mathrm{p}} = m g \Delta h$ with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

parts.prompt: Assuming zero transmission losses and constant resistive work along the same road length, determine the maximum vertical height this flywheel energy release could lift the vehicle.
workingSteps: Work against drag $W_{\mathrm{d}} = F_{\mathrm{d}} s = 6.76 × 10⁴ J$.
Remaining energy for height gain $mgh_{\max} = \Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} - W_{\mathrm{d}}$.

items.stem: A parcel of weight 1550 N slides down a straight slope at a constant speed of 2.5 m s⁻¹. The ramp has length 10 m along the slope and a vertical drop of 6 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses F_f = W sin θ = W h / L at constant velocity.
Obtains 930 N.
Applies P = F_f v.
Obtains 2.33 × 10³ W.

items.stem: A skydiver falls vertically through air and produces the curved velocity–time graph shown. How is the skydiver's instantaneous acceleration at point P correctly determined from this graph?
items.workedSolution: For non-uniform acceleration, a = dv/dt is represented geometrically by the gradient of the tangent line touching the v–t curve at point P. Therefore the correct statement is: Instantaneous acceleration on a curved velocity-time graph equals the gradient of the tangent drawn at that instant.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: instantaneous acceleration on a curved velocity-time graph equals the gradient of the tangent drawn at that instant.

Obtains 0.156 m.

items.stem: A heavy lamp hangs stationary from two cables attached to a ceiling. Which statement correctly defines a Newton third-law force pair in this system?
items.workedSolution: Newton's third law describes mutual interactions: equal magnitude, opposite direction, identical force nature, acting on two separate bodies. Therefore the correct statement is: A Newton third-law force pair consists of two forces of the same type equal in magnitude and opposite in direction acting on two different bodies.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: a Newton third-law force pair consists of two forces of the same type equal in magnitude and opposite in direction acting on two different bodies.

options.text: Two opposing forces acting on the same body whose vector sum equals zero in translational equilibrium.
options.distractorRationale: Balanced forces on one body illustrate Newton's first law, not a third-law interaction pair.

options.label: B
options.text: A Newton third-law force pair consists of two forces of the same type equal in magnitude and opposite in direction acting on two different bodies.

options.label: C
options.text: Gravitational weight of the lamp and upward tension in the vertical cable acting on the lamp.
options.distractorRationale: Weight (gravitational) and tension (contact) are different force types acting on the same body, so they are not a third-law pair.

options.label: D
options.text: Two unequal forces of the same type acting in the same direction on a single accelerating object.
options.distractorRationale: Third-law pairs are always equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on two distinct interacting bodies.

items.stem: An industrial grinding rotor initially spinning at 18.0 rev s⁻¹ decelerates uniformly to rest in 15.0 s once its brake caliper engages. How many complete revolutions does the rotor make while slowing to a stop?
items.workedSolution: Average rotational frequency is $\bar{f} = \frac{18.0 + 0}{2} = 9.00\text{ rev s}^{-1}$. Total revolutions $N = \frac{\theta}{2\pi} = \bar{f}t = 9.00 \times 15.0 = 135 rev$.

markScheme.criterion: Rotor completes 135 rev while decelerating to rest.

items.stem: A crate is towed horizontally through $15.0\text{ m}$ across a warehouse floor by a rope pulling with constant tension $120\text{ N}$ at $35.0^\circ$ above the horizontal. How much mechanical work is done on the crate by the rope tension?
items.workedSolution: $W = Fs\cos\theta = 120 \times 15.0 \times \cos 35.0^\circ = 1.47 × 10³ J$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $W = Fs\cos\theta$ to obtain $1.47 × 10³ J$.

items.stem: A flywheel of moment of inertia $I = 2.50\text{ kg m}^2$ experiences the triangular non-uniform $\alpha$–$t$ pulse shown (peak $\alpha = 12.0\text{ rad s}^{-2}$, total duration $8.00\text{ s}$). Calculate the net angular impulse delivered to the flywheel.
items.workedSolution: $\Delta\omega = \frac{1}{2} \times 8.00 \times 12.0 = 48.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$. Angular impulse $= \Delta(I\omega) = 2.50 \times 48.0 = 120 N m s$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 120 N m s.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a non-uniform access door of length L = 1.4 m and mass 18 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.59 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 26° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) T = 82.80 N ≈ 82.8 N. (b) the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium. (c)(i) R_x = 36.30 N, R_y = 102.2 N, so R = 108.4 N ≈ 108 N. (c)(ii) α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 70.44° ≈ 70.4° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Στ = 0 about O using T cos(angle to vertical) × L = m g x_G.
Obtains T = 82.80 N (82.8 N) matching 83 N.
Identifies horizontal component of angled cable tension directed toward the wall.
States hinge must exert an equal opposite horizontal force away from the wall for ΣF_x = 0.
Computes R_x = 36.30 N and R_y = 102.2 N and applies Pythagoras.
Resultant hinge reaction magnitude R = 108 N.
Uses tan α = R_y / R_x with both hinge components.
Direction α = 70.4° above the horizontal.

workingSteps: Vertical component of cable tension is T cos 26°.
Equate moments about O: T cos 26° × 1.4 = 18 × 9.81 × 0.59.

parts.prompt: Explain why hinge O must exert a horizontal component of force on the door, and state its direction.
parts.expectedAnswer: For horizontal equilibrium, the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium.
workingSteps: Identify that the inclined cable pulls horizontally toward the wall.
Conclude from zero horizontal resultant force that the hinge must push horizontally away from the wall.

items.stem: A metal block of mass 14 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 2 m. It falls freely from rest at the fixed support to point A, where the cord becomes taut. It then stretches the cord by 1.2 m over 0.21 s before stopping at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 6.26 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (14 × 6.26) / 0.21 = 417 N.
Obtains 555 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 732 N.

items.stem: An electric car of mass 1300 kg accelerates along a level road while a small steel sphere hangs from its ceiling at 22° to the vertical. Later, the car climbs a straight 8° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 40 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.55. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 14 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 470 N toward the marker. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg => a = g tan θ.
Obtains 3.96 m s⁻².
Applies μ_s mg = m v_max² / R.
Obtains 14.7 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts resistive work F_res(πR) from initial kinetic energy ½mu².
Obtains 10.3 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By resolving forces on the sphere, calculate the horizontal acceleration when the string hangs at 22° to the vertical.
Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular road without sliding.
Calculate the speed of the car when it reaches the marker at the end of the semicircular bend.

items.stem: A small metal sphere of mass 1.8 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.6 m attached to a light wire. The maximum tension the wire can hold without breaking is 57 N. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Writes T_max − mg = m v_max² / r at the lowest point.
Obtains 3.62 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By considering the forces acting on the sphere at the lowest point, calculate the maximum speed at the bottom so the wire does not break.

items.stem: A small steel ball of mass 0.3 kg hangs on a light string of length 2.2 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a block of clay of mass 0.42 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the speed of the joined objects immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 6.57 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 8.83 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 2.74 m s⁻¹. Target = 2.74 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 2.74 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: A metal block of mass 1.5 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 2.2 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.55 m in 0.2 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum tension in the cord at the lowest point B.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 2.2 + 0.55 = 2.75 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 267 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 147 N. Target = 147 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (2.2 + 0.55) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 147 N (A).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a construction crane has total length L = 15 m and mass 950 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 7 m from rear end A. A 3800 kg concrete counterweight sits 5 m to the left of P (2 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 2.5 m to the right of P (9.5 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 5.5 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) M_cw = 1.864 × 10⁵ N m ≈ 1.86 × 10⁵ N m. (b) Equating clockwise and anticlockwise moments about P gives m_max = 3023 kg ≈ 3.02 × 10³ kg. (c) Vertical force balance yields R = 7.625 × 10⁴ N ≈ 7.63 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses M = m g d with counterweight mass and lever arm from P.
Counterweight moment = 1.86 × 10⁵ N m.
Subtracts boom self-weight moment from counterweight moment and divides by g × load lever arm.
Maximum safe load mass = 3.02 × 10³ kg.
Applies vertical force balance summing counterweight, boom, and load weights.
Upward mast reaction R = 7.63 × 10⁴ N.

workingSteps: Moment M_cw = W_cw × 5 = 1.864 × 10⁵ N m ≈ 1.86 × 10⁵ N m.

parts.prompt: Taking into account the weight of the boom, determine the maximum load mass that can be lifted at the hoist hook so the net moment about P is zero.
workingSteps: Clockwise moment of boom = 950 × 9.81 × 2.5 = 2.330 × 10⁴ N m.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total upward reaction force exerted by the vertical mast pivot P when this maximum load is suspended in equilibrium.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium: R = (m_cw + m_boom + m_max) g.

items.stem: On a smooth level track, cart X of mass 1.6 kg moves right at 10 m s⁻¹ and collides with stationary cart Y of mass 1.2 kg. Immediately after impact, cart Y moves right at 7.23 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of cart X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Momentum conservation: (1.6)(10) = (1.6)v_X + (1.2)(7.23), giving v_X = 4.58 m s⁻¹. K_i = 80.0 J and K_f = 48.1 J, so ΔK_lost = K_i − K_f = 31.9 J. Target = 4.58 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves linear momentum and evaluates kinetic energy budget to obtain 4.58 m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: The figure compares fluid streamlines around a sphere in two regimes. Which statement accurately contrasts laminar flow with turbulent flow?
items.workedSolution: Laminar flow has ordered, non-crossing streamlines; turbulent flow involves unsteady vortices and mixing between layers. Therefore the correct statement is: Laminar flow consists of smooth non-crossing parallel streamlines whereas turbulent flow features chaotic eddies and mixing.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: laminar flow consists of smooth non-crossing parallel streamlines whereas turbulent flow features chaotic eddies and mixing.

options.label: A
options.text: Laminar flow contains rapidly spinning eddies and lateral mixing whereas turbulent flow follows smooth parallel paths.
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the physical definitions of laminar and turbulent flow.

options.label: B
options.text: In laminar flow fluid velocity fluctuates unpredictably with time at every fixed point while turbulent flow is strictly steady.
options.distractorRationale: Steady velocity at each point is a hallmark of laminar flow, not turbulent flow.

options.label: C
options.text: Laminar flow consists of smooth non-crossing parallel streamlines whereas turbulent flow features chaotic eddies and mixing.

options.label: D
options.text: Laminar flow occurs only in gases while turbulent flow occurs exclusively in dense liquids.
options.distractorRationale: Both gases and liquids can show either laminar or turbulent flow depending on speed, size, and viscosity.

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 1.4 kg moves right at 15 m s⁻¹ and strikes stationary trolley Y of mass 5 kg. Immediately after impact, trolley Y moves right at 5.03 m s⁻¹ and trolley X rebounds to the left. Calculate the kinetic energy lost in this rebound collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward positive, (1.4)(15) = (1.4)v_X + (5)(5.03) gives v_X = -2.96 m s⁻¹ (2.96 m s⁻¹ to the left). Scalar final kinetic energies add: K_f = ½(1.4)(2.96)² + ½(5)(5.03)² = 69.4 J. Energy lost = 158 J − K_f = 88.1 J. Target = 88.1 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds rebound speed 2.96 m s⁻¹ and sums scalar kinetic energies to obtain 88.1 J (A).

items.stem: A golf ball is hit from flat ground with an initial speed of 33 m s⁻¹ at 55° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.
items.workedSolution: (a) v_apex = 33 × cos 55°. Answer: 18.9 m s⁻¹. (b) u_y = 33 × sin 55° = 27.0 m s⁻¹. h_max = u_y² / (2 × 9.8). Answer: 37.3 m. (c) T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 5.52 s. R = 18.9 × T. Answer: 104 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes v_y = 0 at apex so v_apex = u cos θ.
Obtains 18.9 m s⁻¹.
Applies h_max = (u sin θ)² / (2g).
Obtains 37.3 m.
Evaluates R = u_x × (2u_y / g).
Obtains 104 m.

items.stem: A small steel ball of mass 0.8 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.9 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal and sticks to a block of clay of mass 0.64 kg at rest at the bottom. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height above the lowest point reached by the joined objects.
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 6.11 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 3.39 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.586 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 6.63 J. Target = 0.586 m.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 0.586 m (D).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform wooden plank AB has total length L = 5.2 m and mass 13 kg. Its centre of gravity G is at its midpoint, 2.6 m from end A. It rests horizontally on a sharp pivot P at 1.87 m from end A. A counterbalance block of unknown mass sits 0.65 m from end A. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) The moment of a force about a pivot is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. (b) Taking moments about P: m_load g (1.220) = (13) g (0.7300), giving m_load = 7.779 kg ≈ 7.78 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Product of force and distance from the pivot.
Specifies perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
Equates opposing moments about P using d_G = 0.7300 m and d_load = 1.220 m.
Obtains balancing mass m = 7.78 kg (4 s.f. 7.779 kg).

workingSteps: Find perpendicular distances from P: d_G = 0.7300 m and d_load = 1.220 m.

items.stem: A sandbag of mass 10 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 4 m. It falls freely from rest at the fixed support to point A, where the cord becomes taut. It then stretches the cord by 1.2 m over 0.36 s before stopping at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 8.86 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (10 × 8.86) / 0.36 = 246 N.
Obtains 344 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 850 N.

items.stem: Two pucks make a glancing collision on a horizontal frictionless air table as shown. Which statement correctly expresses the principle of momentum conservation in two dimensions?
items.workedSolution: Because momentum is a vector, zero net external force guarantees Σp_x and Σp_y are conserved separately. Therefore the correct statement is: Linear momentum is conserved independently along perpendicular x and y axes whenever no net external force acts.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: linear momentum is conserved independently along perpendicular x and y axes whenever no net external force acts.

options.label: A
options.text: Only the scalar magnitudes of momentum add after the collision so p₁ + p₂ always equals p₀.
options.distractorRationale: Momentum is a vector; scalar sums exceed the resultant whenever post-collision velocities diverge at an angle.

options.label: B
options.text: Linear momentum is conserved independently along perpendicular x and y axes whenever no net external force acts.

options.label: C
options.text: Momentum is conserved along the initial direction of motion but perpendicular momentum components can take any non-zero sum.
options.distractorRationale: With zero initial y-momentum and no net external force, the perpendicular components must sum to zero.

options.label: D
options.text: Two-dimensional momentum is conserved only when the collision is completely elastic.
options.distractorRationale: Vector momentum is conserved in both elastic and inelastic isolated collisions.

items.stem: On a smooth level track, cart X of mass 4 kg moves to the right at 7 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with cart Y of mass 2.4 kg moving to the left at 2 m s⁻¹ (arrow on Y not shown). Immediately after impact, cart Y moves to the right at 5 m s⁻¹. Take motion to the right as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) p_before = 4 × 7 + 2.4 × (−2) = 23.2 kg m s⁻¹. Answer: 23.2 kg m s⁻¹ to the right. (b) v_X = (23.2 − 2.4 × 5) / 4 = 2.80 m s⁻¹. Answer: 2.80 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m_X u_X − m_Y |u_Y| with correct signs.
Obtains 23.2 kg m s⁻¹ to the right.
Solves p_before = m_X v_X + m_Y v_Y for v_X.
Obtains 2.80 m s⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform wooden plank of total length L = 5.2 m and mass 56 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is at the left end, and support B is 3.2 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 2 m. A technician of mass 64 kg initially stands 0.7 m from the left end of the plank. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B give F₁ = 593.5 N ≈ 594 N. (b) Vertical equilibrium gives F₂ = 583.7 N ≈ 584 N. (c) the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases. (d) Setting F₁ = 0 about B yields d_tip = 0.5250 m ≈ 0.525 m.

markScheme.criterion: Takes moments about B summing plank and technician anticlockwise moments.
Support A reaction F₁ = 594 N.
Support B reaction F₂ = 584 N via vertical force balance.
States that the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.
Sets F₁ = 0 and equates clockwise overhang moment to restoring plank moment about B.
Tipping distance past B = 0.525 m.

items.stem: A ball is launched from floor level across a flat room at 20 m s⁻¹ and 64° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the total time of flight before returning to the floor.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 20 sin 64° = 18.0 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 20 cos 64° = 8.77 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 3.67 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 32.2 m. Target = 3.67 s.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 3.67 s (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes time to reach the apex u sin θ / g rather than full time of flight.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses total speed u instead of vertical component u sin θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Takes an erroneous square root of 2u sin θ / g.

items.stem: A small lorry of mass 1500 kg accelerates along a level road while a small plumb bob hangs from its ceiling at 22° to the vertical. Later, the lorry climbs a straight 10° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 60 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.55. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 20 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 470 N toward the stop sign. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 22°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 22° = ma and T cos 22° = mg => a = g tan 22° = 3.96 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.55 × 9.8 × 60) = 18.0 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1500)(20)² / 470 = 638 m. Target = 3.96 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 3.96 m s⁻² (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: A skydiver falls at constant terminal velocity where upward air drag equals downward weight. Which force forms the true Newton's third law pair with the skydiver's downward weight?
items.workedSolution: Weight is the Earth's downward gravitational pull on the skydiver; its N3L partner must be the same force type acting on the other body: the gravitational pull of the skydiver upward on the Earth. Therefore option D is correct: gravitational pull of the skydiver upward on the Earth.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: gravitational pull of the skydiver upward on the Earth.

items.stem: A metal box of mass 13 kg slides from rest down a straight ramp of length 5.5 m inclined at 22° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 5.09 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. If the box is instead released from rest halfway down the ramp, calculate its speed at the bottom.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 22° − ½mv² = 94.4 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 5.5 = 17.2 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.60 m s⁻¹. Target = 3.60 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 3.60 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: A stone block of mass 8 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough wooden slope of length 11 m, inclined at 24° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 7.68 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the coefficient of dynamic friction μ_d between the block and the slope.
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 24° = 351 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(8)(7.68)² = 236 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 115 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 24°)L, μ = 0.146. Target = 0.146.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 24° accurately to obtain 0.146 (D).

items.stem: A steel ball of mass 1.3 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.9 m on a light string. At the lowest point, its speed is 5.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.3 × 5.5² / 1.9 = 20.7 N, so T = 20.7 + 1.3 × 9.8 = 33.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 33.4 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A flywheel of moment of inertia I = 1.6 kg m² initially rotates at ω_i = 3.0 rad s⁻¹. A tangential force F = 20 N is applied perpendicularly (θ = 90°) at radius r = 0.40 m for Δt = 4.0 s. What is the angular displacement Δθ during this 4.0 s interval?

markScheme.criterion: Finds ω_f and applies Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t to obtain 52.0 rad.

items.stem: A golf ball is hit from flat ground at 30 m s⁻¹ and 28° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the speed of the projectile at the highest point of its path.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 28° = 26.5 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 28°)² / (2g) = 10.1 m. Target = 26.5 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 28° at apex to obtain 26.5 m s⁻¹ (C).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses u sin θ instead of u cos θ for the speed at the apex.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Assumes speed remains equal to launch speed u throughout the flight.

It falls from rest at the fixed upper support, and the cord obeys Hooke's law once it becomes taut at point A. The cord stretches by a maximum extension of 1.15 m in 0.18 s before the block stops at the lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Uses free-fall relation v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 8.40 m s⁻¹.
Equates mg(L + x) = ½kx² over the complete vertical drop.
Obtains 740 N m⁻¹.
Evaluates a_B = (kx − mg) / m.
Obtains 71.2 m s⁻².

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a horizontal metal bar of length L = 3.6 m and mass 8 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light vertical wires at A and B. The wires are 3.1 m apart. Its centre of gravity G lies 1.18 m to the right of A and 1.92 m to the left of B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Without carrying out a full calculation, which statement correctly compares the tensions in the two wires?
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about the centre of gravity G gives T₁ d_A = T₂ d_B, so the wire with the smaller distance to G carries the larger tension: wire A carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire A.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly concludes that wire A carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire A.

options.text: Both wires carry identical tension because the bar hangs completely horizontal.
options.distractorRationale: Horizontal equilibrium requires zero net moment, which forces unequal tensions when G is off-centre.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.distractorRationale: Reverses the inverse lever-arm relation; the support closer to G bears the larger share of weight.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither wire tension depends on the horizontal location of the centre of gravity.
options.distractorRationale: Moment balance directly couples the tension ratio to the distances of G from each wire.

items.stem: A steel ball of mass 1.6 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1 m on a light string. The string breaks if the tension exceeds 51 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the ball at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((51/1.6) − 9.81) × 1] = 4.70 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 4.70 m s⁻¹ (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds g instead of subtracting g when rearranging T_max − mg = mv²/r.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a control wheel bar has length d = 0.28 m. Two equal and opposite parallel forces of magnitude F = 50 N act perpendicularly at its ends. What is the magnitude of the torque of this couple?
items.workedSolution: Torque of a couple = F × perpendicular separation = 50 × 0.28 = 14.00 N m ≈ 14.0 N m.

markScheme.criterion: Correct couple torque = 14.0 N m.

items.stem: A concrete block of weight 360 N slides at a constant speed down a rough incline. The slope has length 30 m and vertical height 7.2 m. Calculate the magnitude of the resistive force opposing motion along the slope.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed ΔE_k = 0. Potential energy lost = W h = 360 × 7.2 = 2.59 × 10³ J. Parallel equilibrium gives F_res = W sin θ = W h / L = 86.4 N. Target = 86.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses sin θ = 7.2/30 and zero net force to obtain 86.4 N (B).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 2.8 m and mass 7 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 8.5 kg hangs so its centre of gravity acts 2.5 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at 30° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about O give T = 217.6 N ≈ 218 N. (b) Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos θ = 188.4 N ≈ 188 N. (c) Vertical balance: R_y = W_total − T sin θ = 43.27 N ≈ 43.3 N.

markScheme.criterion: Writes full moment balance about hinge O including both rod and sign moments with T sin θ.
Evaluates T = 217.6 N (218 N) showing agreement with 2.2 × 10² N.
Applies horizontal equilibrium R_x = T cos θ.
R_x = 188 N away from the wall.
Applies vertical equilibrium R_y = W_total − T sin θ.
R_y = 43.3 N upwards.

workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium: R_y = W − T sin 30° = 43.27 N ≈ 43.3 N upwards.

items.stem: A parcel of mass 13.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a wooden ramp. The slope is 10 m long and inclined at 40° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 6.18 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = mgL sin θ.
Obtains 851 J.
Subtracts ½mv² from ΔE_p.
Obtains 593 J.
Applies W_f = μ(mg cos θ)L.
Obtains 0.585.

items.stem: Why should the test wire in Required Practical 4 be both long (at least 2 m) and thin (diameter around 0.4 mm)?
items.workedSolution: RP4 mark-scheme principle: A long thin wire produces a larger measurable extension e for safe loads, reducing percentage uncertainty, while an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while perpendicular micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty.

options.text: A long thin wire increases the intrinsic Young modulus E of the metal.
options.distractorRationale: Young modulus is a material property independent of wire dimensions.

options.label: B
options.text: A thicker shorter wire gives larger extensions so Vernier scales are unnecessary.
options.distractorRationale: Since e = FL/(EA), a shorter thicker wire extends much less, worsening percentage uncertainty.

options.label: C
options.text: A long thin wire produces a larger measurable extension e for safe loads, reducing percentage uncertainty, while an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while orthogonal micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty.

options.label: D
options.text: A thin wire eliminates percentage uncertainty in cross-sectional area because %Δd becomes negligible.
options.distractorRationale: A thinner wire actually increases %Δd, which is why precise perpendicular micrometer readings are essential.

items.stem: A lead bob of mass 0.3 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.9 m on a light steel cable. At the lowest point, its speed is 7 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the cable at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 0.3 × 7² / 1.9 = 7.74 N, so T = 7.74 + 0.3 × 9.81 = 10.7 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 10.7 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A spin-stabilised research satellite with extended sensor booms has moment of inertia 24.0 kg m² and spins at 2.20 rad s⁻¹ in deep space. Internal winches retract the booms, lowering its moment of inertia to 8.80 kg m². Calculate the new angular speed of the satellite.
items.workedSolution: By conservation of angular momentum $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$, $\omega_2 = \frac{24.0 \times 2.20}{8.80} = 6.00 rad s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: New angular speed equals 6.00 rad s⁻¹.

items.stem: The turning-moment diagram shows a four-stroke engine coupled to a steady external load. How does the flywheel stop the crankshaft from stalling between power strokes?
items.workedSolution: On the turning-moment graph, the flywheel absorbs excess energy when engine torque exceeds mean load and releases energy during zero-torque strokes (induction, compression, exhaust), keeping $\Delta\omega$ small.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that flywheel absorbs excess energy when engine torque exceeds mean load and releases energy during zero-torque strokes.

options.label: A
options.text: Flywheel increases the mean torque generated by the engine above the thermodynamic power-stroke average.
options.distractorRationale: A passive flywheel cannot create net mechanical energy or raise mean torque.

options.label: B
options.text: Flywheel eliminates the compression stroke so engine torque stays positive throughout the cycle.
options.distractorRationale: A four-stroke cylinder still requires a compression stroke regardless of flywheel inertia.

options.label: C
options.text: Flywheel absorbs excess energy when engine torque exceeds mean load and releases energy during zero-torque strokes.

options.label: D
options.text: Flywheel converts negative torque directly into electrical energy stored in the battery.
options.distractorRationale: Standard engine flywheels smooth speed mechanically via rotational kinetic energy.

items.stem: A metal block of weight 1400 N slides down a rough slope at a constant speed of 2 m s⁻¹. The ramp is 18 m long and drops by 8.1 m vertically. Calculate the magnitude of the friction force acting up the ramp.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed, friction balances downslope weight: F_f = W(h/L) = 1400 × (8.1/18) = 630 N. Rate of thermal energy generation P = F_f v = 1.26 × 10³ W. Target = 630 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_f = Wh/L and P = F_f v to obtain 630 N (B).

items.stem: A metal sphere is thrown from a balcony $25.0\text{ m}$ high at $14.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ angled $36.9^\circ$ below the horizontal ($g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$, negligible fluid resistance). What is the speed of the sphere immediately before hitting the pavement?
items.workedSolution: Combining components (or energy conservation), $v^2 = u^2 + 2gh = 14.0^2 + 2(9.8)(25.0) = 686\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$, so $v = 26.2 m s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Finds resultant impact speed $v = 26.2 m s⁻¹$.

items.stem: A $10.0\text{ kg}$ crate hangs in equilibrium from two light cords attached to a horizontal beam ($g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$). The left cord (tension $T_1$) is at $\alpha = 30.0^\circ$ and the right cord (tension $T_2$) is at $\beta = 60.0^\circ$ to the horizontal. Calculate the tension $T_1$ in the left cord.
items.workedSolution: Since $\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$, resolving parallel to cord 1 (or solving $T_1 \cos 30^\circ = T_2 \cos 60^\circ$ and $T_1 \sin 30^\circ + T_2 \sin 60^\circ = 98.0 N$) yields $T_1 = mg \cos 60^\circ = 98.0 \times 0.500 = 49.0 N$.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves perpendicular components at $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to obtain $T_1 = 49.0 N$.

items.stem: A spoked rotor has a hub inertia of 0.80 kg m² and 4 rim masses of 1.10 kg each at radius 0.50 m. A motor accelerates it uniformly from 4.0 rev s⁻¹ to 16.0 rev s⁻¹ in 10.0 s against a constant bearing friction torque of 2.20 N m. Calculate the driving torque supplied by the motor.
items.workedSolution: Total inertia $I = 0.80 + 4(1.10)(0.50)^2 = 1.90\text{ kg m}^2$. Angular acceleration $\alpha = \frac{2\pi(16.0 - 4.0)}{10.0} = 7.54\text{ rad s}^{-2}$. Driving torque $T_{\mathrm{app}} = I\alpha + T_{\mathrm{f}} = (1.90 \times 7.54) + 2.20 = 16.5 N m$.

markScheme.criterion: Applied driving torque equals 16.5 N m.

items.stem: Marine diesel fuel has a specific energy of $45.0\text{ MJ kg}^{-1}$ and a density of $840\text{ kg m}^{-3}$. What is the volumetric energy density of this fuel in $\text{GJ m}^{-3}$?
items.workedSolution: Volumetric energy density $= (45.0 \times 10^6\text{ J kg}^{-1})(840\text{ kg m}^{-3}) = 3.78 \times 10^{10}\text{ J m}^{-3} = 37.8 GJ m⁻³$.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies specific energy by density to obtain $37.8 GJ m⁻³$.

items.stem: A rotor experiences a non-uniform angular acceleration pulse. Its $\alpha$–$t$ graph is a triangle rising from $0$ to a peak of $8.00\text{ rad s}^{-2}$ at $t = 4.00\text{ s}$, then returning linearly to $0$ at $t = 10.0\text{ s}$. Calculate the total change in angular velocity $\Delta\omega$ over the $10.0\text{ s}$ pulse.
items.workedSolution: Area beneath an $\alpha$–$t$ graph equals $\Delta\omega$: $\Delta\omega = \frac{1}{2} \times 10.0\text{ s} \times 8.00\text{ rad s}^{-2} = 40.0 rad s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 40.0 rad s⁻¹.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a non-uniform access door of length L = 1.6 m and mass 20 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.7 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 26° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium. (b) Moments about O give T = 95.50 N ≈ 95.5 N. (c)(i) R_x = 41.87 N ≈ 41.9 N. (c)(ii) R_y = 110.4 N ≈ 110 N. (c)(iii) R = 118.0 N ≈ 118 N. (c)(iv) α = 69.23° ≈ 69.2° above horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Notes inward horizontal component of cable tension.
States equal opposite outward hinge reaction away from wall.
Equates cable moment T cos(angle to vertical) × L with weight moment m g x_G.
T = 95.50 N (95.5 N) clearly matching 96 N.
Combines perpendicular components via R = √(R_x² + R_y²).
Applies tan α = R_y / R_x.
α = 69.2° above the horizontal.

items.stem: A metal cylinder of mass 11 kg is attached to an elastic rope of natural length 3.8 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the rope becomes taut, and then stretches it by 0.6 m in 0.24 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward force exerted by the rope between A and B.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.8 × 3.8) = 8.63 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.24 + 11(9.8) = 503 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 503 N (B).

items.stem: A small lorry of mass 1800 kg accelerates along a level road while a small plumb bob hangs from its ceiling at 30° to the vertical. Later, the lorry climbs a straight 12° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 45 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.55. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 16 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 380 N toward the stop sign. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular bend of radius 45 m without skidding.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 30° = ma and T cos 30° = mg => a = g tan 30° = 5.66 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.55 × 9.81 × 45) = 15.6 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1800)(16)² / 380 = 606 m. Target = 15.6 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 15.6 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: A heavy ball of mass 1.5 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.8 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a wooden block of mass 3.3 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the speed of the joined objects immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 5.94 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 44.1 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 1.86 m s⁻¹. Target = 1.86 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 1.86 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: Two stationary dynamics trolleys of unequal mass (m₁ < m₂) are pushed apart by a compressed internal spring on a frictionless track. How do their momenta and kinetic energies compare after separation?
items.workedSolution: Since |p₁| = |p₂| = p and E_k = p²/(2m), the kinetic energy ratio is E_k1 / E_k2 = m₂ / m₁ > 1, so the lighter trolley gets more kinetic energy. Therefore the correct statement is: By conservation of linear momentum, because both fragments gain equal and opposite momenta from rest, the lighter mass moves faster and gains the greater proportion of the released kinetic energy.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: because both fragments gain equal and opposite momenta from rest, the lighter mass moves faster and gains the greater proportion of the released kinetic energy.

options.text: By conservation of linear momentum, because both fragments gain equal and opposite momenta from rest, the lighter mass moves faster and gains the greater proportion of the released kinetic energy.

options.label: B
options.text: Both trolleys gain equal kinetic energies because the spring exerts equal and opposite forces on each trolley.
options.distractorRationale: Although forces and impulses are equal in magnitude, the lighter trolley moves further while the spring pushes, gaining more kinetic energy (E_k = p²/(2m)).

options.label: C
options.text: The heavier trolley gains a larger momentum magnitude and more kinetic energy because it has greater inertia.
options.distractorRationale: Total initial momentum is zero, so both trolleys must have exactly equal momentum magnitudes in opposite directions.

options.label: D
options.text: Total kinetic energy before and after release is zero because momentum is conserved.
options.distractorRationale: Elastic potential energy stored in the spring converts into positive kinetic energy for both trolleys.

items.stem: A metal cylinder of mass 12 kg is attached to an elastic rope of natural length 4.2 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.95 m in 0.14 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum tension in the rope at the lowest point B.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 4.2 + 0.95 = 5.15 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 1.34 × 10³ N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 1.28 × 10³ N. Target = 1.28 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (4.2 + 0.95) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 1.28 × 10³ N (B).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a construction crane has total length L = 16 m and mass 1200 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 6 m from rear end A. A 4200 kg concrete counterweight sits 4 m to the left of P (2 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 4.5 m to the right of P (10.5 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 8.5 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum safe load mass at the hook for rotational equilibrium about P.
items.workedSolution: Anticlockwise counterweight moment about P: M_cw = 4200 × 9.81 × 4 = 1.648 × 10⁵ N m. Clockwise boom moment: M_boom = 1200 × 9.81 × 4.5 = 5.297 × 10⁴ N m. Remaining clockwise moment available for load: W_max × 8.5 = 1.118 × 10⁵ N m ⇒ W_max = 1.316 × 10⁴ N ≈ 1.32 × 10⁴ N, m_max = W_max / 9.81 = 1341 kg ≈ 1.34 × 10³ kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct maximum safe load mass = 1.34 × 10³ kg.

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 3.6 kg moves to the right at 7 m s⁻¹. It collides with stationary trolley Y of mass 1.6 kg. Immediately after impact, trolley Y moves to the right at 7.24 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies m_X u_X = m_X v_X + m_Y v_Y.
Obtains 3.78 m s⁻¹.
Sums ½m_X v_X² + ½m_Y v_Y².
Obtains 67.7 J.
Subtracts K_f from K_i = ½m_X u_X².
Obtains 20.5 J.

items.stem: A student uses Stokes' law $F = 6\pi\eta r v$ to analyse a ball bearing descending through glycerol. Which condition is required for Stokes' law to remain valid?
items.workedSolution: Stokes' equation F = 6πηrv is derived for small smooth spheres moving slowly enough to maintain laminar flow without wall interference. Therefore the correct statement is: Stokes law applies only to small smooth spheres moving slowly in laminar flow far from container walls.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: Stokes law applies only to small smooth spheres moving slowly in laminar flow far from container walls.

options.text: Stokes law applies only to small smooth spheres moving slowly in laminar flow far from container walls.

options.label: C
options.text: Stokes law applies at any speed provided the fluid density exceeds the sphere density.
options.distractorRationale: If fluid density exceeds sphere density the sphere floats upwards, and turbulent wakes break Stokes' law at high speeds.

options.label: D
options.text: Stokes law holds only when upthrust is zero and the sphere accelerates uniformly throughout the cylinder.
options.distractorRationale: Upthrust is always present in a liquid and terminal velocity requires zero acceleration.

items.stem: On a frictionless horizontal surface, block X of mass 1.4 kg moves to the right at 15 m s⁻¹. It collides with stationary block Y of mass 3.6 kg. Immediately after the collision, block Y moves to the right at 6.73 m s⁻¹. Take motion to the right as positive.

markScheme.criterion: Applies signed momentum conservation m_X u_X = m_X v_X + m_Y v_Y.
Obtains 2.31 m s⁻¹ to the left.
Adds positive scalar kinetic energies ½m_X v_X² + ½m_Y v_Y².
Obtains 85.2 J.
Evaluates K_i − K_f.
Obtains 72.3 J.

items.stem: A golf ball is hit from flat ground at 30 m s⁻¹ and 24° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the speed of the projectile at the highest point of its path.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 24° = 27.4 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 24°)² / (2g) = 7.60 m. Target = 27.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 24° at apex to obtain 27.4 m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the projectile stops completely for an instant at its highest point, forgetting its constant horizontal velocity u cos θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses u sin θ instead of u cos θ for the speed at the apex.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumes speed remains equal to launch speed u throughout the flight.

items.stem: A small steel ball of mass 1.2 kg hangs from a light string of length 1.4 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the lowest point, it collides with and sticks to a block of clay of mass 0.96 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mgL = ½mu² => u = √(2gL).
Obtains 5.24 m s⁻¹.
Finds v = mu/(m+M) from momentum conservation and evaluates ½mu² − ½(m+M)v².
Obtains 7.32 J.
Applies h = v² / (2g).
Obtains 0.432 m.

items.stem: In a statics experiment, a wooden plank AB has length L = 3.4 m and mass 27 kg. Its centre of gravity G lies 1.7 m from end A. It is balanced horizontally on a pivot P at 1.29 m from end A by placing a 16 kg block to the left of P. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate how far from end B the 16 kg block must be placed for horizontal equilibrium.
items.workedSolution: Distance of CG from pivot P: d_G = 1.7 − 1.29 = 0.4100 m. Taking moments about P: 16 × d = 27 × 0.4100 ⇒ d = 0.6919 m left of P. Position from end A is x_A = 1.29 − 0.6919 = 0.5981 m. Therefore distance from end B is L − x_A = 3.4 − 0.5981 = 2.802 m ≈ 2.80 m.

markScheme.criterion: Correct distance from end B = 2.80 m.

items.stem: A steel ball of mass 8 kg is attached to a rubber cord of natural length 2.4 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the cord becomes taut, and then stretches it by 1 m in 0.24 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward force exerted by the cord between A and B.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.81 × 2.4) = 6.86 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.24 + 8(9.81) = 307 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 307 N (A).

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 4 kg moves to the right at 10 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with trolley Y of mass 3 kg moving to the left at 2 m s⁻¹ (arrow not shown). Immediately after the collision, trolley Y moves right at 5 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of trolley X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward as positive: p_before = (4)(10) + (3)(−2) = 34.0 kg m s⁻¹. From p_before = (4)v_X + (3)(5), v_X = 4.75 m s⁻¹, which is 4.75 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Uses signed head-on momentum p_before = 34.0 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 4.75 m s⁻¹ to the right (A).

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform timber board of total length L = 6.6 m and mass 44 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is at the left end, and support B is 5 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 1.6 m. A technician of mass 60 kg initially stands 4.1 m from the left end of the plank. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Which statement correctly describes the condition at the instant the plank begins to tip clockwise about support B?
items.workedSolution: As the technician moves out onto the overhang, the clockwise moment about B increases until the plank is on the point of lifting off support A, so the upward normal reaction force at support A decreases to zero.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that the upward normal reaction force at support A decreases to zero.

items.stem: A ball is launched from floor level across a flat room at 22 m s⁻¹ and 60° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the floor.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 22 sin 60° = 19.1 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 22 cos 60° = 11.0 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 3.89 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 42.8 m. Target = 42.8 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 42.8 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies horizontal speed by ascent time u sin θ / g instead of full flight time 2u sin θ / g.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cos θ for sin θ in the flight-time expression.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: An electric car of mass 1500 kg accelerates along a level road while a small steel sphere hangs from its ceiling at 34° to the vertical. Later, the car climbs a straight 8° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 55 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.85. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 17 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 530 N toward the marker. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the sphere deflects by 34°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 34° = ma and T cos 34° = mg => a = g tan 34° = 6.61 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.85 × 9.8 × 55) = 21.4 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1500)(17)² / 530 = 409 m. Target = 6.61 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 6.61 m s⁻² (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: Which statement lists all essential AQA criteria for two forces to constitute a Newton's third law interaction pair?
items.workedSolution: Newton's third law pairs must have equal magnitude, opposite direction, same type of force, and act on two different bodies along the same line. Therefore option A is correct: equal magnitude opposite direction same type of force acting on two different bodies.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: equal magnitude opposite direction same type of force acting on two different bodies.

options.text: A Newton's third law pair consists of forces of equal magnitude opposite direction same type of force acting on two different bodies

options.label: B
options.text: A Newton's third law pair consists of equal and opposite forces of different types acting on the same single object
options.distractorRationale: Equal opposite forces on the same object describe Newton's first law equilibrium, never a third-law pair.

options.label: C
options.text: A Newton's third law pair consists of forces acting in the same direction whenever an object moves at constant velocity
options.distractorRationale: N3L pairs are always opposite in direction and hold even during acceleration.

options.label: D
options.text: A Newton's third law pair consists of any two forces whose vector sum is zero on a free-body diagram
options.distractorRationale: A free-body diagram shows forces acting on one body only; N3L pairs act on two distinct interacting bodies.

items.stem: A metal box of mass 13 kg slides from rest down a straight ramp of length 4 m inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 3.76 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the magnitude of the constant friction force opposing its motion.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 30° − ½mv² = 163 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 4 = 40.8 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 2.66 m s⁻¹. Target = 40.8 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 40.8 N (C).

items.stem: A steel ball is fired from a spring launcher on level ground at 15 m s⁻¹ and 28° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height reached above the ground.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 28° = 13.2 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 28°)² / (2g) = 2.53 m. Target = 2.53 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 28° at apex to obtain 2.53 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Converts all initial kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy, forgetting non-zero horizontal speed u cos θ at the apex.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses horizontal component u cos θ instead of vertical component u sin θ in h = u_y² / (2g).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of two in the denominator of h_max = u_y² / (2g).

items.stem: A small stone is thrown from flat ground at 32 m s⁻¹ and 56° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the total time of flight before returning to the ground.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 32 sin 56° = 26.5 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 32 cos 56° = 17.9 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.81 = 5.41 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 96.8 m. Target = 5.41 s.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 5.41 s (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes time to reach the apex u sin θ / g rather than full time of flight.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Swaps sin θ and cos θ when resolving vertical launch speed.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses total speed u instead of vertical component u sin θ.

items.stem: A sandbag of mass 11.5 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 3.4 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 1.15 m in 0.26 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum tension in the cord at the lowest point B.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 3.4 + 1.15 = 4.55 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 776 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 893 N. Target = 893 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (3.4 + 1.15) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 893 N (A).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a non-uniform rod of length L = 3.2 m and mass 10 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light wires at A and B. The wires are 2.5 m apart, and wire A is inclined at 52° above the horizontal rod. Its centre of gravity G lies 0.8 m to the right of A and 1.7 m to the left of B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the tension T₁ in wire A.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: T₁_y × 2.5 = 10 × 9.81 × 1.7 ⇒ T₁_y = 66.71 N, T₂_y = 31.39 N. With wire A at 52°, T₁ = T₁_y / sin 52° = 84.65 N ≈ 84.7 N, horizontal component H = T₁ cos 52° = 52.12 N, and T₂ = √(H² + T₂_y²) = 60.84 N ≈ 60.8 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct wire tension = 84.7 N.

items.stem: A steel ball of mass 2.2 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.6 m on a light string. The string breaks if the tension exceeds 130 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the ball at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((130/2.2) − 9.81) × 0.6] = 5.44 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 5.44 m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds g instead of subtracting g when rearranging T_max − mg = mv²/r.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a control wheel bar has length d = 0.28 m. Two equal and opposite parallel forces of magnitude F = 78 N act perpendicularly at its ends. Which pair of conditions must both hold for a rigid body to remain in complete static equilibrium?
items.workedSolution: For any rigid body to remain in static equilibrium it must have zero resultant force and zero resultant moment about any point.

markScheme.criterion: For any rigid body to remain in static equilibrium it must have zero resultant force and zero resultant moment about any point.

options.text: Zero resultant moment about the centre of gravity while carrying a net upward force.
options.distractorRationale: A non-zero resultant force produces linear acceleration so equilibrium is violated.

options.label: B
options.text: Zero resultant force alone regardless of whether opposing moments balance.
options.distractorRationale: A body can have zero net force yet accelerate rotationally under a couple.

options.label: C
options.text: Equal clockwise and anticlockwise forces acting only at the midpoint of the body.
options.distractorRationale: Equilibrium requires vector force balance and moment balance about any point.

options.label: D
options.text: For any rigid body to remain in static equilibrium it must have zero resultant force and zero resultant moment about any point.

items.stem: A wooden crate of weight 280 N slides at a constant speed down a rough ramp. The slope has length 11 m and vertical height 6.2 m. Calculate the gravitational potential energy lost over the full length of the slope.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed ΔE_k = 0. Potential energy lost = W h = 280 × 6.2 = 1.74 × 10³ J. Parallel equilibrium gives F_res = W sin θ = W h / L = 158 N. Target = 1.74 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Uses sin θ = 6.2/11 and zero net force to obtain 1.74 × 10³ J (D).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 2.6 m and mass 10 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 8 kg hangs so its centre of gravity acts 2.1 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at 50° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the vertical upward component of force exerted on the rod by hinge O.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about hinge O: T sin 50° × 2.6 = (10 × 1.3 + 8 × 2.1) × 9.81 = 292.3 N m. Hence T sin 50° = 112.4 N and T = 146.8 N ≈ 147 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos 50° = 94.35 N ≈ 94.3 N. Vertical balance: R_y = (10 + 8) × 9.81 − 112.4 = 64.14 N ≈ 64.1 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 64.1 N.

items.stem: A plastic box of mass 18 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough ramp. The slope is 2.5 m long and inclined at 32° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 4.18 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = mgL sin θ.
Obtains 234 J.
Subtracts ½mv² from ΔE_p.
Obtains 76.7 J.
Applies W_f = μ(mg cos θ)L.
Obtains 0.205.
