options.text: Wear safety goggles for snapping-wire whiplash and place a sand tray beneath slotted masses; also an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while orthogonal micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty.

options.label: B
options.text: Stand directly beneath the hanging masses to read the Vernier scale vertically without parallax.
options.distractorRationale: Keep feet well clear of hanging masses above a cushioned sand tray and view the Vernier horizontally.

options.label: C
options.text: Measure wire diameter once near the ceiling clamp so the wire is not touched near the midpoint.
options.distractorRationale: Diameter must be measured in perpendicular directions at least three places along the wire.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a plastic thread as the reference wire because plastic stretches less than steel.
options.distractorRationale: The reference wire must be identical material and length to cancel thermal expansion.

items.stem: A small metal sphere of mass 1.5 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1 m on a light wire. At the lowest point, its speed is 6.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the wire at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.5 × 6.5² / 1 = 63.4 N, so T = 63.4 + 1.5 × 9.81 = 78.1 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 78.1 N (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: A reversing mill drum of moment of inertia 2.50 kg m² initially turns clockwise at $+16.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$. A steady reversing torque brings it to $-12.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ (anticlockwise). Calculate the magnitude of the angular impulse delivered to the drum.
items.workedSolution: Angular impulse $T\Delta t = \Delta(I\omega) = I(\omega_2 - \omega_1) = 2.50(-12.0 - 16.0) = -70.0\text{ N m s}$. Its magnitude is 70.0 N m s.

markScheme.criterion: Magnitude of angular impulse equals 70.0 N m s.

items.stem: Motorsport KERS engineers favour carbon-fibre composite flywheel rims over heavier solid cast-iron discs for compact energy storage. Which physical property combination best explains this choice?
items.workedSolution: Maximum stored energy scales with $\frac{1}{2}I\omega_{\max}^2$, and hoop stress scales as $\rho r^2 \omega^2$: a high tensile strength low density composite rim maximises energy stored before bursting.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that high tensile strength low density composite rim maximises energy stored before bursting.

options.label: A
options.text: High density and low tensile strength allow slower rotation while storing greater kinetic energy.
options.distractorRationale: Low tensile strength limits safe centripetal stress and caps $\omega_{\max}$.

options.label: B
options.text: High tensile strength low density composite rim maximises energy stored before bursting.

options.label: C
options.text: Low elastic modulus increases radial expansion so the rim stores energy purely as elastic strain.
options.distractorRationale: Flywheels store rotational kinetic energy, not primarily elastic strain energy.

options.label: D
options.text: High electrical conductivity generates eddy-current braking that boosts stored energy.
options.distractorRationale: Eddy currents dissipate kinetic energy as unwanted heat.

items.stem: A wooden crate of weight 900 N slides down a rough ramp at a constant speed of 5.5 m s⁻¹. The ramp is 16 m long and drops by 7.2 m vertically. Calculate the magnitude of the friction force acting up the ramp.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed, friction balances downslope weight: F_f = W(h/L) = 900 × (7.2/16) = 405 N. Rate of thermal energy generation P = F_f v = 2.23 × 10³ W. Target = 405 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_f = Wh/L and P = F_f v to obtain 405 N (B).

items.stem: A stone is thrown horizontally at $16.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ from the top of a $44.1\text{ m}$ vertical cliff above a calm lake. Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal distance from the cliff base to where the stone hits the water.
items.workedSolution: Vertically from rest, $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{2(44.1)/9.8} = 3.00 s$. Horizontally, $R = u t = 16.0 \times 3.00 = 48.0 m$.

markScheme.criterion: Computes $t = 3.00 s$ and horizontal range $R = 48.0 m$.

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 2.1 kg hangs on a light string of length 2.2 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the lowest point, it collides with and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 4.62 kg at rest. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Uses mgL = ½mu².
Obtains 6.57 m s⁻¹.
Applies T = mg + mu²/L.
Obtains 61.7 N.
Conserves momentum v = mu/(m+M) then uses h = v²/(2g).
Obtains 0.215 m.

items.stem: A solid steel sphere of radius $r = 3.00\text{ mm}$ is completely below the surface of glycerol of density $\rho = 1260\text{ kg m}^{-3}$. Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Calculate the magnitude of the buoyancy force $F_{\text{b}}$ acting on the sphere.
items.workedSolution: Displaced volume $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi (3.00 \times 10^{-3})^3 = 1.13 × 10⁻⁷ m³$. Hence $F_{\text{b}} = \rho V g = 1260 \times 1.13 × 10⁻⁷ \times 9.8 = 1.40 mN$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $F_{\text{b}} = \rho V g$ at $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to obtain $1.40 mN$.

items.stem: A variable driving torque $T$ acts on a lathe spindle as it turns through an angular displacement $\theta$. What physical quantity is represented by the area enclosed beneath the graph of torque $T$ against angular displacement $\theta$?
items.workedSolution: By rotational analogy with $W = Fs$, incremental work is $\Delta W = T\Delta\theta$, so the area under a torque against angular displacement graph equals work done.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that area under a torque against angular displacement graph equals work done.

items.stem: The figure shows a Sankey diagram for a fossil-fuel power station. Which geometric rule applies when drawing and reading a Sankey diagram?
items.workedSolution: Energy conservation requires that the width of the input trunk equals the exact sum of the widths of all output branches. Therefore the correct statement is: The width of every arrow in a Sankey diagram is directly proportional to the energy or power transferred and input width equals the sum of all output widths.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: the width of every arrow in a Sankey diagram is directly proportional to the energy or power transferred and input width equals the sum of all output widths.

items.stem: A centrifugal separator speeds smoothly from rest to $45.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ in $6.00\text{ s}$ (curved $\omega$–$t$ area $= 180\text{ rad}$) and runs at $45.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ for a further $6.00\text{ s}$ up to $t = 12.0\text{ s}$. How many complete revolutions does it complete during the $12.0\text{ s}$ interval?
items.workedSolution: Total area $\theta = 180 + (45.0 \times 6.00) = 450\text{ rad}$. Revolutions $= \frac{\theta}{2\pi} = 71.6 rev$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 71.6 rev.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a non-uniform access door of length L = 2.2 m and mass 28 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.79 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 28° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium. (b) Moments about O give T = 111.7 N ≈ 112 N. (c)(i) R_x = 52.45 N ≈ 52.4 N. (c)(ii) R_y = 176.0 N ≈ 176 N. (c)(iii) R = 183.7 N ≈ 184 N. (c)(iv) α = 73.41° ≈ 73.4° above horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Notes inward horizontal component of cable tension.
States equal opposite outward hinge reaction away from wall.
Equates cable moment T cos(angle to vertical) × L with weight moment m g x_G.
T = 111.7 N (112 N) clearly matching 1.1 × 10² N.
Combines perpendicular components via R = √(R_x² + R_y²).
Applies tan α = R_y / R_x.
α = 73.4° above the horizontal.

parts.prompt: Explain why hinge O must exert a horizontal component of force on the door, and state its direction.
parts.expectedAnswer: For translational equilibrium, the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium.
workingSteps: State that the angled cable exerts an inward horizontal pull toward the wall.
Deduce that the hinge must supply an equal outward horizontal reaction away from the wall.

workingSteps: Clockwise weight moment about O = 28 × 9.81 × 0.79 = 217.0 N m.

items.stem: A heavy block of mass 14 kg is attached to a rubber rope of natural length 3.2 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the rope becomes taut, and then stretches it by 0.6 m in 0.3 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward tension in the rope during this 0.3 s interval.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.8 × 3.2) = 7.92 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.3 + 14(9.8) = 507 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 507 N (D).

items.stem: An electric car of mass 1800 kg accelerates along a level road while a small steel sphere hangs from its ceiling at 18° to the vertical. Later, the car climbs a straight 10° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 75 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.5. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 18 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 470 N toward the marker. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the sphere deflects by 18°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 18° = ma and T cos 18° = mg => a = g tan 18° = 3.19 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.5 × 9.81 × 75) = 19.2 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1800)(18)² / 470 = 620 m. Target = 3.19 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 3.19 m s⁻² (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 1.6 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.8 m attached to a strong string. The maximum tension the string can hold without breaking is 51 N. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Writes T_max − mg = m v_max² / r at the lowest point.
Obtains 4.20 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By considering the forces acting on the ball at the lowest point, calculate the maximum speed at the bottom so the string does not break.

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 1.9 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.8 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 2.66 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string just before the bob strikes the putty.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 5.94 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 55.9 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 2.48 m s⁻¹. Target = 55.9 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 55.9 N (C).

items.stem: A skydiver accelerates downward with increasing air drag, producing the curved velocity–time graph shown. How is the skydiver's instantaneous acceleration at t = 2.0 s determined from the graph?
items.workedSolution: On any curved v–t graph, instantaneous acceleration a = Δv/Δt is found by drawing a long tangent at the chosen instant and measuring its gradient. Therefore the correct statement is: For non-uniform acceleration, instantaneous acceleration equals the gradient of the tangent drawn to the curved velocity-time graph at that instant, rather than the chord from the origin.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: instantaneous acceleration equals the gradient of the tangent drawn to the curved velocity-time graph at that instant, rather than the chord from the origin.

options.distractorRationale: v/t gives the *average* acceleration over [0, 2.0 s], which overestimates the instantaneous acceleration on a concave-down v–t curve.

options.label: B
options.text: For non-uniform acceleration, instantaneous acceleration equals the gradient of the tangent drawn to the curved velocity-time graph at that instant, rather than the chord from the origin.

options.label: C
options.text: Instantaneous acceleration equals the area shaded beneath the curve from t = 0 to t = 2.0 s.
options.distractorRationale: Area under a velocity–time graph represents displacement, not acceleration.

options.label: D
options.text: Instantaneous acceleration remains constant at 9.81 m s⁻² until the curve becomes completely horizontal at terminal velocity.
options.distractorRationale: Drag rises immediately with speed, causing acceleration to fall continuously from 9.81 m s⁻² toward zero.

items.stem: A heavy block of mass 11 kg is attached to a rubber rope of natural length 3.2 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.75 m in 0.3 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the spring constant of the rope.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 3.2 + 0.75 = 3.95 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 1.51 × 10³ N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 1.14 × 10³ N. Target = 1.51 × 10³ N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (3.2 + 0.75) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 1.51 × 10³ N m⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a construction crane has total length L = 22 m and mass 950 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 4.5 m from rear end A. A 3000 kg concrete counterweight sits 3.3 m to the left of P (1.2 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 3.5 m to the right of P (8 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 16 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum safe load mass at the hook for rotational equilibrium about P.
items.workedSolution: Anticlockwise counterweight moment about P: M_cw = 3000 × 9.81 × 3.3 = 9.712 × 10⁴ N m. Clockwise boom moment: M_boom = 950 × 9.81 × 3.5 = 3.262 × 10⁴ N m. Remaining clockwise moment available for load: W_max × 16 = 6.450 × 10⁴ N m ⇒ W_max = 4031 N ≈ 4.03 × 10³ N, m_max = W_max / 9.81 = 410.9 kg ≈ 411 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct maximum safe load mass = 411 kg.

items.stem: On a horizontal frictionless air track, glider X of mass 2.8 kg moves right at 12 m s⁻¹ and collides with stationary glider Y of mass 2.4 kg. Immediately after impact, glider Y moves right at 8.18 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of glider X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Momentum conservation: (2.8)(12) = (2.8)v_X + (2.4)(8.18), giving v_X = 4.99 m s⁻¹. K_i = 202 J and K_f = 115 J, so ΔK_lost = K_i − K_f = 86.5 J. Target = 4.99 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves linear momentum and evaluates kinetic energy budget to obtain 4.99 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: A student measures viscosity using a falling steel sphere in a tall cylinder of liquid. Why is the upper rubber timing band placed several centimetres below the liquid surface?
items.workedSolution: Immediately after release the sphere accelerates until drag grows to balance W − U; timing begins below the surface so v = d/t measures terminal speed. Therefore the correct statement is: To place the first timing marker well below the liquid surface so the sphere reaches terminal velocity before timing begins.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: place the first timing marker well below the liquid surface so the sphere reaches terminal velocity before timing begins.

options.label: A
options.text: To place the first timing marker well below the liquid surface so the sphere reaches terminal velocity before timing begins.

options.label: B
options.text: To prevent the liquid from exerting any Archimedes upthrust while the stopwatch is running.
options.distractorRationale: Upthrust acts whenever the sphere is inside the liquid and is explicitly included in the Stokes terminal-speed equation.

options.label: C
options.text: To ensure the ball bearing accelerates uniformly between the two bands so SUVAT equations apply.
options.distractorRationale: Timing must take place at constant terminal velocity, not during acceleration.

options.label: D
options.text: To increase the turbulence in the wake so that viscous drag becomes independent of radius.
options.distractorRationale: Turbulence invalidates Stokes' law, which requires slow laminar descent.

items.stem: On a horizontal frictionless air track, glider X of mass 0.8 kg moves right at 13 m s⁻¹ and strikes stationary glider Y of mass 2.2 kg. Immediately after impact, glider Y moves right at 6.38 m s⁻¹ and glider X rebounds to the left. Calculate the total kinetic energy of the two objects immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward positive, (0.8)(13) = (0.8)v_X + (2.2)(6.38) gives v_X = -4.55 m s⁻¹ (4.55 m s⁻¹ to the left). Scalar final kinetic energies add: K_f = ½(0.8)(4.55)² + ½(2.2)(6.38)² = 53.0 J. Energy lost = 67.6 J − K_f = 14.6 J. Target = 53.0 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds rebound speed 4.55 m s⁻¹ and sums scalar kinetic energies to obtain 53.0 J (C).

items.stem: A ball is launched from floor level across a flat room at 21 m s⁻¹ and 55° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height reached above the floor.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 55° = 12.0 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 55°)² / (2g) = 15.1 m. Target = 15.1 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 55° at apex to obtain 15.1 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Converts all initial kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy, forgetting non-zero horizontal speed u cos θ at the apex.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses horizontal component u cos θ instead of vertical component u sin θ in h = u_y² / (2g).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of two in the denominator of h_max = u_y² / (2g).

items.stem: A steel bob of mass 0.4 kg hangs from a light string of length 0.7 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the lowest point, it collides with and sticks to a lump of modelling clay of mass 0.8 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mgL = ½mu² => u = √(2gL).
Obtains 3.71 m s⁻¹.
Finds v = mu/(m+M) from momentum conservation and evaluates ½mu² − ½(m+M)v².
Obtains 1.83 J.
Applies h = v² / (2g).
Obtains 0.0778 m.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a non-uniform aluminium beam AB has total length L = 4.6 m and mass 12 kg. Its centre of gravity G lies 2.48 m from end A. It rests horizontally on a sharp pivot P at 1.75 m from end A. A counterbalance block of unknown mass sits 0.7 m from end A. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the upward reaction force R exerted by pivot P on the balanced beam.
items.workedSolution: Take moments about pivot P. Lever arm of beam CG is d_G = 2.48 − 1.75 = 0.7300 m. Lever arm of counterbalance is d_load = 1.75 − 0.7 = 1.050 m. Balancing moments: m_load g d_load = m_beam g d_G ⇒ m_load = (12 × 0.7300) / 1.050 = 8.343 kg ≈ 8.34 kg. Vertical equilibrium gives R = (m_beam + m_load)g = (12 + 8.343) × 9.81 = 199.6 N ≈ 200 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct upward pivot reaction R = 200 N.

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 13 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 3.4 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the cord becomes taut, and then stretches it by 1 m in 0.24 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward tension in the cord during this 0.24 s interval.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.81 × 3.4) = 8.17 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.24 + 13(9.81) = 570 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 570 N (D).

items.stem: Puck A (mass 0.400 kg) travels along the $+x$ direction at 6.00 m s⁻¹ and strikes stationary puck B (mass 0.600 kg) on a frictionless table. After impact, puck A moves at 3.00 m s⁻¹ at 30.0° above the $+x$ axis. Calculate the magnitude of puck B's momentum $p_2$ after the collision.
items.workedSolution: p₀ = 2.40 kg m s⁻¹; p₁ₓ = 1.20 cos 30° = 1.039 kg m s⁻¹, p₁ᵧ = 1.20 sin 30° = 0.600 kg m s⁻¹. Hence p₂ₓ = 1.361 kg m s⁻¹, p₂ᵧ = −0.600 kg m s⁻¹, and p₂ = √(1.361² + 0.600²) = 1.49 kg m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves p₂ₓ and p₂ᵧ and combines via Pythagoras to obtain p₂ = 1.49 kg m s⁻¹.

items.stem: On a smooth horizontal track, trolley X of mass 2.5 kg moves to the right at 13 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with trolley Y of mass 3.6 kg moving to the left at 2 m s⁻¹ (arrow not shown). Immediately after the collision, trolley Y moves right at 2.5 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of trolley X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward as positive: p_before = (2.5)(13) + (3.6)(−2) = 25.3 kg m s⁻¹. From p_before = (2.5)v_X + (3.6)(2.5), v_X = 6.52 m s⁻¹, which is 6.52 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Uses signed head-on momentum p_before = 25.3 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 6.52 m s⁻¹ to the right (A).

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform scaffold plank of total length L = 4.6 m and mass 36 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is 0.8 m from the left end, and support B is 2.4 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 1.4 m. A technician of mass 60 kg initially stands 2.5 m from the left end of the plank. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². The technician steps off and a toolbox is placed at the outer overhanging tip. Calculate the maximum toolbox mass the plank can support without tipping.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: F₁ × 2.4 = (36 × 0.9000 + 60 × 0.7000) × 9.81 ⇒ F₁ = 304.1 N ≈ 304 N. At tipping (F₁ = 0): m_load × d_tip = m_beam × (x_B − x_G) ⇒ d_tip = (36 × 0.9000) / 60 = 0.5400 m ≈ 0.540 m. At the very tip (overhang 1.4 m): m_end = (36 × 0.9000) / 1.4 = 23.14 kg ≈ 23.1 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct solver-verified answer = 23.1 kg.

items.stem: A steel ball is fired from a spring launcher on level ground at 26 m s⁻¹ and 38° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the ground.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 26 sin 38° = 16.0 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 26 cos 38° = 20.5 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 3.27 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 66.9 m. Target = 66.9 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 66.9 m (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies horizontal speed by ascent time u sin θ / g instead of full flight time 2u sin θ / g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cos θ for sin θ in the flight-time expression.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: An electric car of mass 1800 kg accelerates along a level road while a small steel sphere hangs from its ceiling at 34° to the vertical. Later, the car climbs a straight 10° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 55 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.6. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 22 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 620 N toward the marker. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the sphere deflects by 34°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 34° = ma and T cos 34° = mg => a = g tan 34° = 6.61 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.6 × 9.8 × 55) = 18.0 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1800)(22)² / 620 = 703 m. Target = 6.61 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 6.61 m s⁻² (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: At point R on the skydiver's velocity–time graph, the parachute has just opened fully while the skydiver is still moving downwards rapidly. Which statement correctly describes the forces and motion at point R?
items.workedSolution: Opening the canopy multiplies drag above weight, giving an upward resultant force and downward deceleration. Therefore option B is correct: drag greatly exceeds weight producing an upward resultant force and downward deceleration.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: drag greatly exceeds weight producing an upward resultant force and downward deceleration.

options.distractorRationale: Classic misconception! An upward resultant force decelerates downward motion; speed stays downwards (positive) and decreases.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Immediately after canopy deployment, drag equals weight instantaneously so speed drops vertically to zero
options.distractorRationale: Drag rises sharply above weight so speed decreases smoothly over time until reaching the lower terminal speed.

options.label: D

options.distractorRationale: Weight mg stays constant throughout the descent.

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 3 kg slides from rest down a rough wooden ramp of length 6.5 m inclined at 42° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 6 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the magnitude of the constant friction force opposing its motion.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 42° − ½mv² = 74.0 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 6.5 = 11.4 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 4.24 m s⁻¹. Target = 11.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 11.4 N (C).

items.stem: A uniform solid cylinder accelerates down an inclined plane while rolling without slipping. Which statement accurately describes the frictional force acting on the cylinder?
items.workedSolution: At the contact point there is no relative slipping, so static friction points up the ramp, provides torque τ = F_f r about the centre of mass, and does zero dissipative work. Therefore the correct statement is: During pure rolling down the ramp, static friction acts up the incline to supply the torque required for angular acceleration while doing zero net work because the contact point is instantaneously at rest.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: static friction acts up the incline to supply the torque required for angular acceleration while doing zero net work because the contact point is instantaneously at rest.

options.label: A
options.text: During pure rolling down the ramp, dynamic friction acts down the incline and dissipates half of the cylinder's gravitational potential energy as heat.
options.distractorRationale: Pure rolling involves static (not dynamic) friction acting up the incline with zero mechanical dissipation.

options.label: B
options.text: During pure rolling down the ramp, static friction is zero because the cylinder rolls freely without any sliding motion.
options.distractorRationale: Without static friction there would be zero torque about the centre of mass and the cylinder would slide without rotating.

options.label: C
options.text: During pure rolling down the ramp, static friction acts up the incline to supply the torque required for angular acceleration while doing zero net work because the contact point is instantaneously at rest.

options.label: D
options.text: During pure rolling down the ramp, static friction acts downward along the slope to increase the linear acceleration above g sin θ.
options.distractorRationale: Friction opposes the tendency of the bottom point to slide down the ramp, so it acts up the slope and reduces linear acceleration below g sin θ.

items.stem: A steel ball is fired from a spring launcher on level ground at 27 m s⁻¹ and 66° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height reached above the ground.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 66° = 11.0 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 66°)² / (2g) = 31.0 m. Target = 31.0 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 66° at apex to obtain 31.0 m (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Converts all initial kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy, forgetting non-zero horizontal speed u cos θ at the apex.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses horizontal component u cos θ instead of vertical component u sin θ in h = u_y² / (2g).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of two in the denominator of h_max = u_y² / (2g).

items.stem: A tennis ball is fired from a launcher on a level pitch at 34 m s⁻¹ and 34° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the total time of flight before returning to the pitch.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 34 sin 34° = 19.0 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 34 cos 34° = 28.2 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.81 = 3.88 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 109 m. Target = 3.88 s.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 3.88 s (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes time to reach the apex u sin θ / g rather than full time of flight.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Swaps sin θ and cos θ when resolving vertical launch speed.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses total speed u instead of vertical component u sin θ.

items.stem: A wooden block of mass 8 kg is attached to a bungee cord of natural length 1.8 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 0.45 m in 0.32 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the spring constant of the cord.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 1.8 + 0.45 = 2.25 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 1.74 × 10³ N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 785 N. Target = 1.74 × 10³ N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (1.8 + 0.45) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 1.74 × 10³ N m⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a non-uniform rod of length L = 3.8 m and mass 16 kg hangs in equilibrium from two light vertical wires at A and B. The wires are 2.9 m apart. items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: T₁_y × 2.9 = 16 × 9.81 × 1.04 ⇒ T₁_y = 56.29 N, T₂_y = 100.7 N. For vertical wires, T₁ = 56.29 N ≈ 56.3 N and T₂ = 100.7 N ≈ 101 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct wire tension = 101 N.

items.stem: A brass bob of mass 1.2 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 1.6 m on a light nylon cord. The cord breaks if the tension exceeds 38 N. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum safe speed of the bob at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((38/1.2) − 9.81) × 1.6] = 5.91 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 5.91 m s⁻¹ (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds g instead of subtracting g when rearranging T_max − mg = mv²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a steel turning bar has length d = 0.8 m. Two equal and opposite parallel forces of magnitude F = 82 N act perpendicularly at its ends. Which statement accurately defines a couple in mechanics?
items.workedSolution: A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide.

markScheme.criterion: A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide.

items.stem: A concrete block of weight 840 N slides at a constant speed down a rough incline. The slope has length 11 m and vertical height 5.7 m. Calculate the magnitude of the resistive force opposing motion along the slope.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed ΔE_k = 0. Potential energy lost = W h = 840 × 5.7 = 4.79 × 10³ J. Parallel equilibrium gives F_res = W sin θ = W h / L = 435 N. Target = 435 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses sin θ = 5.7/11 and zero net force to obtain 435 N (C).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 2.6 m and mass 11 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 7 kg hangs so its centre of gravity acts 2.4 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at 36° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the tension T in the angled support wire.
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about hinge O: T sin 36° × 2.6 = (11 × 1.3 + 7 × 2.4) × 9.81 = 305.1 N m. Hence T sin 36° = 117.3 N and T = 199.6 N ≈ 200 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos 36° = 161.5 N ≈ 162 N. Vertical balance: R_y = (11 + 7) × 9.81 − 117.3 = 59.24 N ≈ 59.2 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 200 N.

items.stem: A stone block of mass 10 kg is released from rest at the top of a rough wooden slope. The slope is 4 m long and inclined at 32° to the horizontal. It reaches the bottom with a speed of 3.55 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = mgL sin θ.
Obtains 208 J.
Subtracts ½mv² from ΔE_p.
Obtains 145 J.
Applies W_f = μ(mg cos θ)L.
Obtains 0.436.

items.stem: A rubber ball of mass 0.7 kg moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.5 m on a strong string. At the lowest point, its speed is 8.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 0.7 × 8.5² / 0.5 = 101 N, so T = 101 + 0.7 × 9.81 = 108 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 108 N (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: Which SI unit name corresponds directly to angular impulse $T\Delta t$ and angular momentum $I\omega$?
items.workedSolution: Torque has unit $\text{N m}$ and time has unit $\text{s}$, so angular impulse $T\Delta t$ has SI unit $\text{N m s}$, the newton metre second.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that newton metre second.

items.stem: A high-speed flywheel energy-storage unit spins at several thousand radians per second inside a sealed casing. Which design pairing best reduces energy losses while increasing safe energy storage?
items.workedSolution: To store energy efficiently at ultra-high $\omega$, an evacuated casing and magnetic bearings minimise windage and friction losses while high-strength rim permits greater angular speed.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that evacuated casing and magnetic bearings minimise windage and friction losses while high-strength rim permits greater angular speed.

options.label: A
options.text: Pressurised air cooling and greased steel ball bearings with a heavy lead hub.
options.distractorRationale: Pressurised air causes severe windage drag and lead has low tensile strength.

options.label: B
options.text: Open-air spoked housing with oil-bath bearings and soft aluminium spokes.
options.distractorRationale: Open-air spokes cause huge aerodynamic drag and oil churning losses.

options.label: C
options.text: Water-filled containment jacket with solid brass cylinder rotating at low speed.
options.distractorRationale: Fluid drag in water would immediately dissipate rotational energy.

options.label: D
options.text: Evacuated casing and magnetic bearings minimise windage and friction losses while high-strength rim permits greater angular speed.

items.stem: A heavy box of weight 850 N slides down a straight ramp at a constant speed of 6 m s⁻¹. The ramp is 22 m long and drops by 13.2 m vertically. Calculate the magnitude of the friction force acting up the ramp.
items.workedSolution: At constant speed, friction balances downslope weight: F_f = W(h/L) = 850 × (13.2/22) = 510 N. Rate of thermal energy generation P = F_f v = 3.06 × 10³ W. Target = 510 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_f = Wh/L and P = F_f v to obtain 510 N (B).

items.stem: A probe is launched from a cliff edge $35.0\text{ m}$ above level ground at $20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ directed $30.0^\circ$ below the horizontal. Using $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and neglecting air resistance, what is the probe's time of flight to reach the ground?
items.workedSolution: Initial downward speed $u_y = 20.0 \sin 30.0^\circ = 10.0 m s⁻¹$. Solving $35.0 = 10.0 t + 4.9 t^2$ gives positive root $t = 1.84 s$.

markScheme.criterion: Solves vertical quadratic with $u_y = 10.0 m s⁻¹$ and $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to obtain $t = 1.84 s$.

items.stem: A firefighter's hose delivers a horizontal stream of water at mass flow rate $6.50\text{ kg s}^{-1}$ and speed $18.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ perpendicularly against a flat vertical wall. The water runs vertically down the wall with zero horizontal rebound. What horizontal force does the jet exert on the wall?
items.workedSolution: By Newton's second law for changing mass, $F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = v \frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t} = 18.0 \times 6.50 = 117 N$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $F = \Delta p / \Delta t = v (\Delta m / \Delta t) = 117 N$.

items.stem: A test disc of hub inertia 2.10 kg m² carrying 4 masses of 2.00 kg at radius 0.45 m slows uniformly from 12.0 rev s⁻¹ to 4.0 rev s⁻¹ in 6.0 s. Bearing friction contributes a constant retarding torque of 3.50 N m, and a brake pad presses tangentially at radius 0.25 m. What tangential friction force does the brake pad exert?
items.workedSolution: $I = 2.10 + 4(2.00)(0.45)^2 = 3.72\text{ kg m}^2$. Deceleration $|\alpha| = \frac{2\pi(12.0 - 4.0)}{6.0} = 8.38\text{ rad s}^{-2}$. Net retarding torque $|T_{\mathrm{net}}| = I|\alpha| = 31.2\text{ N m}$. Brake torque $T_{\mathrm{brake}} = 31.2 - 3.50 = 27.7\text{ N m}$, so $F = \frac{T_{\mathrm{brake}}}{r} = \frac{27.7}{0.25} = 111 N$.

markScheme.criterion: Brake pad tangential force equals 111 N.

items.stem: A student drags a heavy suitcase horizontally across a level floor by pulling on a strap inclined at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. How do the components of the pulling force contribute to mechanical work?
items.workedSolution: From W = Fs cos θ, F cos θ along displacement transfers energy while F sin θ perpendicular to horizontal displacement does zero work. Therefore the correct statement is: Only the force component parallel to displacement does mechanical work whereas the perpendicular force component does zero work.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: only the force component parallel to displacement does mechanical work whereas the perpendicular force component does zero work.

items.stem: In the analogy between translational and rotational dynamics required by AQA Engineering Physics, which correspondence is completely correct?
items.workedSolution: Every linear law maps directly onto its rotational counterpart: torque parallels force moment of inertia parallels mass and I omega parallels linear momentum ($T = I\alpha$, $W = T\theta$, $P = T\omega$, $E_{\text{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$).

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that torque parallels force moment of inertia parallels mass and I omega parallels linear momentum.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a non-uniform metal hatch of length L = 1.6 m and mass 16 kg is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. It is held horizontally in equilibrium, and its centre of gravity G lies 0.64 m from hinge O. A steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at 44° to the vertical. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium. items.stem: A heavy block of mass 2 kg is attached to a rubber rope of natural length 2 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the rope becomes taut, and then stretches it by 0.8 m in 0.18 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward force exerted by the rope between A and B.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.8 × 2) = 6.26 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.18 + 2(9.8) = 89.2 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 89.2 N (C).

items.stem: A delivery van of mass 1700 kg accelerates along a level road while a small pendulum bob hangs from its ceiling at 34° to the vertical. Later, the van climbs a straight 10° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 95 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.55. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 14 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 440 N toward the checkpoint. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 34°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 34° = ma and T cos 34° = mg => a = g tan 34° = 6.62 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.55 × 9.81 × 95) = 22.6 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1700)(14)² / 440 = 379 m. Target = 6.62 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 6.62 m s⁻² (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: A brass ball of mass 2.3 kg hangs on a light string of length 1.4 m and is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the bottom, it collides with and sticks to a wax block of mass 3.22 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the tension in the string just before the ball strikes the block.
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 5.24 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 67.7 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 2.18 m s⁻¹. Target = 67.7 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 67.7 N (B).

items.stem: The diagram compares the path of a projectile launched from a cliff in a vacuum (solid blue) with its path in air (dashed red). How does air resistance change the projectile's path?
items.workedSolution: Because drag opposes velocity throughout flight, both peak height and range fall, and horizontal slowdown steepens the descent. Therefore the correct statement is: Comparing the two curves, air resistance opposes motion continuously, reducing both maximum height and horizontal range while producing an asymmetric path with a steeper downward descent.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: air resistance opposes motion continuously, reducing both maximum height and horizontal range while producing an asymmetric path with a steeper downward descent.

items.stem: A metal cylinder of mass 5.5 kg is attached to an elastic rope of natural length 2.4 m. It is released from rest at the upper support, becomes taut at point A, and stretches by 1.35 m in 0.16 s to stop at lowest point B. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum tension in the rope at the lowest point B.
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 2.4 + 1.35 = 3.75 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 222 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 299 N. Target = 299 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (2.4 + 1.35) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 299 N (C).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a dockside crane has total length L = 18 m and mass 400 kg. It rests on a vertical pivot P located 7 m from rear end A. A 3200 kg concrete counterweight sits 5.6 m to the left of P (1.4 m from A). The boom's centre of gravity G lies 4.5 m to the right of P (11.5 m from A). The hoist hook hangs 9 m to the right of P. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum safe load weight at the hook without tipping clockwise about P.
items.workedSolution: Anticlockwise counterweight moment about P: M_cw = 3200 × 9.81 × 5.6 = 1.758 × 10⁵ N m. Clockwise boom moment: M_boom = 400 × 9.81 × 4.5 = 1.766 × 10⁴ N m. Remaining clockwise moment available for load: W_max × 9 = 1.581 × 10⁵ N m ⇒ W_max = 1.757 × 10⁴ N ≈ 1.76 × 10⁴ N, m_max = W_max / 9.81 = 1791 kg ≈ 1.79 × 10³ kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct maximum safe load weight = 1.76 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: On a frictionless horizontal surface, block X of mass 5.2 kg moves right at 5 m s⁻¹ and collides with stationary block Y of mass 1.2 kg. Immediately after impact, block Y moves right at 6.07 m s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of block X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Momentum conservation: (5.2)(5) = (5.2)v_X + (1.2)(6.07), giving v_X = 3.60 m s⁻¹. K_i = 65.0 J and K_f = 55.8 J, so ΔK_lost = K_i − K_f = 9.21 J. Target = 3.60 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves linear momentum and evaluates kinetic energy budget to obtain 3.60 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: A column of syrup used in a falling-ball viscosity practical is warmed from 18 °C to 35 °C while using the same steel ball bearing. What happens to the liquid's viscosity and the sphere's terminal speed?
items.workedSolution: In liquids, higher thermal kinetic energy helps molecules overcome cohesive forces, reducing η and raising v_t = 2r²(ρ_s − ρ_f)g/(9η). Therefore the correct statement is: Increasing liquid temperature weakens intermolecular cohesion so liquid viscosity decreases and terminal speed increases.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: increasing liquid temperature weakens intermolecular cohesion so liquid viscosity decreases and terminal speed increases.

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing liquid temperature strengthens intermolecular bonds so liquid viscosity increases and terminal speed decreases.
options.distractorRationale: Applies the gas-viscosity trend to a liquid; warming a liquid reduces its viscosity.

options.label: B
options.text: Liquid viscosity stays constant with temperature so the sphere reaches the exact same terminal speed.
options.distractorRationale: Liquid viscosity is strongly temperature-sensitive and must be controlled during viscometry.

options.label: C
options.text: Liquid viscosity decreases so upthrust vanishes and the sphere accelerates at 9.81 m s⁻².
options.distractorRationale: Upthrust depends on fluid density rather than viscosity and does not drop to zero when warmed.

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing liquid temperature weakens intermolecular cohesion so liquid viscosity decreases and terminal speed increases.

items.stem: On a horizontal frictionless air track, glider X of mass 1 kg moves right at 7 m s⁻¹ and strikes stationary glider Y of mass 3.2 kg. Immediately after impact, glider Y moves right at 2.82 m s⁻¹ and glider X rebounds to the left. Calculate the kinetic energy lost in this rebound collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward positive, (1)(7) = (1)v_X + (3.2)(2.82) gives v_X = -2.02 m s⁻¹ (2.02 m s⁻¹ to the left). Scalar final kinetic energies add: K_f = ½(1)(2.02)² + ½(3.2)(2.82)² = 14.8 J. Energy lost = 24.5 J − K_f = 9.73 J. Target = 9.73 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds rebound speed 2.02 m s⁻¹ and sums scalar kinetic energies to obtain 9.73 J (B).

items.stem: A golf ball is hit from flat ground at 42 m s⁻¹ and 33° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the maximum vertical height reached above the ground.
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 33° = 35.2 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 33°)² / (2g) = 26.7 m. Target = 26.7 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 33° at apex to obtain 26.7 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Converts all initial kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy, forgetting non-zero horizontal speed u cos θ at the apex.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses horizontal component u cos θ instead of vertical component u sin θ in h = u_y² / (2g).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of two in the denominator of h_max = u_y² / (2g).

items.stem: A metal bob of mass 2.4 kg hangs from a light string of length 1.3 m. It is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the lowest point, it collides with and sticks to a lump of putty of mass 1.92 kg at rest. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mgL = ½mu² => u = √(2gL).
Obtains 5.05 m s⁻¹.
Finds v = mu/(m+M) from momentum conservation and evaluates ½mu² − ½(m+M)v².
Obtains 13.6 J.
Applies h = v² / (2g).
Obtains 0.401 m.

items.stem: In a statics experiment, a wooden plank AB has length L = 2.8 m and mass 10 kg. Its centre of gravity G lies 1.4 m from end A. It is balanced horizontally on a pivot P at 0.84 m from end A by placing a 12 kg block to the left of P. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate how far from end B the 12 kg block must be placed for horizontal equilibrium.
items.workedSolution: Distance of CG from pivot P: d_G = 1.4 − 0.84 = 0.5600 m. Taking moments about P: 12 × d = 10 × 0.5600 ⇒ d = 0.4667 m left of P. Position from end A is x_A = 0.84 − 0.4667 = 0.3733 m. Therefore distance from end B is L − x_A = 2.8 − 0.3733 = 2.427 m ≈ 2.43 m.

markScheme.criterion: Correct distance from end B = 2.43 m.

items.stem: A sandbag of mass 14 kg is attached to an elastic cord of natural length 2.8 m. It falls from rest at the support to point A, where the cord becomes taut, and then stretches it by 1.4 m in 0.12 s to stop at point B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the average upward force exerted by the cord between A and B.
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.81 × 2.8) = 7.41 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.12 + 14(9.81) = 1.00 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 1.00 × 10³ N (C).

items.stem: Ball A (0.300 kg) moves along $+x$ at 10.0 m s⁻¹ and makes a glancing collision with stationary ball B (0.500 kg). After impact, ball A moves at 5.00 m s⁻¹ at 40.0° above $+x$. Using momentum conservation and $E_k = p^2/(2m)$, calculate the total kinetic energy lost in the collision.
items.workedSolution: E_k0 = 15.0 J. From vector momentum conservation p₂ = 2.09 kg m s⁻¹, so E_k,after = 3.75 J + 4.36 J = 8.11 J. Loss = 15.0 − 8.11 = 6.89 J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes kinetic energy loss ΔE_k = 6.89 J.

items.stem: On a smooth level track, cart X of mass 2.5 kg moves to the right at 5 m s⁻¹. It collides head-on with cart Y of mass 2.4 kg moving to the left at 6 m s⁻¹ (arrow not shown). Immediately after the collision, cart Y moves right at 4 m s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of cart X immediately after the collision.
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward as positive: p_before = (2.5)(5) + (2.4)(−6) = -1.90 kg m s⁻¹. From p_before = (2.5)v_X + (2.4)(4), v_X = -4.60 m s⁻¹, which is 4.60 m s⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: Uses signed head-on momentum p_before = -1.90 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 4.60 m s⁻¹ to the left (A).

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a uniform timber board of total length L = 5.2 m and mass 60 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is 0.8 m from the left end, and support B is 2.6 m to the right of A, leaving an overhang of 1.8 m. A technician of mass 84 kg initially stands 2.3 m from the left end of the plank. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². How do the two upward support reaction forces change as the technician walks from support A toward the overhanging end?
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B shows that reducing the technician's anticlockwise lever arm lowers F₁; because F₁ + F₂ equals total weight, the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.

items.stem: A ball is launched from floor level across a flat room at 26 m s⁻¹ and 38° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. Calculate the horizontal range before landing on the floor.
items.workedSolution: u_y = 26 sin 38° = 16.0 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 26 cos 38° = 20.5 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 3.27 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 66.9 m. Target = 66.9 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves horizontal and vertical components accurately to obtain 66.9 m (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies horizontal speed by ascent time u sin θ / g instead of full flight time 2u sin θ / g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cos θ for sin θ in the flight-time expression.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses the 45° maximum-range formula u²/g without the angle factor sin(2θ).

items.stem: A small lorry of mass 1700 kg accelerates along a level road while a small plumb bob hangs from its ceiling at 18° to the vertical. Later, the lorry climbs a straight 10° slope at constant speed. It then moves around a flat semicircular bend of radius 70 m where the coefficient of static friction is 0.45. Finally, its engine is switched off and it slows down along the bend from 19 m s⁻¹ against a constant resistive force of 560 N toward the stop sign. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the horizontal acceleration during the straight-line phase when the bob deflects by 18°.
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 18° = ma and T cos 18° = mg => a = g tan 18° = 3.18 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.45 × 9.8 × 70) = 17.6 m s⁻¹. Stopping distance with engine off: s = ½(1700)(19)² / 560 = 548 m. Target = 3.18 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 3.18 m s⁻² (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses g sin θ as if on an inclined plane rather than resolving T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg to obtain g tan θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio of horizontal to vertical components, evaluating g / tan θ instead of g tan θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies g by cos θ instead of tan θ.

items.stem: A $1250\text{ kg}$ test vehicle travelling at $16.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is brought uniformly to rest in $0.400\text{ s}$ by its front crumple zone. Calculate the average stopping force exerted on the vehicle.
items.workedSolution: $\Delta p = 1250 \times 16.0 = 2.00 \times 10^4\text{ N s}$; average force $F = \Delta p / \Delta t = 2.00 \times 10^4 / 0.400 = 5.00 × 10⁴ N$. Option C (5.00 × 10⁴ N) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Average stopping force $= 5.00 × 10⁴ N$ (5.00 × 10⁴ N, option C).

options.distractorRationale: Divides kinetic energy by time (average power in watts) instead of dividing momentum by time.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Quotes the impulse (N s) without dividing by the 0.400 s collision time.

items.stem: A heavy crate of mass 11.5 kg slides from rest down a rough wooden slope of length 5.5 m inclined at 34° to the horizontal. Against a constant friction force, it reaches the bottom at 5.05 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. If the crate is instead released from rest halfway down the slope, calculate its speed at the bottom.
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 34° − ½mv² = 200 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 5.5 = 36.4 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.57 m s⁻¹. Target = 3.57 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 3.57 m s⁻¹ (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes final speed scales linearly with distance (v/2) instead of with √s (v/√2) under constant acceleration.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides speed by four instead of √2 when halving the release distance.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes frictionless half-ramp speed and ignores the constant friction force.
